en: Regarding the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra-śāstra*:

I have heard that the wisdom of the Buddha is profoundly deep; even the most eminent sages cannot fathom its limits. The sacred words are supremely wondrous; how could those of common station perceive their source?
When Śāriputra proclaimed "non-explanation," flowers rained down as he cast his thread of doubt in secret darkness; when Asaṅga ascended to Tuṣita...
Although the oral instructions have been divided into sections, they still appear contradictory; thus we know that Prajñā is boundless and that only the Vajra [Sūtra] is supreme.

To investigate it thoroughly is no easy task, and its faithful acceptance is truly rare. Fortunately, the verses were expanded by the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya), providing a complete set of guiding rules;

the Great Being (Nāgārjuna) joyfully extolled them in verse, where the "knocking" and the "singing" harmonize like a matching tally. Xiqian Gongdeshi clearly illuminated the principles of emptiness and the conventional, while Changshui edited [the commentary].
This is the definitive exposition. I shall briefly set forth the principles of their synthesis. Together with Vasubandhu as our wings, we shall resolve the twenty-seven doubts once and for all.
The essential aim is to unfold the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and to shatter all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) as being entirely non-existent.

Yet, while the principle of "shattering marks" becomes increasingly subtle, the contemplation of "illusory-like" reality becomes progressively more refined. Having already entered and abided in the stages (*bhūmi*), one still speaks of "correspondence to non-abiding."
As soon as the thought of saving sentient beings arises, it is held that universally bringing them to the state of no-more-saving is the ultimate ideal.

One rescues those who are biased within the realm of emptiness and resolves the critical pivot in the region of profound mystery. This is because attachment lies hidden within the co-emergent; thus, the Vajra [Wisdom] serves as the medicinal remedy for its direct realization.

When one’s rank ascends to that of Equal Enlightenment, this Vehicle possesses the power to reach the further shore—a state known only by the Buddhas and unfathomable by ordinary beings. To accord with this...
The profound meaning returns to those of the highest capacity. In the past at Huangmei, it was said that this sutra alone enables one to see one's nature;
at that time, the Sixth Patriarch truly understood its essence upon hearing these words. Once the five petals had blossomed, every person held the seal of the Tathāgata.

As the single lamp continued its succession, it was specifically termed the "transmission outside the teachings. Awakening does not depend on a teacher, and their words frequently accord with the Way.

The sharp edge of the spiritual pivot is revealed far and wide, like the shimmering light of a precious sword; its illumination and function manifest together, like the brilliant radiance of a mani jewel.
Truly, in these final five hundred years, one should not say there are no such people. If one upholds even a single four-line verse of the sutra, one will ultimately find entry.

In my study of the *Fengyi*, I am ashamed of my lack of specialized mastery; in my understanding, I regret my failure to seek through universal inquiry. The flavor of the Way delights my heart, as if it were a fulfillment of long-standing affinities;
to find joy in the Zen gate for the rest of my years may perhaps not obscure my past causes. At this time of strife and contention, I have ventured forth a view of harmony and accord:
that the school (*zong*) is identical to the teaching (*jiao*), and that the blazing, uninterrupted discourse belongs entirely to verbal expression; and that the teaching is identical to the school.

Whether it be the Tathāgata-dhyāna or the Patriarchal-dhyāna, one must in all cases sit in meditation and dissolve [all phenomena] back into oneself. Is picking up a flower any different from picking up a phrase?
Once that other shore is thoroughly realized, what difference is there between what is seen and what is heard?

This is how the penetration of the essence (zongtong) opens the key to the scriptures, while the penetration of the teaching (shetong) likewise serves as the gateway to awakening. When all obstructions are completely integrated, True Suchness (Tathatā) is suddenly revealed. As for...
Kumārajīva translated [the texts]. Through his work, the faculty of the tongue was shown to be the locus of faith, and the unseen Lord manifested his spiritual efficacy.

By imperial decree, the omissions were supplemented upon stone carvings. Thus, for sentient beings, a portion of their wisdom-life was incidentally increased. Even regarding those who perceive through form or seek through sound, there still remained four lines of verse;

as for that which is like dew or lightning, three kinds of conditions were particularly lacking. Since the verses and treatises already provide clear evidence, how could the scriptural text be otherwise?
This may be abridged; I have ventured to record the Tang dynasty translation for the purpose of providing a comprehensive view. A re-explanation of the verses is appended at the end of this section.
Recently, due to the sudden passing of my late father, I recited this scripture daily while attending to his grave.

Consequently, I compiled this collection, hoping for a slight touch of the profound dew and praying that it might provide a small measure of moisture to these withered remains. Relying upon the Vajra to conceal my form, I venture to aspire toward purity.
This cool cave happens to share a name with a mountain, providing a modest means for the perfuming of Prajñā. Here, the Dharma and the earth are both spiritually potent;
the profound and the luminous are forever relied upon. I respectfully entrust this to the carver’s tool to be widely circulated.
Should one thereby attain realization of the unborn, may all equally receive boundless gratitude.

Preface to the First Fascicle of the *Zongtong* (Compendium of the Essential Meaning) of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, composed by Jinjian Ceng Fengyi (style name Shunzheng), a native of Mount Nanyue,
and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva (translated here as Tongshou) of the Yao Qin dynasty.
The Treatise on Breaking Attachment to Grasping While Not Destroying Provisional Designations by Bodhisattva Guṇadatta of the Western Heaven;
with Verses by the Great Master Fu of the Liang Dynasty;
and the *Vajra-kāṇḍa-viniścaya-ṭīkā* by Dharma Master Zixuan of Changshui in Jiahe during the Song Dynasty.
The Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Nan-yue Shan Jien Zeng Fengyi, whose dharma name is Zongtong, said:
"The title of this sutra is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. It is the foremost *pāramitā*.
The Tathāgata preached it for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle; it is not for those of ordinary wisdom."
This is indeed appropriate. Furthermore, Subhūti praises the Tathāgata for skillfully protecting and mindful of all bodhisattvas, and for skillfully entrusting all bodhisattvas.
It is only within the stage of a bodhisattva that one can resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
therefore, the Tathāgata protects and mindfully cares for them so that they may abide permanently [in this resolve], and entrusts them so that they may deliver sentient beings. Subhūti...
Having attained sublime wisdom and subdued the mind, one is then able to realize the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata; therefore, the Buddha addressed him with the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

Having already realized the three types of emptiness during the stages of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) and application (*prayoga-mārga*), and having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one reaches the stage of penetration (*prativedha-mārga*).
At this point, the Bodhisattva of the first bhūmi attains partial realization of *tathatā* (suchness), yet there remains...
Regarding innate self-grasping, it is abandoned upon reaching the eighth bhūmi; however, innate grasping at phenomena still remains.

These two types of grasping each have a subtle ignorance regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) and an extremely subtle ignorance regarding the objects of knowledge, which are only severed upon reaching the stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
That which severs [these obstacles] is none other than the profoundly deep Vajra-like Illusory Samādhi, which serves as the antidote.
What is attained on the first bhūmi is destroyed on the second; what is attained on the second is destroyed on the third.

Progressing thus through each successive stage, one reaches the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), at which point there is nothing further to be destroyed—namely, the maturation (*vipāka*) that follows the Vajra Path.

"Emptiness" refers precisely to this meaning. Furthermore, regarding the ten kinds of profound metaphors of the *Vajra*, such as "like an illusion, like a dream," and the verses at the end of the sutra comparing things to dew and lightning:

since even the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are viewed through the lens of illusion and dreams, how could one not employ such a contemplation unless one possesses extremely profound wisdom? This is the function of Subhūti.
He shed tears and marveled at what he had never heard before. The *Kanding ji* (Record of Critical Determination) states:
"Vajra" refers to the precious mace of Śakra, possessing the two meanings of being extremely hard and extremely sharp. What is meant by 'extremely hard'? That no object can destroy it.
What is meant by 'extremely sharp'? That it is capable of shattering all other objects. If there were even a single object capable of destroying it, it would not be 'extreme' [in its hardness].

"Solid": if a single object does not break, it is not yet extremely sharp. For example, though silver and iron are solid, they melt when meeting fire; though swords and blades are sharp, they chip when striking stone.

These are not examples of being both extremely solid and sharp. Prajñā has two aspects: the *bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā* (wisdom of true reality) and the *vipaśyanā-prajñā* (wisdom of contemplative observation).
It likewise possesses the meaning of being both solid and sharp. "Solid" refers to the *bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*, because even after passing through many... [text continues]
Though one wanders through the six realms throughout the flow of kalpas, the nature of awakening remains unimpaired; it has never arisen nor ceased, and it has never been diminished or deficient.
Therefore, it is called "solid" (*kaṭhina*). "Sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*) refers to the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*);

this means that when this wisdom manifests, it illuminates the emptiness of all phenomena, such that afflictions, fetters, ignorance, and the darkness of delusion are all severed and destroyed. Therefore, it is called "sharp. Based on these two meanings—
Because it resembles that vajra, the hardness of the vajra is cited as a metaphor for the essence of prajñā, and the sharpness of the vajra is used as a metaphor for the function of prajñā.
Since both the dharma and the metaphor are manifested together, it is called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. In the Sanskrit language, it is called *pāramitā*.

This is called "reaching the other shore. It means leaving behind this shore of birth and death for sentient beings, crossing the middle current of the great river of afflictions, and reaching the other shore of the nirvana of all Buddhas.
However, upon realizing that birth and death are fundamentally empty and that afflictions are fundamentally non-existent, one has already reached the other shore;
it is not that there is truly a distinction between this and that shore. There is simply a difference between sudden and gradual in reaching the other shore.
In the case of the sudden approach (*tun*), as soon as wisdom arises, one perceives the emptiness of the five aggregates; in a single kṣaṇa, one reaches the other shore.

Because it does not require the passage of much time, it is called "sudden. In the case of the gradual approach (*jian*), although one is able to suddenly illuminate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), due to the habitual tendencies accumulated over many lifetimes, spontaneous conceptual clinging persists such that moment-to-moment correspondence has not yet been attained; therefore, one must listen to the true Dharma.
One contemplates its meaning and employs that wisdom of sudden enlightenment to observe deluded sentiments.
By diminishing them again and again until they reach non-existence, one ultimately arrives at the other shore; yet because this process takes a long time to traverse, it is called "gradual."
Although they differ in speed, both are designated as the wisdom that reaches the other shore. The Sanskrit term *sūtra* is translated in meaning as "scripture" (*jīng*).
This signifies being in accord with principle and in accord with capacity. To be in accord with principle means to explain phenomena as they truly are and to explain principles as they truly are.
To be in accord with capacity means to cause listeners to awaken to understanding, to rejoice, and to accept with faith. "Scripture" (*jīng*) means "to string together."
It is a compendium. It penetrates the meanings that ought to be explained and sustains those beings who are to be converted.
That sentient beings have been able to hear the True Dharma for more than two thousand years since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is entirely due to the power of penetration and sustenance.
In India, there was the Bodhisattva Asaṅga, who entered the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* (Sunlight Samādhi) and ascended to the Tuṣita Heaven palace to inquire of Maitreya.
The World-Honored One Maitreya expounded eighty verses to reveal the purport of the sutra.

Asanga, in turn, transmitted these verses to his younger brother Vasubandhu. Based on these verses, Vasubandhu composed a treatise in three fascicles, which summarizes the severing of doubts and attachments.
This is to explain the true meaning of this *Vajra*. Those who interpret it otherwise and fail to investigate this thoroughly are entirely engaged in erroneous discourse.

I have therefore taken the treatise composed by the Bodhisattva Guṇadakṣa as my basis, cross-referenced it with Changshui Zixuan’s *Kandingji* (Record of Collated Determinations), and interspersed it with the机缘 (kaiyuan) dialogues and phrases of various elder masters. Thus, I have entitled it *Zongtong* (The Penetration of the Essential School).
A monk asked Zhimen, "What is the essence of prajñā? Zhimen said, "An oyster contains the bright moon. The monk asked, "What is the function of prajñā?
Zhimen said, "A rabbit carries a fetus. Xuedou’s verse says: "A single expanse of void stillness, utterly beyond conceptualization;
From this, humans and devas behold the birth of emptiness. The oyster containing the dark rabbit is a profound meaning; It has once been bestowed upon..."
The Chan school engages in a battle of wits. In the *Verses on the Perfected Nature* (*Phalendriya-pariniṣpanna-svabhāva-gāthā*), Fayan says:

"When principle reaches its limit, sentiments are forgotten; how can it be compared to anything? In the end, the frosty night moon falls naturally into the stream before one. "The fruit ripens, and the monkeys grow heavy."
The mountain is so distant it seems the path is lost; lifting my head, the setting sun remains—yet it was all along to the west of my dwelling.
Students must penetrate such phrases through investigation before they can know the intimate essence of Prajñā, thereby avoiding the proliferation of futile and unprofitable disputes.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Then, at the time for eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having gone through the city begging for alms in order, he returned to his original place and ate his meal.
Having finished [his meal], he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.
He said: "This entire *Prajñāpāramitā* consists of six hundred fascicles and was preached in sixteen assemblies across four locations:
first, seven assemblies at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha; second, seven assemblies at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park; third, [at] the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven..."
There was one assembly in the Palace of the Mani-Jewel Treasury; another assembly by the White Heron Pond in the Bamboo Grove Garden at the City of the Four Kings.
In total, there were nine assemblies where light was emitted. All who saw this light attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This light is the light of wisdom. The Buddha said that this sutra is profoundly deep and subtle. Why?
It is because he does not emit light. Since the Buddha manifests the wisdom of equality, he emits light from within that very equality, yet the multitude does not perceive it.
At that time, at the hour of eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes and took up his alms bowl; this was the emission of light from his hand.
Entering the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms is the emission of light from his feet.
Having completed his sequential begging within that city is the emission of light from his eyes. Returning to his original location and finishing his meal is the emission of light from his mouth.
Having set aside his robes and bowl and washed his feet, he spreads out his seat and sits down; this is the emission of light from his entire body. Furthermore:
This sutra, for the sake of protecting, mindful of, and entrusting the bodhisattvas, explains the dharma-gate of the six perfections as being without marks (*animitta*).
He begs for food in order to teach sentient beings the practice of giving; he wears robes and carries an alms-bowl to manifest his morality (*śīla*);
he begs for alms in successive order to manifest his patience (*kṣānti*); his feet do not touch the dust, and he washes his feet to manifest his diligence (*vīrya*). [He] returns...

Returning to his original location, he spreads his seat and sits to manifest meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). When it is said that he was at Jetavana, he is also shown entering the city to beg for food;
when it is said that he was begging for food, he is also shown returning to his original location. In each instance, he does not abide in any sign (*nimitta*);
is this not the manifestation of the profoundly deep *prajñāpāramitā*? For those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, observe how the World-Honored One emits [light] like...
This light immediately enables one to attain the Vajra-like Illusory Samādhi and reach the other shore;

what need is there, then, for further instruction? The *Kanding ji* states: "There are two kinds of prefaces: first, the Preface of Certification (Saddharmapratyaya-nidāna); second, the Preface of Origination (Utpatti-nidāna).
The first, from 'Thus have I heard' up to 'the assembly of fifty people,' is the Preface of Certification. 'Certification' means to manifest the speaker and the listener."
The time and place are each clearly elucidated to prove that there is no error.
"At one time" refers to the time when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and the great assembly listened and received it. "Buddha" refers to the master who preached the Dharma.
"The tree offered by Prince Jeta" and "the garden purchased by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada" refer to the location where this Dharma was preached. Together with the Great... [comparison].
"Kiu et al. refers to the assembly listening to the Dharma. "Together" (ju) means being at the same time and in the same place.
As for placing such phrases at the beginning of all sūtras: when the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda asked the Buddha, "What words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?
The Buddha replied, "One should place: 'Thus have I heard at one time' (evam mayā śrutam ekasmin samaye)."

The Buddha was at such-and-such a place, with such-and-such a retinue of such-and-such a number. It is not only my Dharma that is thus; the Dharmas of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise so.
Therefore, Ānanda followed the Buddha’s command and placed it at the beginning [of the sūtra], to certify that what he transmitted contains no divergent teachings.
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the prepared seat and sat down; this constitutes entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is the section on the Precepts (*śīla*).
Virtue supports meditative concentration; concentration can give rise to wisdom. Thus, through virtue and concentration, one brings forth the true essence of Prajñā. Regarding the time for eating:
from the hours of the Tiger (寅), Rabbit (卯), and Dragon (辰) is the mealtime of the devas; from the Snake (巳), Horse (午), and Sheep (未) is the mealtime of humans according to the Dharma;

from the Monkey (申), Cock (酉), and Dog (戌) is the mealtime of ghosts and spirits; and from the Pig (亥), Rat (子), and Ox (丑) is the mealtime of animals. Now, it is the mealtime of humans; therefore, begging for alms will not be difficult.
If one begs at an improper time, the donor may have nothing to give; yet to refuse the gift would cause embarrassment.

Thus, one would disturb the other. If the request is unsuccessful, one suffers the loss of food and hunger, thereby disturbing oneself. "Wearing robes" refers to wearing the twenty-five-fold *saṃghāṭī*.
"Holding an alms-bowl" refers to holding the dark-blue lapis lazuli bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings at the time of his past enlightenment.
Nevertheless, one must wear robes and carry an alms bowl in order to remain free from the two extremes of suffering and pleasure.
Laypeople, who take delight in fine silks, flowery and clean garments, and precious vessels, increase their negligence and become overly attached to the extreme of pleasure.
Monastics and non-Buddhist ascetics, who practice austerities such as going naked and holding food in their hands, incur reproach and shame, becoming overly attached to the extreme of suffering.
The Buddha dwells in the Middle Way; therefore, he wears robes and carries an alms bowl.
Śrāvastī—here translated as "Hearing of Things"—means that this country produces many people of renowned excellence and extraordinary, precious treasures. (From the *Xiyu ji*).
The kingdom is over sixty *li* in circumference, while the inner city is twenty *li* in circumference; thus it is said that the area is vast.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are nine hundred million households; thus it is said that the population is great. When the Buddha entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms in sequence, [he proceeded in this manner].
He did not bypass the poor to follow the wealthy, nor did he abandon the lowly to follow the noble; his great compassion was impartial and made no distinctions.
"Returning to his original place" means that once his work of transformation was complete, he returned to the Jeta Grove.

Regarding "taking food," it is because the Buddha wished to cause those who practice giving to attain fulfillment of their merit. Some say that when the food reached the mouth, a deity of majestic power stood by his side.
He vanished from sight and traveled to other realms to perform buddha-work; this was a manifestation of eating, not actual eating.

As for putting away his robes and bowl, it signifies resting from攀緣 (pān-yuán, mental attachments) so that the mind is free from weariness and anxiety. Washing his feet signifies purifying physical karma so as to remain unstained by worldly entanglements.
These two acts were manifested for the sake of providing models for future generations; thus he displayed them. He then spread out his seat.

As for his sitting: he personally spread out his seat, sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), and remained with his body upright and unmoving in right mindfulness, manifesting his intention to preach the Dharma.
Whenever the Tathāgata preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* in an assembly, he always personally spread out his seat.
Because the *Prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to all Buddhas—that is, she is the Mother of Buddhas—he personally spreads the seat to express his reverence for the *Prajñā*. Thus, it is wisdom.

The verse says: The Dharma-body is fundamentally not food; the same is true for the Response and Transformation bodies. To increase the merit of humans and devas, they act as fields of blessings through compassion.
Having gathered their robes and stilled all weary anxieties, they wash their feet to leave behind worldly conditions. They desire to realize the principle of the three emptinesses.

He sat cross-legged, manifesting entry into dhyāna. Formerly, Chan Master Xinxin of Longtan asked Emperor Tianhuang, "Since I arrived here, I have not received instruction on the essential point of the mind.
The Emperor said, "From the moment you arrived, I have never failed to point out the essential point of your mind.
Xinxin asked, "Where did you point it out? The Emperor said, "When you brought me tea, I accepted it from you; when you walked..."
"Come and eat; I shall receive it for you. When you perform the *vaṃdana*, I shall bow my head. "Where else would you not point out the essential heart?
Xinxin bowed his head for a long time. The Emperor said, "If you see, see directly and immediately. Any attempt at deliberation is already a deviation."
Xin immediately attained understanding. He asked again, "How does one maintain this? Huang said, "Roam freely according to your nature; let go and relax in accordance with conditions.
Simply exhaust the ordinary mind; there is no separate 'sage's' understanding. Later, while residing at Longtan, Prefect Li Ao asked, "What is true suchness and prajñā?
Xin said, "I have no true suchness or prajñā. Li said, "Fortunately..."
Upon meeting the Master, Xinxing said, "These are still words that go beyond the ordinary. Furthermore, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "I am a student newly entered into this forest monastery;
I beg the Master for instruction. Zhaozhou said, "Have you finished eating your gruel yet? The monk replied, "I have finished."
Zhaozhou said, "Go wash your bowl. Because of this, the monk attained awakening. Tiantong’s verse says: After the gruel was finished, he ordered him to wash his bowl;
Suddenly, the ground of his heart accorded with it of its own accord. Nowadays, there are guests who have "participated to satiety" in the monastic forests;
Tell me, among them, is there awakening or not? Judging from these two cases, one can know that the Tathāgata himself [demonstrated] wearing robes and holding [the bowl].
When the bowl had been set down, he spread his seat and sat upon it. Having finished explaining the Prajñāpāramitā of True Suchness (tathatā), what further need was there for words?
At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;

he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all [bodhisattvas]..."

“Bodhisattvas, you have well entrusted yourselves to the bodhisattvas. World-Honored One, how should sons and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds?
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and mindfully cares for all bodhisattvas; he has well entrusted them.”

He addressed the bodhisattvas: “Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you. Sons of good family and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this manner and subdue their minds in this manner.
“So be it, World-Honored One,” they replied, “we wish and desire to hear it.”
Tong said: "Subhūti was originally the Buddha Qinglongta of the East; he manifested in the body of a śrāvaka and entered the assembly of Śākyamuni.

For many lifetimes he cultivated the understanding of emptiness, yet he realized only partial emptiness. Upon hearing of the 'Jewel-Bright Sea of Emptiness,' he finally realized that emptiness is not empty.
He is a Great Arhat dwelling in the eighth stage; one who abides in this Immovable Stage is called 'Dwelling'."
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva up through the subsequent ninth and tenth stages, they preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, not dwelling in any fixed state.
Subhūti establishes this point of inquiry here in order to eliminate the doubts and attachments of all bodhisattvas.
Since generating the unsurpassed bodhicitta, from the very first stage onward, bodhisattvas have often been inclined toward quiescence; [Subhūti] asks this solely to encourage their further progress.
Once you have attained the blissful dwelling in the present life while abiding in the ground, the Buddhas of the ten directions will again exhort you, saying:
"Arise, arise! Son of good family, you must deliver sentient beings. Turn your wisdom toward compassion; turn away from stillness toward activity.
In the interim, could there not be moments when thoughts arise or the mind stirs? If you do not subdue such a mind, you will violate the state of abiding. If...
To be solely attached to dwelling is to contradict the salvation of sentient beings.
Within the act of saving sentient beings, one subdues the mind without losing the intent of dwelling; thus, even while in motion, one is still. Therefore, the question should be asked:
"How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind? What is called "dwelling" does not mean dwelling in signs as ordinary people do. Nor...
It does not abide in emptiness as the followers of the Two Vehicles do; rather, it is the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

It is neither provisional nor empty, for it abides in the Middle Way Truth. What is called "subduing the mind" does not mean suppressing the six consciousnesses as ordinary beings practice, nor does it mean annihilating the seventh consciousness as the followers of the Two Vehicles practice; rather, it concerns the field of the eighth consciousness.
Subtle habitual tendencies are permeated by True Suchness (tathatā), causing the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna) to be transformed into wisdom (jñāna).

This is likened to subduing a band of rebels and making them one's own good citizens; hence it is called "subduing" (parājaya). This is like Ānanda attaining the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) without passing through the kalpas of a bodhisattva.
I hope you will further examine and eliminate even the most subtle delusions; none but Subhūti is capable of reaching the ultimate conclusion—how could one dare to speak lightly of this?
The *Kanding ji* states: "At this time, the Elder arrives to entrust [the teaching] to the various Bodhisattvas, arranging his appearance to praise the Buddha.
One of high virtue is called 'Elder' (*zhǎnglǎo*); one of many years is called 'Old' (*lǎo*). Subhūti is here translated as 'Born of Emptiness' (*kōngshēng*), and also as 'Good' (*shàn*).

Regarding "rising from one's seat": in the way of teacher and disciple, the distinction between honor and humility is fundamental. When one wishes to seek counsel, it is improper to do so while remaining seated.

for those whose faculties are not yet mature, one has compassion for them so that the Buddha-dharma already arisen may remain and increase, and so that the supreme Dharma not yet arisen may be entrusted to them so that it may arise.

The "Supreme Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) means awakening to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) through correct wisdom and knowing it according to its true nature;

thus, it is not the false awakening of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). It means awakening to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through universal wisdom and knowing it as it is; thus, it is not the partial awakening of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are five kinds of bodhi from cause to fruit: first, the bodhi of generating the mind (*cittotpāda-bodhi*);...

Fifth is the unsurpassed bodhi, which refers to the stage of the Tathāgata. Now, in terms of that which can give rise to the mind, it corresponds to the first; in terms of that which is given rise to, it corresponds to the others.

Regarding "how to subdue the mind": before generating the resolve, whenever deluded thoughts arise, one immediately pursues those delusions; now that...

"Listen now attentively"—this is an exhortation to listen. "I shall speak for you"—this is a promise to speak. "Attentively" (*dṛṣṭi*) means the sense of examining with precision;

The Obstructing Demon King, leading his retinue, followed the Bodhisattva Vajrasama for a thousand years seeking the place of his arising, but could not find it.
Suddenly, one day, he beheld him and asked: "Upon what do you rely to abide? For a thousand years I have sought the place of your arising, yet I have not found it."
Vimalakīrti said, "I do not dwell by relying on dwelling, nor do I dwell by relying on non-dwelling;
I dwell in this manner. "Excellent, excellent! If one can dwell in such a way, one will not be spied upon by the obstructing Māra King.
This is truly one who has been able to subdue the mind. Thereupon, Vajrasama Bodhisattva said:
"Is it not perhaps because he was skilled in the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* that he thereby acquired his name?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner:
'Regarding all categories of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether they possess [form]..."

Whether they have form or are formless, whether they possess perception, lack perception, or possess neither perception nor non-perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.

In this way, although I liberate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, in truth there is no sentient being who has been liberated. Why is that? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses a self...
The mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span—these are not the Bodhisattva.
Master Fu’s verse says: When Subhūti first asked his question, the Sugata responded according to the occasion.

First he answered how one should dwell; next he taught how one should practice. Whether born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or by transformation, all are gathered within compassion and wisdom. If one gives rise to [these marks]...
This gives rise to views; it is no different from seeking through attachment to marks (*nimitta*).
[The Master] replied: "This is precisely the answer to your question. In your question, both 'abiding' and 'subduing' were mentioned together; why is it that here only 'subduing' is indicated?
It is because supreme bodhi is fundamentally without characteristics and is inherently free from subject and object. To give rise to this..."
As for the mind, one desires it to abide permanently and never fall away; yet this is the most difficult thing to accomplish.
Because it arises obscurely, conditioned by subtle ignorance, even the slightest stirring of a single thought causes it to depart from its original station, such that it cannot be called "abiding.
If one strives to guard and restrain it so that it does not arise, one falls into the trap of guarding and restraining, such that it cannot be called "abiding. If, at every moment of thought...
It is associated [with them], dwelling in attachment and not relinquishing them; furthermore, it falls into dwelling in attachment and cannot be called "dwelling" [in the true sense].
Only the self-substance of True Suchness (tathatā), fully endowed with diamond-like wisdom (vajra-prajñā), is sufficient to illuminate and shatter them so as to subdue them.
This sutra emphasizes the functional application of prajñā-wisdom; therefore, "subduing" is taken as its fundamental principle. Possessing this wisdom of subduing, not only...
When the mind does not abide, one can subdue it so that it abides; thus the mind attains its place of abiding.
Furthermore, one can subdue it so that it does not abide; to abide in non-abiding is true abiding. Therefore, if one speaks only of "subduing," then peaceful abiding is naturally contained within it.
However, if one speaks only of "peaceful abiding" while omitting "subduing," then peaceful abiding is not achieved. Thus...
This is because it alone stands out as the means of subduing. The function of subduing is great indeed. If the mind is narrow, one desires it to become vast;
if the mind is base, one desires it to be supreme; if the mind is attached to pleasure, one desires it to be equanimous;
if the mind is inverted, one desires it to possess correct wisdom. Therefore, those who give rise to the bodhicitta must fully possess these four kinds of mental states.
Only then will one be in accord with Bodhi; only then can one be called a "Bodhisattva" (an awakened being). As Maitreya Bodhisattva stated in verse:
"Vast, foremost, and eternal, his mind is non-erroneous; abiding in a deeply beneficial resolve, the merit of this vehicle is fulfilled.
This reveals the profound fourfold correspondence through which the Bodhisattva’s fruition benefits sentient beings.
The mind. All Bodhisattvas should abide in this. What is meant by the "vast mind"?
It refers to all categories of sentient beings—those who breathe, possess feelings, and are conscious; whether born from eggs, such as various birds;

born from wombs, such as various humans; born from moisture, such as various insects; or born by transformation, such as various devas. These beings of the four modes of birth and six realms of existence, each...
There are many classes [of beings]. Where do these sentient beings reside? Those who possess form reside in the Desire Realm and the celestial abodes of the Form Realm.
Those who are formless reside in the celestial abode of the Sphere of Infinite Space within the Formless Realm.
Furthermore, how many types are there? Those who possess perception arise in the celestial abode of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.

Those who possess conceptual thought are these [beings]. Those who are without conceptual thought are the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), who are free from even slight conceptual thought.

Those who are neither with nor without conceptual thought are the gods of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), who lack coarse conceptual thought but possess subtle conceptual thought.
All sentient beings of the three realms are entirely subsumed within these. Thus, all such [beings] are...
The mind by which I have brought them across—how vast it is! What is called the "supreme mind"? It is not difficult to deliver sentient beings;
it is difficult to deliver sentient beings into nirvana. It is not difficult to deliver sentient beings into nirvana;
it is difficult to deliver all sentient beings into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder). There are four kinds of nirvana: first, *svabhāva-nirvāṇa* (nirvana by its own nature).

1. Nirvana shared by both ordinary beings and sages (*sādhāraṇa-nirvāṇa*). 2. Nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), which refers to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) who have emerged from the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) yet still possess a body that is the basis for suffering.
3. Nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), which refers to the two vehicles who have extinguished their physical bodies and ceased their cognitive wisdom (*jñāna*);

because their bodies have emerged from the suffering of birth and death, they no longer have a basis [for rebirth]. 4. Non-abiding nirvana (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*), in which compassion and wisdom are combined, such that one does not abide [in the realm of] Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*): not abiding in the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles—which is a cessation like ashes—is the true state of non-abiding.
The former three [nirvāṇas] constitute *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder), while the latter one constitutes *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder); this is the realm of the Buddha.

By means of this, he intends to deliver all sentient beings within the triple world—those of the nine classes, whether possessing the nature for enlightenment or lacking it—and cause them all equally to attain the Buddha-way. This is...
This is the supreme, foremost mind. What is meant by the "constant mind"? It is because all sentient beings and one's own body are equal in *tathatā* (suchness) and without distinction.
Thus, although immeasurable sentient beings are brought to extinction and all enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, in reality, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "All sentient beings are themselves quiescence."
The mark of extinction does not undergo further extinction. If one perceives that there are sentient beings who can be saved, this is a mind of attachment and fondness;

such attachment involves coming and going, and thus cannot be permanent. Only by being able to subsume all affection—whether saving or not saving—with a mind that is non-dual, is it called "permanent.
The salvation of sentient beings is no different from one's own self; how could one then give rise to [attachment] toward one's own self?
Regarding the perception of others: suppose one sees a single sentient being as someone to be delivered by oneself—what fault is there in this?

It is because of delusion regarding the ultimate truth that one gives rise to the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, and the notion of a life-span; thus turning one's back on awakening and uniting with the sensory dust.
This is called perversion. One who holds perverted views is what is known as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); such a one is not called a bodhisattva.
If one realizes the true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the notion of "sentient beings" will certainly not arise.

Just as a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) does not give rise to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), since there is no self-characteristic, there is likewise no other-characteristic. Self and others are equal; all sentient beings [are thus].
All these are unattainable. Master Zhi said: "Because my own body is empty and all dharmas are empty, the thousands of grades and myriad species are entirely the same.
This is precisely what is meant by that. Correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is not the same as *er-yan*. *Er-yan* here means the cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
To have the cognitive obscuration is called perversion; to be without the cognitive obscuration is called correct wisdom. It is for this reason that it is termed "correct."
Wisdom is a mind free of discrimination, whereas *er-yan* (the radiance of consciousness) possesses a discriminating mind.

The realization and awakening through the four aforementioned marks is precisely where the consciousness of *er-yan* resides. To perceive that there is a nirvana to be realized is itself the mark of self (*ātman*).

To realize that what has been attained is non-existent is the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*). To thoroughly understand that awakening and realization should be relinquished is the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*).
To maintain a consciousness that perceives there is something realized is the mark of a life-span (*jīvita-nimitta*).

These four marks are fundamentally no different from those in the *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith* (or the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*). What is meant by "carefully eliminating subtle delusions" refers precisely to this. The Bodhisattva, having already...
Only one who has resolved to attain enlightenment and can further deliver sentient beings may be called a Mahāsattva.
Although this Great Bodhisattva possesses a trace of ignorance regarding the appearance of birth, he does not abandon sentient beings.

Within this context, the single phrase "there is truly no sentient being who attains parinirvāṇa" is precisely the essential method for subduing [the mind]. If one perceives even a single sentient being who attains parinirvāṇa...
This refers to being attached to the marks of realization and awakening, which is not right knowledge; therefore, it must be subdued.
By subduing these four marks, one attains abiding in oneself within *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and is also able to cause sentient beings to abide in *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
While remaining within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one is not turned by birth and death; hence, it is called "non-."
Above is nirvāṇa; while abiding amidst afflictions (*kleśa*), one is not turned by them. Therefore, it is called unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*).
These two transformations of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) constitute dwelling in the Buddha-ground at the stage of perfect fruition.
Thus it is said: "The merits of this vehicle are fulfilled. Could this be possible without the wisdom of *prajñā* as its cause? Shi Shanren asked Guifeng.

[The Buddha] is eternally abiding. Or, it is said that he enters parinirvāṇa. If he were eternal, he would not cease; if he ceased, he would not be eternal.
Is this not a contradiction? The answer says: To be free from all marks is precisely what is called the Buddhas. How could there be any reality to "appearing in the world" or "entering extinction"?
Those who perceive his appearance and disappearance do so according to the conditions of sentient beings' capacities. When the capacity and conditions respond, he appears beneath the Bodhi tree.
When the conditions [for teaching] are exhausted, he enters nirvana amidst the śāla groves. This is like pure water that is mindless: no image fails to appear within it, yet the image is not "mine.
It is merely the coming and going of external forms; these appearances are not the Buddha-body, so how could they be the appearance or disappearance of the Tathāgata?
These two questions and answers are sufficient to analyze the profound meaning of this chapter. Páng [Jiǎo] resided—
A scholar once visited a lecture hall and, out of sympathetic joy, attended a recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
When he reached the passage concerning "no self" and "no person," he asked, "Master, if there is neither self nor person, who is it that lectures and who is it that listens? The Master had no reply.
The scholar said, "Although I am a layman, I have a rough understanding and a sincere faith. The Master asked, "In that case, what is your own view, Layman? The scholar—
He replied in verse: "No self and no person; how can there be distance or intimacy? I urge you to cease wandering through the seats; do not seek the Truth indirectly.
The nature of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is utterly free from even a speck of dust outside itself.

What I have heard and what I accept with faith are all merely conventional designations. When the Master heard this verse, he sighed in admiration and said: "If such is the Bodhi of a layman as this..."

therefore, Prajñāpāramitā always serves as the precursor to the five perfections. Without Prajñā, the five perfections cannot be called "reaching the other shore.
As previously stated, when the four qualities—the vast mind, the foremost mind, the constant mind, and the non-perverted mind—are fully possessed, it is called "subduing. Being thus able to subdue...
Prostrate. One is then able to be free from signs (*nimitta*). Being able to be free from signs, one is then able to practice the gift of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita-dāna*).
Therefore, "cultivation" refers precisely to the dwelling in accordance with and the subduing [of the mind] through the six *pāramitās* as revealed below.

Therefore, it is said that a bodhisattva, within the Buddha-dharma, should not abide in phenomenal characteristics (*vastu-nimitta*) when practicing giving. There are three kinds of giving, the meaning of which encompasses the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). First:
There are three kinds of giving: first, the gift of material sustenance; second, the gift of fearlessness; and third, the gift of the Dharma. Regarding the gift of material sustenance:

it consists of bestowing wealth and resources to support the lives of others. Regarding the gift of fearlessness: because one upholds the precepts and practices patience, one has no intent to harm living beings;
even if one encounters an enemy, one does not seek retaliation, thereby causing no fear to arise. Regarding the gift of the Dharma: it arises through diligence...

Because of progress, the mind does not slacken or retreat from virtuous deeds. Because of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one understands the minds of others as clearly as a mirror reflects still water.
Because of wisdom (*prajñā*), one teaches the Dharma without error, in accordance with principle and reality.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "The meaning of giving (*dāna*) is subsumed within six types: material support, fearlessness, and the Dharma; among these, there are two and one [respectively]."
Third is called "dwelling in practice. The first is the provision of life's necessities; the second is fearlessness; the third is the Dharma. What is meant by "not dwelling in signs"?
It means not dwelling in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, dharmas, and so forth.
One practices giving without seeking external objects. First, this is because one does not [cling to] the present self. Therefore, [one does not dwell in signs].
One practices giving for two reasons: first, to repay the kindness of others from the past;
second, to hope for the fruit of future abundance. One must dispel all such [motivations].
Whether the mind perceives emptiness or existence, the mere arising of a thought deviates from the essence of the Dharma. One must simply maintain an equanimous mind at the time of giving. Do not...
When one perceives the gift, the giver, and the recipient, it is only then that non-abiding is truly established. Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse:
"One is not attached to oneself, to gratitude, or to the karmic fruit; One does not withhold out of self-preservation, nor does one seek other worldly matters."

For the sake of one's own self, there is the fault of being attached to oneself and failing to practice giving. For the sake of repaying kindness or seeking karmic retribution, there is the fault of seeking after external things.
"Not dwelling on form and so forth" mentions only the category of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*);

if all were mentioned, they would include the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the four noble truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*), and the thirty [mental states].
The seven factors of enlightenment, up to bodhi, nirvāṇa, and so forth—altogether eighty-one categories—all should be without abiding.
Practicing the six pāramitās in this manner results in purity; therefore it is said that a bodhisattva should practice giving in this way, without dwelling on signs.
This means that within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there is neither giver nor receiver.
When neither the donor, the recipient, the gift, nor the conceptualizations regarding names, meanings, and objects of knowledge arise, this is the cause for subduing the mind through purification.
To address the objection that "if one is free from the characteristics of giving and so forth, how can one obtain the benefit of merit?
it is said that "the merit produced is exceedingly great," because that bodhisattva does not depart from conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
One practices giving without departing from the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and thus does not dwell upon signs. Not dwelling upon signs is itself subduing;
the purity of giving is itself abiding. One cultivates both merit and wisdom so that wisdom is not one-sided;
one cultivates both wisdom and merit so that merit is beyond measure—just as, for example, the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
The empty space of the ten directions pervades all places; it is vast, sublime, and ultimately inexhaustible, beyond the reach of conceptual thought.
Yet, the pure cultivation of causes by the Bodhisattva is such that no marks can be apprehended. The resulting merit and reward they induce is likewise inconceivable.
Being fully endowed with both merit and wisdom, they are called the "Honored One of Two Fullnesses" (Dvipadottama); this is the ultimate fruition. Therefore—
It is said: "The merit of this vehicle is fulfilled. Thereupon, he concluded with an exhortation, saying: "A bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed.
The Wei translation says: "One should simply practice giving in this manner.
Based on Subhūti’s question regarding how one should abide—fearing that one might fail to find such an abiding—the World-Honored One taught that one should practice giving.
To abide in signs while causing the mind to not abide—how could these be contradictory? It is because abiding without abiding is precisely abiding in true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Just as a bird does not abide in space yet is able to abide in space—if one were to abide in space, one would not be abiding in space at all.
The *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra* states: The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "How should one abide in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?"
Regarding the *pāramitās*, Mañjuśrī said: "By means of the dharma of non-abiding, one abides in the *prajñāpāramitā*. He was further asked:
"In what way is the dharma of non-abiding called abiding in the *prajñāpāramitā*? Mañjuśrī replied:
"By means of the characteristic of non-abiding, one abides in the *prajñāpāramitā*. The *Samādhi-sūtra* says: "All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata..."
"In non-abiding. I come from the place of non-abiding; it is there that I pay homage to the Tathāgata.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should indeed abide in non-abiding, just as he has been taught. Long ago, Dongshan asked a monk, "Where have you come from?

The monk replied, "I have come from wandering the mountains. Dongshan said, "Have you reached the summit? The monk replied, "I have. Dongshan said, "Is there anyone at the summit? The monk replied, "There is none."
Zhaozhou said, "If that is so, then you have not reached the summit. Tian replied, "If I had not reached the summit, how could I know there is no one?
Zhaozhou said, "Why do you not stay for a while? Tian replied, "I am not unwilling to stay; it is just that someone in the Western Heavens would not approve.
Zhaozhou said, "I have always suspected this fellow. Tiantong cited Zhaozhou, saying: "Where there is a Buddha, one may not [stay]."
He stays. Where there is no Buddha, he runs past in haste. [The Master] picks up the case and says:

"To sink into emptiness or linger at a trace, to mishandle the hand or wound the blade—none of these constitute the coming and going of a patch-robed monk. You must simply not enter the marketplace of others; do not sit upon their beds or stools.
When you neither establish the profound nor attach yourself to things, only then do you have the freedom to hold fast or let go. These two venerable ones—"
Xu Su deeply clarified the principle of non-abiding and thereby came to know that the unsurpassed true teaching of Caodong does not establish two extremes nor settle upon a middle way;
this is the true bloodline path of Prajñā.
The direct answer above is concluded. Below, the text traces the steps to sever doubts.
It states in general: "The preceding questions and answers have dispelled Subhūti’s subtle doubts and revealed the true lineage of the Tathāgata."
Universally delivering all sentient beings, they gather them back into the ocean of the Tathāgatagarbha. Practicing the signless, they mysteriously identify with the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
They extinguish the cognitive obscurations at the stage of Buddhahood, equalizing the Dharma-realm with empty space.
Abiding in nirvāṇa yet without abiding, acting through all phenomena yet without action, they achieve all merit, power, and majesty; this is precisely in accord with the sūtras.

This concludes the section on the dissemination (*parivarta*). Based upon the questions posed by Subhūti, [it was shown that] to pursue quiescence is to oppose the saving of sentient beings, and to save sentient beings is to oppose the pursuit of quiescence;
thus, conceptual discrimination arises and the two are not harmonized. The World-Honored One erected the great banner of the Dharma to decisively resolve this:
"In saving, there is no saving; how could this obstruct quiescence? In quiescence, there is no quiescence; how could this hinder saving?"
One must bring matters such as giving and discipline under control, remaining detached from the mind that grasps at signs, and dwelling in non-dwelling;
this is what is meant by "constant dwelling. Within this, the subtlety is particularly difficult to comprehend: it is mindfulness without mindfulness, and signs without signs.
To speak while there is no speaking, and to realize while there is no realization—how can one not have doubts regarding such manifold contradictions?

When the former doubt has subsided, the latter doubt arises again. If the doubting mind does not cease, that is not subjugation. If one claims to be without doubt yet remains attached and settled, this is precisely the formation of a mind.
As long as this formed mind is not eliminated, one dwells where one should not dwell. Therefore, various means of subduing are employed.
This is for the purpose of severing subtle doubts. This sutra merely speaks of their severance, but not of their arising.
The locus of their arising is so extremely subtle that it is difficult to manifest through words;

only the Buddha’s World-Honored One’s eye can illuminate each and every instance, silently severing them without waiting for a question. How could such adamantine wisdom be fathomed by ordinary intellect?

Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke in verse: "In the matter of disciplining those [afflictions], one should distance oneself from the mind that grasps at signs, sever various doubts, and also guard against the arising of conceptualizing minds. This verse was transmitted to Asaṅga;
Asaṅga, in turn, transmitted it to Vasubandhu. Asaṅga divided this sūtra into eighteen stages (*vihāra*), while Vasubandhu divided this sūtra into two.

Seventeenth, the elimination of doubts: Why is it that in some cases there are two or three doubts within a single dwelling (*vihāra*), while in other cases there are three or four dwellings within a single doubt, such that the treatises differ from one another?
Asaṅga assigns the first dwelling to the stages of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) and the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicittotpāda*);
the second dwelling to the first six of the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*); and the third dwelling...
The fourth dwelling corresponds to the stages of the seven practices; the fifth dwelling through the fourteenth dwelling correspond to the ten stages of dedication;
the fifteenth dwelling corresponds to the four stages of application; the sixteenth dwelling corresponds to the stage of the World’s Foremost;
and the seventeenth dwelling corresponds to the first bhūmi. The eighteenth dwelling...

From the second bhūmi up to the stage of Buddhahood, these are collectively termed the Tathāgata-bhūmi. Since this sutra takes non-characteristic (animitta) as its central tenet, how could it be appropriate to enumerate the stages according to their relative depth?
Although delusions may gradually thin out and one’s position on the stages may become increasingly exalted, the essential meaning remains largely the same;
thus, it would not be improper to provide a brief correspondence between them. However, to force a synthesis with other sutras merely results in being hindered by names.

Consequently, the profound meaning and intent [of the sūtra] are, on the contrary, obscured. This is why Vasubandhu specifically took it upon himself to resolve doubts, following the instructions of Maitreya.
Those who uphold this sūtra hereafter should collectively adhere to this [work].
