The Essential Meaning of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume Two. 01.
Dispelling Doubts Regarding Abiding in Marks While Practicing Generosity with the Desire for Buddhahood.
This doubt arises from the preceding passage concerning giving without dwelling on signs (*animitta-dāna*). The *Puṇyaprasaraka-bodhisattva-śāstra* states:
"If a bodhisattva does not dwell even upon dharmas when giving, how can they practice giving for the sake of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*)?"
The collection of dharmas consisting of merits such as the hundred marks of excellence is called the World-Honored One.
If he did not abide in these dharmas, how could he achieve the essential characteristics of a Buddha? To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of his physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not physical marks.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All marks whatsoever are empty and illusory. If one perceives all marks as being no-marks,"
One immediately beholds the Tathāgata. Master Fu’s verse says: The Tathāgata displays his physical form To accord with the sentiments of the world.

Fearing that people might give rise to the view of annihilation, He provisionally establishes empty names. He speaks of the thirty-two marks; Even the eighty secondary characteristics are but hollow sounds. To have a body is not...
The essence of awakening is formless; this is its true form.
It is said that the Dharmakāya Tathāgata comes, yet has never come; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Ordinary beings see his coming and grasp it as having form, constantly dwelling in existence as they cultivate their causes. The followers of the Two Vehicles see...
Regarding that which does not come, they grasp it as being without marks (animitta) and constantly abide in non-existence as the cause for their cultivation.

The Bodhisattva, already knowing that the retributive and transformation bodies are not existent, leaves behind the views of ordinary beings; already knowing that the Dharma-body is not non-existent, he leaves behind the views of the Two Vehicles.
Although you are intent upon the Buddha-vehicle, you still harbor attachment to the Dharma.

Now that you have heard that at the time of practicing the Six Perfections, one should not dwell upon or cling to any phenomena—from the six sense objects up to Bodhi and Nirvana—by what means can you maintain your practice and realize the Dharma-body?
The Buddha replied: "If the Dharma-body were identical to characteristics, then by means of those very characteristics, [one could realize it]."
Regarding the vision of the Tathāgata: if the Dharma-body were separate from its marks, then one could see the Tathāgata by means of being separate from those marks;
yet this is neither possible through identity nor through separation. Therefore, one should not abide in dharmas in order to realize the Dharma-body.
Because it is not identical, one sees that it has never come; because it is not separate, one sees that it has never not come. Hence it is said: "To see it through identity."
The Tathāgata’s three truths are perfectly interfused; when cause and effect coincide as one, only then does one correspond with unsurpassed bodhi.
The *Kanding ji* states: The Buddha asked Subhūti, “In your view, can the body of the thirty-two marks be used to see the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, or not?
When Śūnyatā-ja (Subhūti) saw the Buddha raise up these marks...
Question: Since it is known that one cannot seek [the Tathāgata] through marks, the answer says: "No. One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
Fearing that sentient beings of the final age would fail to understand this principle and mistake grasping at marks for reality, he further inquires into his own intent, saying:
"For what reason can the Dharma-body not be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?"
Is it the Tathāgata? Because the body characterized by the thirty-two marks spoken of by the Tathāgata is not the mark of the Dharma-body.

Since these thirty-two marks are accomplished through cultivation over many kalpas, they fall within the category of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and must be subject to the transitions of the four marks:
arising, abiding, change, and cessation. How much more so when, for the sake of responding to the capacities of sentient beings, they may appear or not appear?
This is definitive. How could this be taken as the Dharmakāya? If it were the essence of the Dharmakāya Buddha, it would not have arisen in the past, nor would it perish in the future;
it would be without transition and indestructible, being distinct from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, it is said that the thirty-two marks are not the marks of the Dharmakāya. As Maitreya Bodhisattva stated in verse: "One discriminates the conditioned."
[The Buddha said: "The essence [of the Tathāgata] prevents the attainment of those [three marks], because the three marks are distinct from the essence. To be apart from them is the Tathāgata.
The three marks are identical to the four marks, for since abiding and change occur simultaneously, they are combined into one. This is what Subhūti perceives:
he already knows that the Dharma-body is without marks, yet he has not yet clarified that the Dharma-body is not separate from marks. Therefore, the Buddha confirms this."
He said: "All that has marks is entirely illusory and false. All conditioned phenomena arise from deluded thoughts.
Deluded thoughts are fundamentally empty and lack intrinsic nature. If even the thought itself lacks a nature, how much more so the marks manifested by it—how could they truly exist?
Not only are the thirty-two marks like illusions and unreal, but all things, both mundane and supramundane,"
All characteristics of both the holy and the ordinary are not real. Since these characteristics are not real, that which is non-characteristic is real.
Might one not, therefore, seek a Buddha free from characteristics apart from these delusive characteristics? Thus, he further refutes this, saying:
If one perceives that all marks are no-marks, one sees the Tathāgata; that is to say, the Dharma-body is markless.
It is not that the Dharma-body exists separately outside of all marks, for form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form.
By simply extinguishing conceptual discrimination, marks do not arise of themselves. Since marks do not arise, there is only the single reality. This reality is...
It dwells within the midst of the false and illusory; it is both true and false, and both false and true. People perceive only its appearances, whereas I perceive that which is beyond appearance.

Just as one who examines a horse grasps it outside of whether it is a mare or a stallion, or black or yellow, so too does one perceive the Tathāgata, the Dharma-body, the self-nature of True Suchness.
The Tathāgata Ratnakūṭa explained: "The true body of the Tathāgata..."

Fundamentally, there is neither birth nor extinction; it is serene and eternally abiding. Entrusting itself with the aggregates to receive a physical form, it manifests its transformation in common with ordinary beings.
Upon entering the womb of the divine mother, it assumes these various distinct mundane appearances. Therefore, it is said: "If one sees all phenomena as non-phenomena, then one sees the Tathāgata."
The verse says: When all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) cease, their nature does not cease; the essence of the realization of *tathatā* is free from defilement.
To fully awaken to the distinction between the roots and fruits of annihilationism and eternalism—this is called seeing the Tathāgata with the Buddha-eye. It is not merely the thirty-two marks;
that the marks are themselves non-marks is what is called the Tathāgata. All marks, whether mundane or supramundane, are ultimately markless.
There is nothing that is not the unconditioned essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*); it is the singular, true equality, without duality or distinction.
The entire nature of the Dharma-realm constitutes the single Dharmakāya. Those who see thus know it through realization;
therefore, one does not perceive the Tathāgata by means of illusory marks, but perceives the Tathāgata by means of subtle and wondrous marks. Since the Dharmakāya is... [inexpressible].
One cannot perceive [the Buddha] by means of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), nor can one perceive him by being apart from marks.

Thus, those who seek the Buddha must certainly not seek him by clinging to marks, nor must they seek him by departing from marks. The fruit is fundamentally non-abiding; the cause is likewise non-abiding.
If one can remain far removed from the hopes and expectations of sentient beings and does not dwell in existence, then even the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is ultimately unobtainable. Not...
Abiding in non-existence, one constantly practices in this manner without dwelling upon signs; thus, one will swiftly achieve the fulfillment of the Buddha-body.
Why, then, should one doubt that cause and effect do not correspond? The Celestial Youth (Tiantong) cites the Sūtra, saying:
"If one sees that all signs are non-signs, then one sees the Tathāgata. Fayen says: "If one sees that all signs are non-signs, then one does not see the Tathāgata."
Come. [Wansong] picks up the topic and says: "The World-Honored One spoke of Tathāgata Chan; Fayen spoke of Patriarchal Chan. If you understand it, how extraordinary!
Even if you do not understand, I grant you my approval. Wansong praises his own portrait, saying: "All that has marks is entirely illusory.
If you see that all marks are no-marks, then you will see them right upon the eyebrows and eyes—without expending even a grain of effort."
By exerting power, he demarcated the boundaries and established the jurisdictions within the Dharma-eye of Śākyamuni, bringing peace through skillful means and unifying all under heaven;
how could this not be a good thing? As for the Chan of the Tiantong Tathāgata, the Patriarchal Master of Chan, I dare not give rise to further deluded discrimination.
Setting aside for a moment the fact that you have attained something extraordinary, since you have not yet attained it, why do you grant me permission? Have you not heard it said:

"Even if one were to shatter the Great Tang Empire, one could not find a single person who has not attained [enlightenment]"? The aforementioned venerable masters have each revealed their own unique insights regarding the message that all phenomena are non-phenomena;
they have each displayed their own hands and eyes. It is certainly not the case that they are not the Tathāgata face-to-face.
One is able to exercise such mastery.
○ Second, regarding the severance of both cause and effect, there is deep lack of faith and doubt.
This doubt arises from the two preceding sections of the sutra: "practice giving while abiding in the non-abiding" and "not seeing the Buddha through signs. There is no [other source].

Abiding in and practicing the giving [of the Dharma] is profound in its cause. Perceiving the Buddha through signlessness is profound in its fruit. Only those like me, who have received it directly, are able to comprehend and awaken to it.
How can those of dull faculties in the final age believe and accept it? If they do not believe and accept it, will this not be a case of empty preaching?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, is there any sentient being who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, will give rise to true faith?
The Buddha told Subhūti, “Do not speak thus. After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit;
they will be able to give rise to faith in these phrases and regard them as true.”
Master Fu’s verse says: The cause is profound, and the fruit is likewise profound; The principle is subtle and esoteric, difficult to fathom.
In the future age of the Dharma-ending period, I fear only that the Dharma will sink. Though emptiness arises, my feelings have not yet reached it; Hearing its meaning, I fear I cannot bear it.
If one can believe in this Dharma, One is surely a person of awakened mind.
It should be known that such persons have not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;
rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas.

Subhūti, when these beings hear these phrases and give rise to pure faith for even a single moment, the Tathāgata knows them all and sees them all. These sentient beings shall obtain such immeasurable [merit].
Regarding merit, Master Fudai composed a verse: "A single thought born from the faculty of faith, all Buddhas can fully know. The cause was produced on this very day;

the fruit shall be realized in the future. Throughout three great kalpas and many eons, the six perfections were long practiced and bestowed. Through this perfuming, the unconditioned [Dharmakaya] is formed."
The seeds of outflows are then termed "inconceivable.
Why is this? These sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a being, or the notion of a life-span.
They possess neither the notion of phenomena nor the notion of non-phenomena. Why is this? If these sentient beings were to take up signs with their minds, they would immediately become...

To cling to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; or if one grasps at the characteristics of dharmas, that is likewise clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Why is this? If one grasps at the characteristics of non-dharmas, that too is clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Master Fu’s verse says: “Sentient beings are empty, and phenomena are also empty; these two aspects are fundamentally the same. The parikalpita (imagined) nature is false discrimination;
the paratantra (dependent) nature is obstructed and does not penetrate. The pariniṣpanna (perfected) nature sinks into the ocean of consciousness, wandering like a tumbleweed in saṃsāra.
If you wish to know the place of non-arising, cut off all traces of activity outside the mind.”
Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas.
Master Fu’s verse says: Because there is a cause, there is the name "non-existence"; Where there is no mark, there is the pursuit of fame. Existence and non-existence have no distinct essence;

Non-existence has existence, yet existence has no form. Existence and non-existence lack self-nature; Delusively, the sentiments of existence and non-existence arise. Existence and non-existence are like...
Like an echo in a valley, there is no sound of existence or non-existence.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said: "O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft."
"Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas.
Master Fu’s verse says: "To cross a river one must use a raft; Upon reaching the shore, the boat is no longer needed.

When one knows that both person and dharmas are without self, Awakening to this principle, why labor over the trap? If one is still drowned in the middle of the stream, Who will discuss being on either side? Existence and non-existence are like..."
If you grasp at one [aspect], your mind-field will immediately be defiled.
It is said: "This passage of scripture encapsulates the essential purport of the entire sutra; therefore, Master Fu (Bodhidharma’s successor) commented upon it in great detail.

This sutra takes non-characteristic (*animitta*) as its essence (*tattva*) and non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*) as its principle (*siddhānta*). Since its essence is non-characteristic, it cannot be grasped by the intellect."
One should contemplate this. Because it is non-abiding, it cannot be fathomed through the attachment of the deluded mind. An ancient master said:
"Just as a silkworm can alight anywhere except upon a flame, the minds of sentient beings can take as their objects anything whatsoever."
It alone cannot take *prajñā* as its object; this is why it is profoundly deep. What is meant by "signless" (*animitta*)?
It means there is no sign of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*) and no sign of a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātman*). What is meant by "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*)?
It means not abiding in signs, not abiding in phenomena (*dharma*), and not abiding in non-phenomena (*adharma*). Why is signlessness the fruit? Why is non-abiding...
This is taken as the cause. The Dharma-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it does not fall into any numerical categories and is originally without marks (*animitta*).
It is only because the mind dwells upon something that one fails to attain the perfection of this markless essence.

Therefore, the means by which all that possesses marks is gathered back into the markless lies in the wisdom of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). As stated in the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*: "If one emerges from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and realizes nirvāṇa..."
The realms, the fruits of the desirable and the undesirable, and the causes of the dharmas and the non-dharmas—all these are to be relinquished.

Even though they are correct causes and correct fruits, they are still included among what is to be relinquished; this profound Prajñāpāramitā is the most difficult of all teachings to believe. The *Kanding ji* states:
At first, when Subhūti heard these profound passages concerning both cause and effect, he was filled with immeasurable joy and gratitude.
Previously, he had only known the signless (*animitta*), yet he did not know the profound fruit that is sign-lessness within signs;

previously, he had only known eternal abiding, yet he did not know the profound cause that is abiding while being non-abiding. Even during the time of the Buddha, there were those who found it difficult to believe in such profundity.

Regarding the Dharma, one does not know whether, in the present or the future, there might be sentient beings who, upon hearing these phrases, give rise to true faith, thinking that such a thing truly exists.
To dispel this doubt, the Buddha rebuked and exhorted him, saying:
"Do not speak thus. All sentient beings possess buddha-nature; how could it be said that they do not give rise to faith upon hearing the Dharma?"
There will be no one [to uphold the Dharma]. It is as if after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the five periods of five hundred years:
in the first five hundred years, liberation will be firm; in the second five hundred years, meditative concentration will be firm;
in the third five hundred years, learning will be firm; in the fourth five hundred years, stūpas and monasteries will be firm; and in the final five hundred years, contention will be firm. This is...

When the power of the teachings gradually declines and the True Dharma is about to perish, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, who are fully endowed with ethical discipline and meditative concentration, and who are able to give rise to wisdom and awakening.
Taking this as reality, they will correctly understand the profound meaning of cause and effect, free from the delusion of inversion.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "The profound meaning of cause and effect was taught for the sake of later [generations]..."
In this degenerate age, it is because they are not empty that they possess reality. A bodhisattva is fully endowed with the three virtues;
if one lacked the three virtues of precept, concentration, and wisdom, who could take this as real and give rise to faith?

One should know that such a person has long served virtuous friends under many Buddhas and has habitually heard the True Dharma; thus, their conditions are superior. They have planted various roots of goodness, and the three poisons have long been...
I prostrate. When the six perfections increase, the causes are superior. Only when both causes and conditions are superior does genuine faith arise.
Thus we know that genuine faith is truly not easy to obtain. It is not merely a matter of hearing these words and phrases;

rather, it is to have genuine faith that all Buddhas are fundamentally pure and that all sentient beings will ultimately attain the Buddha-way, even to the point of conceiving a single thought of pure faith in this sutra.
This is the cause of all Buddhas; this is the fruit of all Buddhas.
Those who believe in this sutra in such a manner shall obtain immeasurable merit, as vast as the empty space of the ten directions, beyond all calculation. Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke in verse:

"Having cultivated precepts in the past, And having planted various roots of goodness, The Tathāgata, whose precepts are complete among all Buddhas, Also declares his merits to be fulfilled. The Tathāgata, regarding...
They all know and see [these things]. Ordinary persons know through inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*) and see with the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*);
therefore, there are things they do not know and do not see. The Tathāgata knows at the very moment of seeing; he does not know through inferential cognition.
He sees at the very moment of knowing; he does not see as the fleshly eye does. Therefore, there is nothing he does not know and nothing he does not see. As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse:
The Buddha does not know this by perceiving its fruit; rather, he perceives it directly through the power of his wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).

One who seeks offerings and honor cannot explain [this matter]. There are two ways in which merit is acquired: namely, acquisition through birth (*upapattilabdha*) and acquisition through effort (*pratilambhika*).

"Birth" refers to those who, while correctly practicing meritorious deeds, are able to produce wholesome causes—that is, those who possess faith, understanding, retention, and exposition. "Effort" refers to the seeds currently being perfumed, which will subsequently bring about results.
This is the resulting retribution. These various offerings and respects cannot be known by inferential wisdom (*anumāna-jñāna*), nor can they be seen with the physical eye;
therefore it is said that such a person cannot describe them. For what reason does one who believes in the sutra obtain such immeasurable merit?

It is because these sentient beings uphold and expound [the teaching] in this way, cultivate and practice it in this way, and are no longer subject to the notions of "self" (*ātman*) or "person" (*pudgala*).

Sentient beings possess the marks of a life-span and a self. Having already attained the wisdom of the non-self of persons, they no longer cling to the marks of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), nor do they cling to the marks of unconditioned non-phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-adharma*). Having attained the wisdom of the non-self of dharmas, both person and dharma are empty;
their measure is equal to the great void. Therefore, their merit is immeasurable. As for the four marks, they are indeed called "marks."
Indeed, dharma and non-dharma belong to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Why, then, are they also called "characteristics" (*nimitta*)?

That which is conceptually discriminated does not exist apart from the characteristics of "self" and "what belongs to self" (*ātma-ātmīya-nimitta*); it is based on these that one gives rise to the notions of dharma and non-dharma.

One does not give rise to such discrimination regarding things like inanimate matter or wood, which are devoid of self. As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "Those [notions of] a living being and dharmas are far removed..."

Regarding the grasping of signs, it is also said that one knows those signs by means of eight distinct categories of meaning. These consist of the four signs of the selfhood of persons (*pudgala-ātman*) and the four signs of the selfhood of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*), which together constitute the eight meanings.
Briefly stated, there are levels of depth; wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to know these eight meanings while remaining detached from signs, and this is what is meant by being "endowed with wisdom.
For example, just as one might grasp the various distinctions among one's own five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a self, so too does one conceptualize the aggregates [as such].
Having already passed away, one again takes birth among the various realms as a human being.

To reckon the continuous flow and uninterrupted succession of the aggregates (*skandha*) as a "sentient being" (*sattva*), and to reckon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of a single lifetime as eternally abiding as a "life-principle" (*jīva*), are the coarse characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in which ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) cling.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "The substance of differentiated continuity, Uninterrupted until the end of life, remains. Furthermore...
This refers to the four kinds of self-characteristics that lead one toward heterodox paths. If these four characteristics are eliminated, they may be removed by eliminating their very marks.
Why, then, would one not abide in neither phenomena nor non-phenomena?
If the mind grasps at the marks of form, it becomes attached to the objects of the five sensory realms; with this as its cause, it clings to the illusory substance of the aggregates.

The four characteristics. If the mind grasps conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and seeks the mind apart from its objects, taking this as a cause, one then becomes attached to the four characteristics of correct awakening and clear realization.

Observing by analogy: if the mind grasps unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), wherein all phenomena are empty, taking this as a cause, one then becomes attached to the four characteristics of abandoning and concealing the dharma-grasping. How can these be described?
Is it the signless Dharma-body? Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verse says: "All things are empty and without substance; their actual existence is ineffable.
It is by relying on words and phrases that they are spoken of; these are the four kinds of dharmic characteristics. This refers precisely to this.

"All things are empty" refers to the insight into the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena (*pudgala-śūnyatā* and *dharma-śūnyatā*). When both person and phenomenon are empty, there is no discrimination at all; this is "actual existence."

It is ineffable. Although it is ineffable, it is not a dull void; rather, it is spoken of by relying upon the terminology of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is itself the Middle Way Truth (*madhyamā-satya*).
If one has attachment or dwelling toward this [ineffability], one does not depart from the two grasps of the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*);
consequently, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) sinks into the ocean of consciousness, and one is unable to realize the fruit of signlessness (*animitta-phala*).
Therefore, those who cultivate the true cause of unsurpassed bodhi should not grasp at dharmas, nor abide in the dharmas of saṃsāra.
They should not grasp at non-dharmas, nor abide in the dharmas of nirvāṇa. By not abiding in these two extremes, one returns to the Middle Way;
yet even this ultimate Middle Way should not be clung to or adhered to. As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse:

Those people give rise to faith and, out of reverence, give rise to the perception of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). They do not grasp the sound incorrectly; they grasp what is correctly taught in this way.

What is the meaning of this? It means that those who give rise to pure faith in the Prajñā for even a single moment do not grasp the meaning according to the literal expression (*yathāruta*), but rather accord with the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*), because its meaning is non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*). Thus, the Tathāgata has always said to you:

Monks, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft. Just as one who wishes to cross a river must first take up a raft, yet once they have reached the other shore, they should leave it behind;
so too, those who wish to cross the great torrent of afflictions should cultivate all wholesome dharmas.
Once one has already ascended to the shore of *nirvāṇa*, even the Dharma should be relinquished.

Since even wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) should not be grasped—because the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is signless (*animitta*)—how much more so unwholesome and non-Dharmic states, which lie outside of the true mark?
Because all dharmas characterized by existence or non-existence are non-Dharmas, they should not be grasped. As the Bodhisattva Maitreya said in verse: "He does not..."
Abiding in accordance with the teachings, one realizes wisdom within the Dharma. Just as a person abandons a boat or raft, so it is with the meaning within the Dharma.
That realized wisdom does not originally abide within the teachings that accord with practice;
yet for one who has not yet realized it, wisdom must be realized within those teachings that accord with practice, for they are like a raft that can be relied upon and then abandoned. Nevertheless...
If that is so, why should one also abandon the *prajñā* of words? It is for the sake of eliminating the subtle attachments of those who believe in the sutras.
Previously, it was stated that through the purity of faith one obtains immeasurable merit; this is not an incorrect cause leading to an incorrect result.

However, if these subtle attachments are not eliminated, they will ultimately become an obstacle to the Holy Path. Therefore, one must be able to transcend the sutra within the sutra, and transcend the Dharma within the Dharma.
To depart from dharmas is merely to eliminate their disease, not to eliminate their substance; this is the excellent and profound purport of Prajñāpāramitā. A monk asked Tong’an:
“To interpret the meaning based on the scriptures is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three ages; to depart from even a single word of the scriptures is to speak like a demon.
What is the principle behind this? Tong’an said: “A solitary peak rises in sublime beauty, unclad by misty vines; a sliver of the moon—”
Spanning the void, the white clouds are naturally distinct. Danxia’s verse says: The clouds fly high on their own, the waters flow on their own;
The sea and sky are vast and wide, as the empty boat drifts. At nightfall, it does not seek lodging in the reed coves; It stands far beyond both the middle and the two ends.
This single phrase, "standing apart from both the middle and the two extremes," fully encompasses the profound meaning of Prajñā.
Master Fu’s verse, which states, "Even in the middle flow, one may still be drowned," precisely means that even Prajñā should be relinquished. How profound!
Regarding the third [point], the severance of the signless (*animitta*):
how can one speak of attaining it? This doubt arises from the first doubt, which holds that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of bodily marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
It was previously stated that the Buddha’s body is signless. If one realizes the signless, both dharma and non-dharma are abandoned; thus, there is no longer any conjunction.

There is that which is attained and that which is taught. For what reason does the World-Honored One, through the awakening to reality by means of the right knowledge associated with a single thought-moment, speak concerning all phenomena?
Some say that speaking itself falls within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); how then can it be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti replied, “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma named anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata could [attain].”
[The Buddha] said: "Why is this? All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Master Fu composed a verse on this: "Bodhi transcends verbal expression; From the beginning, no one has attained it. One must rely upon the two kinds of emptiness."
In principle, one shall realize the body of the Dharma King. Where there is mind, all is delusion; freedom from attachment is called the True.
If one awakens to that which is neither dharma nor non-dharma, one wanders at ease beyond the six sense objects.
Why is this so? Because all noble ones and sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Master Fu’s verse says: "Both persons and dharmas are called attachments; To realize them is the two kinds of unconditioned.

Bodhisattvas can realize both equally; Śrāvakas abandon one but not the other. When the objects of knowledge and afflictions are exhausted, There is nothing to rely upon within emptiness. They are always able to act..."
"This contemplation will undoubtedly lead to noble concentration.

Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? This merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is someone who receives and upholds even as little as a four-line verse from this sutra and explains it to others, their merit shall surpass the former.
Why is this? Subhūti, all Buddhas and the unsurpassed... [of all Buddhas]... arise from this Dharma.]
The Dharma of *samyaksambodhi* all issues from this sutra. Subhūti, what are called the Buddha-dharmas are, in truth, not Buddha-dharmas.

Master Fu’s verse says: Even if one fills the three thousandfold world-system with jewels and offers them as a field of merit, One will only accomplish out-flowing karma and ultimately remain within the realms of humans and devas.
But by upholding even four lines of this sutra, one creates a virtuous affinity with the Sages;
To enter the ocean of non-conditioned reality, one must board the ship of Prajñā.
Tong said: "The Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma of non-abiding is truly inconceivable. When discussing the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is nothing at all to be attained.
Nevertheless, for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings, it does not hinder the manifestation of various forms and sounds.
All who see or hear them obtain benefit; yet in truth, regarding the nature of all phenomena, it is free from all conceptual discrimination."
It is not attained through mental application; attainment itself is non-attainment. It is not explained through verbal expression; explanation itself is non-explanation.

This is the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-satya). Although Wuxing merely clarified matters pertaining to the dharma-body (dharmakāya), he stated that the Tathāgata has neither attainment nor explanation, and that all worthies and sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
The World-Honored One, however, pointed directly to the dharma-body.
Regarding the matter of transcending [the mundane]: it is not that all Buddhas do not arise from this, nor that the Dharma of unsurpassed Bodhi does not emerge from this.
However, what are called "Buddha" and "Dharma" are in fact neither Buddha nor Dharma, for they are entirely unattainable.
If there are those who can believe in and accept such a wondrous Dharma, their merit is truly immeasurable. The *Kanding ji* states:
The Buddha asked Subhūti: "In your mind, what do you think? Do you say that I have attained bodhi, or that I have not attained it?
Do you say that I have preached the Dharma, or that I have not preached it? Subhūti had exclusively understood emptiness;
how could he not know that there are three kinds of Buddhas: first, the Dharmakāya Buddha; second, the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha; and third, the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha?
The World-Honored One of the present is a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This has never been one who attained awakening, nor does he preach the Dharma to save sentient beings.
Therefore, there is no fixed dharma called "attaining bodhi," nor is there any fixed dharma that a Tathāgata can preach.
Why is this? Because the unsurpassed dharma of bodhi preached by the Tathāgata cannot be heard with the ears. It is not...

Because it can be apprehended, yet it cannot be proclaimed by the mouth; because it is ineffable. If one wishes to say it exists, it has no form and no name, for all dharmas lack substantial reality and characteristics;
fundamentally, it has never existed. Therefore, it is called "not-dharma" (*adharma*).

If one wishes to say it does not exist, then the Sages rely upon it for their spiritual power, for True Suchness (*tathatā*) truly exists as being devoid of the mark of self (*anātman-lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, it has never...
It is non-existent. Therefore it is said that it is neither dharma nor non-dharma. To take it as dharma is again not dharma; to take it as non-dharma is again not non-dharma.
Since the speaker does not speak dualistically, the listener likewise does not grasp dualistically.
Thus, it is said that the Tathāgata has neither attainment nor teaching. Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verse says: "The manifested transformation is not the true Buddha, nor is it..."
Regarding the one who preaches the Dharma: they preach the Dharma without dualistic grasping. There is no preaching, for it is free from the characteristics of words.

"Without dualistic grasping" means not grasping at either dharma or non-dharma. How could this be true only of the Tathāgata? All worthy sages (ārya) derive their names from the purity of the *tathatā*-dharma;
all are this unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma. Since the unconditioned is fundamentally devoid of any activity, it is therefore not...
One perceives its existence but does not perceive its non-existence. Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is beyond differentiation, it cannot be grasped and cannot be described.
Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is far removed from the characteristics of language, for it is not an object that can be expressed.
Only the wise partially realize this principle and partially attain purity; the noble ones (*ārya*) fully realize this principle and possess complete purity.
They are all purified by practicing and realizing this Dharma of Bodhi; it is only that there are differences in their resultant stages.
It is like elephants, horses, and rabbits crossing the same river: while there are differences in their ability to cross, there is no distinction in what they have crossed.

The World-Honored One did not establish a formal thesis regarding all unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), fearing that people, upon hearing that these dharmas are unconditioned, might think they cannot be grasped.
[He] spoke thus, intending to utterly disparage and abolish [the teaching], saying: "The Tathāgatas would have no source from which they arise;
supreme enlightenment would have no means by which it is realized. Would not that which is called the Buddha-dharma fall into emptiness?
Thereupon, he compared the merit of upholding this sutra and questioned Subhūti: "What do you think? If a person were to use gold, silver, lapis lazuli..."
Crystal, coral, agate, red pearls, and glass—these seven treasures fill the trichiliocosm.
From the small chiliocosm to the medium chiliocosm, and from the medium chiliocosm to the great chiliocosm, there are ten billion suns and moons and ten billion sets of four continents.
One takes such treasures as these and uses them for giving; such are the preciousness and abundance of these jewels. Thus they are distributed.
If one were to give such extensive gifts as these, would the resulting merit and reward not be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very much.
"For what reason do you say it is so much? [The Buddha said: "The merit from giving away such vast treasures is merely the merit of material things;
it cannot sustain the burden of bodhi, for it is not the seed-nature of the merit of *prajñā*. If one practices in reliance upon *prajñā*..."
Practice so that one’s own nature does not fall into the various realms of existence; this is called the nature of merit (*puṇya*).

To shoulder the Tathāgata upon one’s shoulders, with a nature that pervades the entire *sāhasra-lokadhātu*, the accumulation of such merit is likewise like this; this is merit according to principle (*yukti-puṇya*). It cannot be described as merit or non-merit.

Since merit does not exist [in an ultimate sense], there is no basis for speaking of its abundance. That which exists conventionally (*saṃvṛti*) possesses characteristics and is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); it can...
Regarding "merit": because there is merit, one may also say it is "great. For this reason, the Tathāgata said that the merit is great.

The Buddha then confirmed this, saying: "It is as you have said. Furthermore, if there is someone who, regarding these verses of the Prajñāpāramitā, believes, accepts, upholds, and recites them—this benefits oneself—and explains them for others—this benefits others—whether in their entirety or not..."
Maintaining this from beginning to end—even down to the recitation of a single four-line verse—one does not depart from the self-nature of Prajñā as one's merit.
This merit surpasses that of giving away jewels; it is immeasurable and boundless, beyond the reach of the mind.
As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "To receive, uphold, and explain the Dharma is not in vain in terms of meritorious virtue."
Merit does not lead to Bodhi; two things can lead to Bodhi. These two are precisely upholding and explaining. Regarding the four-line verse, there is no single interpretation.
Some say it refers to the four lines on the mark of non-self (*anātman*). Some say it refers to the four lines beginning with "Whatever marks exist.
Some say it refers to the four lines beginning with "If one sees me by means of form" and "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Or else, [some] take a single...
There are two lines, three lines, and up to four lines; for example, the Sixth Patriarch took the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as consisting of four lines.

While these various explanations are not uniform, if one simply uses the Buddha’s words to seal whatever is spoken with the four-line formula, then all are four lines, all can be upheld and recited, and there will be no room for dispute. For what reason should they be upheld?
Is it because this sutra is superior to the gift of material wealth? It is because unsurpassed bodhi emerges from this sutra.
Its fundamental, true principle is neither born nor extinguished; when shrouded by afflictions, it is hidden, but when realized through wisdom, it is revealed.
By upholding and expounding this Dharma, wondrous wisdom manifests spontaneously and the Bodhi-Dharmakāya appears; this is called the "cause of realization" (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*).
It is because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are born from this sūtra. The retributive and transformation bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) are fundamentally non-existent.
By upholding and expounding this Dharma, others receive their retribution, adorning their bodies with boundless forms and colors, and traveling throughout the lands of the ten directions.
It is unimpeded; this is called the cause of arising. Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "Regarding the truth, it is the cause of realization, and it is also the cause of other arisings.
The merit of upholding the sutra can thus accomplish all the Buddha-dharmas of enlightenment."

How could the worldly merits of outflows ever compare with this? Furthermore, if one becomes attached to the merit of upholding the sutra and perceives the Buddha’s Dharma-body as something manifest, or perceives it as having a fixed nature, one has not yet awakened to the Dharma; instead, one merely increases one's own obstacles.
Therefore, he further declares: "That which is called the Buddha and the Dharma is not the Buddha and the Dharma. To speak of the Buddha and the Dharma is merely a provisional designation.

They exist from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet they are not the Buddha or the Dharma. From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they do not exist at all.

This means that within the characteristics of conventional truth, there are distinctions between delusion and awakening, defilement and purity, and ordinary beings and sages; therefore, it is said that the Buddha and the Dharma emerge from the scriptures.

However, the principle of ultimate truth is free from the characteristics of delusion and awakening, defilement and purity, and ordinary beings and sages; ultimately, there is no Buddha or Dharma to be found.
It is so. Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verse says: "Only the Buddha-dharma achieves the foremost essence of merit.

When one discusses the Buddha and the Dharma, there is no worldly merit that can be compared to them. Yet, when viewed from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), nothing exists at all;
this is what is meant by "achieving the foremost essence of merit. In sum, it is neither graspable nor expressible.
To take these dharmas and reduce them to non-action (*wuwei*) seems to fall into a one-sided emptiness.

It is better to regard what is Buddhist and what is not as the Middle Way Truth (*madhyamā-satya*), wherein they do not lose their nature. To abide while having no abiding, and to have no abiding while abiding—is this not the most subtle, the most subtle?
Formerly, Xuefeng asked Deshan: "Regarding the ancestral vehicle of the past, does a student..."
Deshan struck him with a staff and asked, "What do you say? Feng said, "I do not understand. The next day, Feng requested further instruction.
Deshan said, "In my school there are no words or phrases; in truth, there is not a single dharma to give to anyone. Because of this, Feng attained realization.
When Yantou heard of this, he remarked, "The old man Deshan has a backbone as hard as iron; it cannot be bent."
Nevertheless, even so, within the gate of proclaiming the teaching, there still remains a slight discrepancy.
Fayan said, "Those who realize the stage of Buddhahood are called those who uphold this sutra.
The sutra states, "All Buddhas, as well as the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma of all Buddhas, all emerge from this sutra. Now tell me, what do you call "this sutra"?
"Is it not these yellow scrolls and red axes? Do not mistake the zero point on the scale.
Furthermore, a monk asked Shoushan, "All Buddhas emerge from this sutra; what is this sutra? Shoushan said, "Lower your voice, lower your voice.
The monk asked, "How does one uphold it? Shoushan said, "Without defilement. Tiantong Zongjue’s verse says: "Water..."
Clouds arise from Mount Kunlun; the fisherman and the woodcutter are ignorant of their origin.

They know only the vastness of the surging waves and the mountain crags, yet they refuse to cast their lines or abandon the sound of their axes. If they could cast their lines and abandon their axes, they would directly exhaust the path that leads upward.
Then the water would emerge from oneself and the clouds would rise from oneself; what need would there be for attachment to language and writing?
How defiled! ○ Fourth, the severing of the śrāvaka’s attainment of fruition is grasping;
this doubt arises from what was previously called "the Buddha-dharma is not the Buddha-dharma. — Vasubandhu Bodhisattva’s Commentary.

It is said: Previously it was stated that the Sage is designated by the name "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) because of this principle; therefore, those dharmas cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed.
If the noble ones, such as the *srotāpanna* and others, were to grasp their own respective fruits, how could it be said that those dharmas cannot be grasped?
Since they are realized and explained in such a manner, how can they be established as inexpressible? To dispel this doubt, [the following] is established:
The Dharma cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken.
Thus, a sutra says: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna have the thought: 'I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna'?
Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A srotāpanna is called one who has entered the stream, yet..."
There is no entering. One does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena;
this is called a *srotāpanna*. Subhūti, what do you think? Does a *sakṛdāgāmin* have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin*"?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A *sakṛdāgāmin* is so named because they return once more, yet in reality there is no coming and going."
"This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? An Anāgāmin is so named because he does not return;
yet in reality there is no such thing as 'not returning. For this reason, he is called an Anāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think?"
"How so? Can an Arhat have this thought: 'I have attained the path of Arhatship'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma that is called 'Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have this thought, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' he would thereby be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span."
"World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention and am foremost among men;
I am a foremost Arhat who is free from desire. World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought as 'I am an Arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One, if I were to harbor such a thought as 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti delights in [the emptiness of] dharmas."
The practitioner of *araṇā* (the state of non-conflict) is Subhūti, for in reality he practices nothing at all; yet he is named Subhūti, the one who delights in the practice of *araṇā*.
Master Fu’s verse on the first three fruits says: "Having abandoned the mundane and first entered the holy, afflictions gradually become light and subtle. [He] severs..."

Having eliminated the grasping at a self among persons, one first reaches the unconditioned. Regarding the perception of objects and the view of a personal body, it is only now that one knows them to be false.
After seven returns among humans and devas, one proceeds toward quiescence, unaware of the way back.
Furthermore, the verse on the fourth fruit says: Without birth, there is no extinction; No self, and likewise no person. The obstacles of affliction are forever eliminated;
One bids eternal farewell to future existence. When objects vanish, the mind also ceases; No longer do greed or hatred arise.
Without compassion, yet possessing wisdom within emptiness, One dwells in solitary tranquility, abiding alone in the Real.
Subhūti said: "The previous statement that 'the dharma of non-action is neither to be grasped nor to be spoken' was Subhūti’s own words.
Why, then, do you harbor doubt regarding your own speech? For what the Buddha calls 'Buddha-dharma' is precisely not Buddha-dharma."
This directly refutes their [view of] unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). They seek to obliterate all phenomena and return to non-existence;
the Buddha, however, manifests the arising of all phenomena without perceiving them as having existence—even unconditioned phenomena are not perceived as having existence.
Therefore, Subhūti suspects that if even unconditioned phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), then all noble and holy ones (*ārya*)—such as the four [types of fruits]...
The fruits of the śrāvakas and others are each distinct and each has that which is attained. How is it that, having already attained a fruit, it is yet not a fruit?

The Buddha questioned him regarding the existence or non-existence of the four fruits because, although the fruits have never been non-existent, he did not personally realize them; thus, he saw no fruit as something to be attained.
Therefore, the Buddha interrogated him with the presence or absence of the four fruits. He himself realized that, fundamentally, he had not formed such a thought.
Since no such thought is produced, what marks of fruit could there be?

Thus one gains faith that what the Tathāgata has taught—that which is the Buddha-dharma and that which is not the Buddha-dharma—is truly the wondrous Dharma of non-abiding. The subsequent text tests this by asking whether the Tathāgata has any dharma he has attained;
thereby one knows that in reality nothing is attained. It further tests this by asking whether a Bodhisattva adorns Buddha-lands.
[The Buddha] said: "Know that this is truly not adornment. Therefore, the Buddha confirmed it, saying: "One should give rise to a pure mind in this way;
one should give rise to that mind without abiding anywhere. This does not mean that by abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one may thereby constitute the dharma of the worthy and holy ones.
The *Kanding ji* says: "What do you think? Do you suppose that a person who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna* would harbor such a thought?"
"Does one attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*? He replied, "No. "If that is so, by what meaning is one named a *srotāpanna*? [The Buddha said:
"Because, from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one enters the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*) while the mind has no attainment."
What is meant by "non-attainment"? It is because there is no grasping toward the objects of the six sense-fields, such as form and the rest.

If one grasps at the six sense-fields, one enters the stream of ordinary beings and goes against the stream of the sages. Only by not grasping or clinging does one enter the stream of the sages and go against the stream of ordinary beings.
Therefore, one is called a *srotāpanna*. Among the four fruits, the first constitutes the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); the next two constitute the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*);

and the last is that of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the first, the Path of Seeing: it refers to the sixteen moments of mind (*ṣoḍaśa-citta*), which sever the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*)—the coarse afflictions of discrimination—underlying the Four Truths of the three realms.
What are these sixteen moments? They refer to one moment of Patience (*kṣānti*) for each of the Four Truths of the Desire Realm.

One wisdom (*jñāna*) brings about eight moments of mind. Furthermore, by combining the two upper realms into one set of four truths (*catuḥ-satya*), and observing them as being abandoned in the same manner as the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there likewise arise one patience (*kṣānti*) and one wisdom for each, thus forming eight moments of mind; these constitute the sixteen moments of mind.

Patience is the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*), which is the time when delusions are correctly severed. Wisdom is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which is the time when the severance is finalized. As it is said:

The receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*)—and so on, up to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).

From the first moment until the fifteenth moment of mind, which is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path, one is called a candidate for the first fruit (*prathama-phala-pratipannaka*). Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), one is said to have realized the first fruit. This refers to a person.
There are two distinctions among the gods. [The first is] "at most seven returns. Why seven births? Because of the remaining seven fetters (*saṃyojana*).
What are these seven fetters? They are: greed, hatred, and delusion of the desire realm; and craving, restlessness, pride, and ignorance of the form and formless realms.

Among these, one further abandons the four afflictions of the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), namely: greed, hatred, delusion, and pride. These are the subtle innate [afflictions].

Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) that arise spontaneously: because they are difficult to sever, they are divided into nine grades, namely from the "upper-of-the-upper" (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) down to the "lower-of-the-lower" (*mṛdu-mṛdu*).

These nine grades of affliction are severed by those who have attained the second or third fruits. When one has severed up to five grades, one is called a "candidate for the second fruit" (*dvitīya-phala-pratipannaka*).

When the six grades are completely severed, one is called the "second fruit" (*dvitīya-phala*). Within the stage of the candidate for the second fruit, there are two types of "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*), namely those among the gods...

Regarding "those who go from family to family among gods and humans": those who go from family to family among gods are said to transmigrate through one, two, or three families within the celestial realm before attaining parinirvāṇa.
Those who go from family to family among humans are said to do so within this continent [of Jambudvīpa].
Alternatively, they may pass away through transmigration among various families within other regions and attain parinirvāṇa.

Having already exhausted six births, with only one birth remaining, they must therefore go once to the heavens and return once more to the human realm to take birth and sever their remaining afflictions.
In this sequence, one further abandons two grades [of afflictions] and, with one birth remaining as an interval, shall attain parinirvāṇa;

this is termed the candidate for the third fruit. When the nine grades are permanently abandoned, it is called the third fruit. One will no longer return to be born in the desire realm, having severed all entanglements;
thus, there is no returning. This is precisely the eight unconditioned [attainments] of the path of seeing, followed by the nine [grades] of the path of cultivation.

The ninth category of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) serves as the essence of this fruit. When these two or three fruits are attained, the person’s abandonment of afflictions is like cutting wood across its grain.

Likewise, when one abandons the desires of the first dhyāna stage up to the ninth category of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), at the moment of the path of immediate succession (ānantaryamārga), one is called an Arhat-designate (arhattvapratipannaka). This path of immediate succession is also termed the "Vajra-like [Samādhi]."

The simile for concentration: because it can permanently destroy the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of all afflictions up until the path of liberation, it is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).
Since it arises simultaneously with the attainment of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-prāpti*), one is thus said to abide in the fruit of Arhatship.

In total, the eighty-nine categories of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) constitute the essence of this fruit. Regarding the phrase "non-arising," it means: "My births are exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been lived."

He stands firm; his task is accomplished; he shall not undergo further existence. Now, the first three phrases constitute the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), while the final phrase constitutes the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*.
This means that one will no longer receive a body of suffering within the three realms.

Since worldly causes have perished and their fruits have been lost, the supramundane cause has been realized and its fruit attained; thus, one should perform deeds for the benefit of oneself and others.
Therefore, they should be venerated by all humans and devas who possess attachment. Thus, these four types of persons do not harbor the thought, "I have attained the fruit.
Why is this? Because at the time of realization, there is nothing to be attained.
As it is said: "In truth, there is no dharma named 'stream-enterer,' ... up to ... in truth, there is no dharma named 'arhat. Why?
Therefore, does the thought of attaining the fruit not arise? If such a thought were to arise, there would be grasping at a self and so forth, and one would be no different from an ordinary person.

Those who have attained the four fruits are all free from the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); because they lack that grasping, once the mind of grasping is absent, realization itself is non-realization.
Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke in verse: "It cannot be grasped nor can it be described, for its own fruit is not grasped. In former times, the Buddha said of himself:
"I have attained this *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-contention). I do not afflict sentient beings, for I am able to cause them not to give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*).
If someone dislikes him standing, he will instead sit; he even avoids going to the homes of the poor.

He begs for alms solely to avoid causing distress to others. As for those who are foremost among men, each of the great disciples possesses a particular excellence and is thus acclaimed as "foremost," such as Kāśyapa, foremost in ascetic practices (dhūta), and Ānanda, foremost in erudition (bahuśruta).
Subhūti is foremost in the absence of contention (araṇā); among all Arhats free from desire, he is called the foremost.
Although the Buddha praised me, at that time I did not have such a thought.
Had I, at that moment, thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship and practice in non-contention," I would not have realized immediate emptiness.

Why then did the Tathāgata praise me, saying I am foremost? He said I am foremost because I realize immediate emptiness; for this reason, I am called one who delights in supreme tranquility. Because of this...
Bodhi does not form such thoughts; truly, there is nothing practiced. Therefore, the Buddha praised me as foremost in the absence of strife (*araṇā*).
"Absence of strife" means being free from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and free from the obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhivaraṇa*).

Because one attains arhatship by being free from the obstacle of afflictions, and because one attains the absence of strife by being free from the obstacle to meditative concentration. As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "Relying on..."
That Subhūti speaks of being free from the two kinds of hindrances. Subhūti abides in this samādhi; thus, neither hindrances nor disputes accompany him.
Therefore, in accordance with worldly convention, it is called "the practice of non-dispute" (araṇā-vihāra). Yet, in reality, there is no practice at all.

Furthermore, what doubt could there be that attaining the fruit constitutes grasping? This was the World-Honored One’s way of causing him to understand and awaken for himself, silently removing his doubts.
Long ago, when Chan Master Cuiwei Wuxue was making offerings to an Arhat, a monk asked:
"When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why does the Master offer to an Arhat? The Master replied: "Even burning, it is not burning."
