○ Fifth, the refutation of the doubt concerning Śākyamuni’s attainment [of the fruit] under Dīpaṃkara:
this also derives from the third doubt mentioned previously. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* by Guṇaprabha states:

"If those such as the Stream-enterers do not attain their own respective fruits, how is it that the World-Honored One, upon meeting the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)? That Buddha..."
For this reason, the Buddha teaches the Dharma. If it is thus, why is that Dharma ungraspable and unseizable?
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says:
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "What do you think? Did the Tathāgata, when he was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma?
No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained no dharma."
The Verse of Master Fu says: In former times I was called Shanhui; today I am named Nengren.
Observe that conditions are illusory; the essence of consciousness is not real. Dharmatā is neither cause nor effect; according to the principle, it does not arise from causes.
I claim to have received the prediction of Dīpaṃkara; who would know this to be my final birth?

The *Kanding ji* says: "What do you think? When I was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, regarding the words of the prophecy, was there any dharma that was obtained, or was there nothing obtained? He replied: "No.
When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, regarding the words of the prophecy, in reality there was no dharma that was obtained."
It is so. Indeed, that which was spoken by Dīpaṃkara Buddha was merely words; that which Śākyamuni heard was likewise only words.

Words arise from conditions, and conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since that which is expressed by speech does not constitute the realization of the Dharma, how then is it that one receives the prediction?

It is simply because, through one's own non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one realizes the principle of non-differentiation within oneself; thus, wisdom and [the principle]— [...are non-dual. (The text ends here.)
The principle is profound; the object and the spirit meet in union. There is only a single reality, with no further branches or leaves.
How could there be anything to be spoken of or attained? Thus we know that the realized Dharma is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, and therefore cannot be spoken;

the realized Dharma is free from the characteristics of mental objects, and therefore cannot be grasped. As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "Regarding the words of Dīpaṃkara, the Buddha did not grasp them."
In reality, this is wisdom; because it is the true meaning, it establishes that teaching of non-apprehension.
The *Bodhisattvaguṇaprabhāsa-śāstra* states: Furthermore, a sūtra says: "All dharmas that I possess are unapprehendable.
Whether by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or tathāgatas, one cannot apprehend the dharma of realization through speech; it is not that wisdom does not apprehend it. This is what is taught.
This contradicts the sūtras. The sūtras state that the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is not within the sphere of cognition, let alone that of words.
Furthermore, in another sūtra, the Blessed One himself explained how he attained the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and did not grasp at any phenomena.
As that sūtra says: "Sāgaramati, you should know that there are four kinds of bodhisattvas: namely, the bodhisattva who has first resolved [to attain enlightenment], the bodhisattva who practices..."

Bodhisattvas—bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive and bodhisattvas in their final birth before enlightenment—among these, the bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening sees the Tathāgata as a form-body (*rūpakāya*);
the practicing bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata as the accomplishment of merit;
the non-retrogressive bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); and, Sāgaramati, the bodhisattva in his final birth does not see [the Tathāgata] as a form-body.
It is not a vision of the accomplishment of merit; it is not a vision of the Dharma-body. Why is this?
Because that bodhisattva observes with the eye of pure wisdom; he abides in pure wisdom and acts in accordance with pure wisdom.
Pure wisdom is without activity, free from conceptual proliferation, and is no longer a "vision. Why is this? Vision and non-vision are two extremes; [pure wisdom] is far removed from both.
These two extremes are themselves the seeing of the Buddha. If one sees the Buddha, one sees one’s own self.
Seeing the purity of the self, one sees the purity of the Buddha. Seeing the purity of the Buddha, one sees that all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely pure.
Within this, the wisdom that perceives purity is likewise pure; this is called seeing the Buddha. Sāgaramati, it was in this way that I saw Dīpaṃkara.

The Tathāgata, having attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and realized the principle of non-attainment and non-apprehension, at that very moment ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees;
the wisdom of all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) became clearly manifest before him, and he severed all categories of views.
Transcending all conceptualization, distinct conceptualization, and pervasive conceptualization, I did not dwell within the domain of any consciousness.
I attained sixty thousand samādhis, and the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara then bestowed upon me this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Yet that sound of the prediction did not reach my ears, nor was it perceived by any other cognition.

It is not that I am deluded and utterly unconscious; rather, there is nothing to be attained, nor is there the notion of a Buddha, nor the discourse of a prophecy, nor the notion of a prophecy, and so forth, as explained at length.
To say "there is no notion" (*asaṃjñā*) reveals that this is a realization through wisdom, because there is nothing to be grasped.
"Notion" (*saṃjñā*) is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*), not a verbal expression. One should know that this is what is being taught herein.
This is the domain of wisdom; therefore, it is said that one observes with the eye of pure wisdom.

Furthermore, the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) is a mental phenomenon (*citta-dharma*), not a vocal phenomenon (*vāk-dharma*). Furthermore, it is the realization of neither attainment nor non-attainment.
Because phenomena lack intrinsic nature, there is nothing that can be apprehended. Within this principle of non-apprehension, could there be anything to be apprehended?

Since there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended, how could cognition grasp it? Furthermore, by severing the category of views and transcending all conceptualization, one abandons the conceptualization of the category of views.
Wisdom is not speech. Furthermore, it does not abide within the sphere of any consciousness; it neither speaks nor relies upon any linguistic domain.
Therefore, it is without grasping—this is the sphere of wisdom. Why, then, do other teachers claim that [wisdom] is defined by the negation of speech?
In the past, the Venerable Siṃha asked the Venerable Huali: "I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind?
The Patriarch said, "If you wish to seek the Way, do not apply your mind to anything. He asked, "If there is no application of the mind, who performs the Buddha-work?
The Patriarch said, "If you have any application, it is not a meritorious deed. If you have no action, that itself is the Buddha-work."
The Sūtra says: "Regarding the merit I have performed, there is no sense of 'mine'.

Upon hearing these words, Siṃha immediately entered the Buddha-wisdom, and the Patriarch entrusted him with the Dharma-eye. He spoke in verse: "When the nature of mind is recognized, It may be called inconceivable.
When it is clearly understood, nothing can be grasped; When it is attained, one does not speak of knowing. This is non-attainment and non-action—Subhūti..."
Śāriputra also knew this. However, Subhūti is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva who perceives the Dharma-body Tathāgata;
whereas the bodhisattvas described by the Buddha as being in their "one-life-to-enlightenment" stage do not perceive the Dharma-body. This is the reason for their difference.
Therefore, the Buddha revealed it to him with the eye of pure wisdom, saying: "What is called the Buddha-dharma is itself not the Buddha-dharma. Thereupon, he remained silent.
He has realized it for himself; it is truly beyond the scope of ordinary measurement.
○ Sixth, the doubt that the adornment of the land contradicts the principle of non-attachment.
This also derives from the third doubt of the preceding section regarding "that which cannot be grasped. (From the *Puṇyavardhana-bodhisattva-śāstra*).

It is asked: "If wisdom cannot also grasp the qualities of all Buddhas, for what reason does a bodhisattva, by means of wisdom, grasp the merits of a Buddha-field and give rise to vows? To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is that?
To 'adorn a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely called adorning.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form."
When the mind arises in dependence on sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas, one should give rise to that mind without dwelling anywhere.
Master Fu’s verse says: Sweeping away the ground of mind and intellect Is called the cause of the Pure Land.
Regardless of merit or wisdom, First, one must depart from greed and anger. Adornment transcends subject and object; There is neither self nor person. Both annihilationism and eternalism...
Unstained, he emerged from the clamor and dust like a sprouting grain.
Tong said: "Subhūti stated that all worthy sages are distinguished by means of the dharma of non-action (asaṃskṛta-dharma)."

Although one knows that dharmas cannot be grasped—because they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and thus ungraspable—the World-Honored One holds that what is called "Buddha-dharma" is not actually Buddha-dharma;
it is ungraspable and inexpressible, yet it is precisely within this that the Buddha-dharma resides.
Those who merely cling to the dharma of the unconditioned are, in their very clinging to the ungraspable, truly grasping.
Thus, at first one doubts that the four fruits are grasping, yet one believes that their essence is originally free from the thought of attainment;
this is for the four fruits to transcend the four fruits. Subsequently, one doubts that the bestowal of prediction is grasping, yet one believes that in reality there is nothing to be obtained;
this is for the prediction to transcend the prediction. Finally, one doubts that adornment is grasping, yet one believes that it is precisely non-adornment.

This is precisely the adornment that is free from adornment. Furthermore, having doubted that the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) is something grasped, yet believing that the Buddha’s teaching is not a body, this is the Reward Body that is free from the Reward Body.
The four fruits, the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), adornment, and the Reward Body—all these are the Buddha-dharma;
yet they are "not" the Buddha-dharma, pointing directly to the matter that transcends the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Subhūti clings to them.
The Dharma-body exists; therefore, one desires it to abide and desires it to subdue [afflictions], yet one does not realize that non-abiding is itself abiding.
This non-abiding constitutes the fundamental principle of this entire sutra and is taught for those who set forth upon the Supreme Vehicle (Agryayāna).
How could it be easily understood? The *Kanding ji* states: "The World-Honored One, wishing to clarify the true land of the Dharma-nature, therefore raised [this topic]."
When Bodhisattvas perform meritorious deeds and practice the six perfections, they dedicate their merit toward the arousal of the bodhicitta to adorn and purify the Buddha-fields.
Subhūti answered, "No. For what reason? It is because adorning the Buddha-fields by grasping at signs is not true reality.
There are two kinds of lands: first, the land of dharmic characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa-bhūmi*), which refers to—
There are two kinds of lands that can be apprehended through form: first, the land of *dharmatā*, which is free from all marks and is beyond seeing or hearing;

second, the land of adornments, which is also of two types: first, those with formal characteristics, such as golden ground and jeweled ponds; second, those characterized by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This refers to the cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which penetrates the true nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
It is the outflow of purified wisdom and is manifested as representation-only; it is adorned by the manifestation of merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges.

This [wisdom] is incapable of any grasping or appropriation. If one were to say that there is a real form or substance, that would be of a nature capable of being grasped. I am able to accomplish the realm...

To claim that the excellence of the land’s adornment is a false statement would be a lie. Maitreya Bodhisattva states in verse: “When wisdom practices the penetration of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), one thus takes hold of the Pure Land.

It is not a form; it is the primary essence. It is not an adornment; it is the intention of adornment. That which is ‘not adorned’ distinguishes it from the lands of the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), which possess natures such as form and so forth—it is not a true adornment.

This is what is called ‘adornment. This means that while the lands of the Dharma-characteristics have natures such as form and other sensory qualities, these are not true adornments. What is called “adornment” is that which transcends such characteristics.
This reveals the *dharmatā*-realm (*dharmatā-kṣetra*), which is adorned by the perfection of all merits;
it is devoid of any material form that can be grasped, and this is the foremost adornment. Therefore, below, the Buddha exhorts based on the adornment of the pure mind. Thus he says:
"For this reason, you bodhisattvas should give rise to a pure mind. If a person were to [regard it] as having a physical form..."
The true Buddha-field is not something one seeks to adorn with physical forms, nor is it something one claims to create or achieve.
To do so is to dwell within the objects of the senses, such as form (*rūpa*). Once one dwells in form, the mind becomes defiled;
how, then, can it be called pure? To prevent this, it is said: "One should give rise to a pure mind in this way; one should not dwell upon the six sense-objects, such as form."
To "give rise" means to produce the mind that seeks to attain the fruit. Not abiding in any phenomena such as form and so forth, the mind is then without abiding.
This non-abiding mind is pure; therefore, one should give rise to this pure mind. If there were no mind at all, it would be identical to the view of emptiness (śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi);
thus, one is instructed to give rise to this true mind. The true mind of heaven is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished.

However, to take an abiding object as a condition is inconsistent with this. If the mind does not abide, then Prajñā is vividly clear; yet this is not brought about through volitional effort (*manasikāra*).
Fearing that people might be confused by this, it is clarified and such [effort] is excluded. The previous instruction not to abide in form and so forth excludes "existence" (*sat*);
the subsequent instruction to give rise to the mind excludes "non-existence" (*asat*). Since one is thus free from both existence and non-existence, it is called the Middle Way (*madhyama*).
The Way: to realize its essence in this manner is true adornment. How could there be a buddha-field that is not pure?
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "If you wish to purify your land, you should purify your mind; according as the mind is purified, so too is the buddha-field purified."
One achieves through wisdom without dwelling in attachment. How could this apply only to a single adornment? One should, wherever one is born, maintain a mind that dwells nowhere.

Formerly, when the Fifth Patriarch was expounding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the Sixth Patriarch, upon reaching the passage, "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," the Sixth Patriarch attained great enlightenment at those words.
He then exclaimed, "How unexpected! Self-nature is originally..."
"Pure! How unexpected that the self-nature is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing! How unexpected that the self-nature is fundamentally and spontaneously complete!
How unexpected that the self-nature is fundamentally without movement! How unexpected that the self-nature can give rise to the myriad dharmas! The Fifth Patriarch said:
"If you do not recognize your own mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit. If, upon these words, you recognize your own fundamental mind and see your own original nature, then..."
He was named Mahāpuruṣa, Teacher of Gods and Humans, and Buddha. [The Master] protected and sustained him well, and finally entrusted him with his robe and bowl, saying in verse:
"When sentient beings come to sow seeds, The fruit arises again according to the ground. Since insentient things have no seeds, That which lacks nature has no arising.
Chan Master Huairang of Nanyue said: "All dharmas arise from the mind; the mind has nothing from which it arises."
The Dharma has no abiding place. If one penetrates the ground of the mind, all actions will be unimpeded; yet unless one encounters a person of superior capacity, one must be cautious with words.
This single phrase, "the mind arising from non-abiding," which the Sixth Patriarch attained, subsequently became the secret transmission of the Mind-Seal of Nanyue.

Severing Doubts Regarding the Attainment of the Reward Body through the Cessation of Feeling and the Presence of Appropriation.
This doubt also arises from the third doubt, which cannot be grasped [as a separate entity]. The *Bodhisattvaguṇālaṃkāra-śāstra* states:
"If one does not grasp at any phenomena (*dharma*), how is it that one receives the retribution of bliss? Why does the Buddha assume the body of the Dharma-King?"
How is it that other worldly beings further perceive him as the body of a Dharma King? To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, for example, suppose there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Would that body be large?
Subhūti replied, "It would be very large, World-Honored One. [The Buddha said: "Why is this? The Buddha says it is not a body; it is merely named 'large'."
The Body. Master Fu Daoshi’s verse says: Mount Sumeru is high and vast, used as a metaphor for the body of the Dharma King. The seven treasures surround it in equal measure;
the six perfections follow one another in succession. The four colors form the appearance of the mountain; compassion serves as the cause for Buddhahood. That which has form must ultimately...
"Not so. Formlessness is what is truly real.
Tong said: "Subhūti asked, 'How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind? This was because he wished to attain the cultivation and realization of unsurpassed bodhi.
The World-Honored One [responded] that unsurpassed bodhi does not depend on cultivation and realization; even if one were able..."
Cultivation and realization are not the Buddha of the original self-nature and natural spontaneity.

If one cultivates the immeasurable merit of the six perfections and myriad practices, one accomplishes a land of reward, which is called the Pure Land Adorned with Golden Light, and accomplishes the body of reward.
That which is called the body of Vairocana a thousand *zhang* in height is ultimately sustained by the power of karma; it is the fruit of outflows (*sāsrava*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
It is difficult to compare with the fruit that is pure, fundamental, and without outflows or conditioning (*anāsrava-anabhisaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, the land that is pure and fundamental is the true Pure Land; the body that is pure and fundamental is the true Great Body—namely, the Buddha-body.
It is this that pervades the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). If one attains faith in this, there is no need for cultivation or realization;
it is primordially and spontaneously perfected. Is this not indeed most difficult and rare? The *Kanding ji* states:
"For example, suppose there were a person whose body was like Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains. Such phrases as these use metaphors to demonstrate the sovereign mastery of those analogous dharmas.

Regarding this body, in what sense is it called "great"? Just as Mount Sumeru is called "great" because its power is lofty and far-reaching, yet one does not grasp at the substance of that king of mountains, thinking, "I am the king of mountains," for the mountain is devoid of discrimination;
so too is the Reward Buddha (vipākabuddha). Because he has attained the essence of the Unsurpassed Dharma King, he is called "great," yet [he does not grasp at it].
One takes up the essence of that Dharma King; I am the Dharma King because of non-discrimination. How does one attain this non-discrimination?
By practicing various meritorious deeds throughout immeasurable kalpas, all worldly concerns are entirely forgotten, and like wisdom, one becomes tranquil;
thus, there is no discrimination. As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "Like the king of mountains, there is no grasping; even when receiving retribution, it is likewise."

It is likewise so, because it is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). As the Sūtra says: "For what reason? The Buddha taught that what is not a body is called the 'Great Body.
It is not that the existence of a body is called the Great Body. That which receives the retribution of bliss is the Buddha-body, which is free from all outflows.
If it is thus, then there is no substantial entity; this is precisely what is meant by "not a body. Because of this [non-substantiality], it is...
There is a body; it is called a "body" because there is only the pure body.

It is brilliantly refined and pure, possessing a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for it is not produced in dependence upon other causes and conditions, and it is far removed from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
How, then, could it be characterized by grasping? Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked the World-Honored One, "What is called the 'Great Body'? The World-Honored One replied, "It is not..."
This body is called the "Great Body. Because it is fully endowed with all precepts, concentrations, and wisdom, and has realized the dharma of purity, it is named the Great Body.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, "That which is not a body is called the Great Body";
this is based on that very principle. A monk asked Dàlóng, "The physical body perishes; what is the indestructible Dharmakāya? Lóng replied, "Mountain flowers bloom like brocade."
The mountain stream water is as deep blue as indigo. Xuedou’s verse says: Questioning, one knows not; answering, one still does not understand. The moon is cold and the wind is high;
the ancient cliff holds frosty cypresses. How laughable it is to meet a person who has attained the Way And not respond with either speech or silence!
Holding a white jade whip in hand, he shatters the dragon pearls all at once. If he did not shatter them, they would remain like flawed jade. The land has its laws and statutes.

Regarding the three thousand offenses: if we discuss the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), even the firm Dharma-body is not permitted to dwell in attachment, let alone that which is not the Dharma-body.
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—what do you think?
"How so? Would those grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers be many? Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One.
Even the Ganges Rivers alone are already countless; how much more so their sands? "Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth:
if there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers..."
"If one were to give as a gift a thousand worlds, would the merit obtained be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One.

The Buddha told Subhūti, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to even receive and uphold a four-line verse or the like and explain it for others, this merit would surpass the former merit. Furthermore, Subhūti..."

Wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
How much more so for those who can fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it?
Subhūti, you should know that such persons have accomplished the most supreme and rarest of dharmas. If...
"Wherever the sūtras reside, there is a Buddha, as well as his honored disciples.
Master Fu’s verse says: "If the sands of the Ganges were used as a measure, And divided into six kinds of 'many,' Holding even four lines of this sūtra Would surpass the value of the seven treasures.
Wherever one travels through the gates of the Dharma, One's offerings will move the asuras. Thus it is proclaimed within the sūtras..."
"Most excellent and venerable, resembling a Buddha.
The *Kanding ji* (Record of Determination) states: "After the three preceding doubts and before the four fruits, the parable of the precious gift has already been explained."

If it is asked, "Is it not redundant to speak of this again?"—it is because the previous discourse described the gift of jewels within a single trichiliocosm, whereas this discourse describes the gift of jewels within immeasurable trichiliocosms.

Although both cases involve a vast quantity and both represent superior comparisons, the latter is the most numerous of the many and the most excellent of the excellent; therefore, it is stated again. Maitreya Bodhisattva...
The verse says: "By explaining many distinctions of meaning, one also achieves a superior comparison; the subsequent merit exceeds the former, therefore a superior analogy is stated again.
This is a repetition of the words, but not a repetition of the meaning. Why was this superior analogy not presented first?
Because ordinary people have not yet seen the reality; if it were explained extensively at the outset, they would not give rise to faith or understanding."
By hearing this gradually, one gives rise to faith; therefore, what is emphasized here is the person (*pudgala*).

Furthermore, the previous analogy did not yet speak of the four fruits being mindless, Śākyamuni having nothing attained, the purification of the land being pure without being adorned, or the cultivation and realization of the Buddha-body being realized without being realized.
Only after these meanings have been clarified is the principle of the Dharma profound; thus, what is emphasized here is the Dharma (*dharma*).
This is a comprehensive analogy. Because this comparison is likewise most excellent, he asks Subhūti:
"Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think? Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous?
Subhūti replied, "They would be very numerous, World-Honored One, for the circumference of the Gaṅgā River is forty..."
The sand is as fine as flour. If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of such sand, those Ganges Rivers alone would already be beyond counting;
how much more so the sand within all those Ganges Rivers? Therefore, it is said to be exceedingly vast.

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who filled as many trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven treasures...
"If one were to give these as a gift, would the merit obtained not be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very much so. [The Buddha continued:
"If one were to give the seven treasures of even a single world-system as vast as the sands of the Ganges as a gift, that merit would already be great;

how much more so if one were to give the seven treasures of worlds as numerous as the sands of all the Ganges Rivers—would it not be exceedingly great? The Buddha said: "If one were to practice only such giving and not uphold this sutra..."

Such a person does not advance toward Bodhi; their merit is not superior. However, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, receives and upholds even a four-line verse and explains it to others—thereby benefiting themselves and others—they will be able to advance toward Bodhi.
Their merit shall surpass the merit of the previous gift of the seven treasures, being immeasurable and boundless.
It is beyond calculation. How can one perceive the superiority of its merit? The merit of upholding it is vast;
indeed, there are thirteen kinds of superior causes by which this merit is accomplished. To speak first of the places that are worthy of veneration and the persons who are worthy of reverence:
furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even so much as a single four-line verse, [there such merit is established].
One should know that this place is itself a caitya; all the world should offer it worship.

Just as when Śakra preaches the Dharma for the assembly of devas, all the devas turn toward his seat with reverence and pay homage—not out of respect for the person, but because they revere the Dharma and thus honor the site.
Enshrining the Buddha’s śarīra is called a stūpa; enshrining the Buddha’s image is called a temple; and the preaching of the Dharma [is likewise honored].
A place where [this teaching exists] is like a Buddha-stūpa or temple; such a place of illumination is worthy of reverence. Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "One should revere two places:
The place where the four-line verse is proclaimed is already worthy of the offerings of gods and humans, let alone one who can receive and uphold the entirety of this sutra's text.
The former [verse] spoke of the place; this speaks of the person. The former clarified the four-line verse.
This clarifies the extent to which they can receive and uphold [the teaching]. It is stated repeatedly for this reason, hence the phrase "how much more so.

One should know that such persons are fully capable of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [it], and are fully capable of believing in and understanding the profound and wondrous meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
By means of this, they are able to accomplish the supreme *dharmakāya*, the foremost *saṃbhogakāya*, and the rare *nirmāṇakāya*.
This Dharma, which excels all vehicles and is peerless in the world—wherever this sutra resides, in whatever place, there is a Buddha and his disciples;

it is a place worthy of honor by wise men. This is because the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* must necessarily rely upon the *dharmakāya*, and the *dharmakāya* is, in turn, manifested through the sutras.
Since the teaching that manifests it exists, there must necessarily be [the reality it reveals].

The Buddha is that which manifests it; furthermore, the Sūtra is the Dharma of teaching, while the Buddha is the Dharma of fruition. Fruition is manifested through principle, and principle is attained through practice.
Thus, the three Buddhas are fully present and the four Dharmas are all perfected. Wherever this exists, how could one give rise to feelings of inferiority?

Furthermore, all noble ones and saints are named after the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Since the sūtras manifest the unconditioned, there must necessarily be noble ones and saints who are their honored disciples.
Moreover, the sūtra itself is the Dharma Jewel; where there is a Buddha, that constitutes the Buddha Jewel.
If there are honored disciples, they constitute the Saṅgha Jewel. Wherever the scriptures are located, the Three Jewels dwell together. If [that is so]...
In the case of one who gives jewels or the place where jewels are given, such a thing does not exist; therefore, this [sūtra] is superior.

What was previously stated—that all Buddhas are born from this sūtra—is still believable. However, what is now stated—that wherever this scripture resides, there is a Buddha—is truly difficult to believe.
As for what was previously stated—that unsurpassed bodhi emerges from this sūtra—it is still acceptable...
It is indeed true. To now say that merely upholding and reciting these four lines can bring about the accomplishment of the most supreme and rare Dharma is truly difficult to believe.
This unsurpassed and wondrous Dharma transcends all things; how could it ever be measured by the abundance of offerings of the seven treasures?
During the Sui dynasty, there was a man of the Xun clan from Shu who once gazed into the distance across an empty field.
Kong. He transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* by hand, whereupon he was moved by the protection of the various devas.
When it rained, this spot remained dry; cowherds all sought shelter here. During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, a monk said to the villagers:
"In the past, someone transcribed a scripture at this location, and the devas established precious canopies above to protect it. You must not [allow it to be desecrated]."
People used to trample upon it, but later a railing was erected around it and an image of the Buddha was enshrined there. One constantly hears the sound of celestial music;

this is a case where the evidence is clear and manifest. Formerly, when Linji arrived at the stupa of Bodhidharma, the caretaker asked, "Shall I first pay homage to the Buddha, or shall I first pay homage to the Patriarch?
Linji replied, "I pay homage to neither the Patriarch nor the Buddha. The caretaker said, "The Patriarch and the Buddha are both with you, Elder."
There was a most formidable adversary. Ji shook his sleeves and departed; this was solely to accomplish a matter of supreme rarity, which enabled him to act with such perverse and contrary conduct.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it? The Buddha told Subhūti: “This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By this name, you should uphold it. Why is this so? Subhūti, when the Buddha speaks of *prajñāpāramitā*, it is...”
It is not that the Prajñāpāramitā exists [as something] from the beginning; this is called the phrase "Prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti, what do you think?
"Did the Tathāgata preach any Dharma? Subhūti replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has preached nothing.
Master Fu composed a verse: Within names there is no meaning; Upon meaning, moreover, there is no name.
The diamond-like true wisdom Can shatter the hardness of evil. If one reaches the further shore, One enters into principle and emerges from deluded sentiment. The mind of the wise person...
Self-awakening. The foolish seek sound externally.
Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within the great trichiliocosm many?
Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One. Subhūti, those atoms—the Tathāgata has said they are not atoms.
Dust. This is called a minute particle (*paramāṇu*). The Tathāgata said: "The world is not a world;
it is called a world. Master Fu’s verse says: Accumulated dust forms the world; Dividing the world produces minute particles. The world is a metaphor for the fruits of humans and devas;
Dust represents the causes of outflows (*sāsrava*). Since the cause of dust is unreal, The fruit of the world is not true. Thus one knows the nature of cause and fruit.
This is an illusion. O Subhūti, you who are carefree and self-sovereign, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? "No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that the thirty-two...
These two marks are themselves non-marks; this is what is called the thirty-two marks.

Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who were to give away their bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in alms, [it would not equal the merit of one who hears this teaching].
Master Fu’s verse says: Giving one's life as numerous as grains of sand, the karma of humans and devas grows ever deeper.

Having obscured the marks of Bodhi, it can obstruct the mind of Nirvana. A monkey reaches for the moon in the water; a cicada picks up a flower-needle. In the river of craving, floating and then sinking;
in the sea of suffering, emerging and then drowning again.
If there should be another person who, from this sutra, even receives and upholds as little as a four-line verse and explains it for others, their merit will be exceedingly great.
Master Fu’s verse says: "The sutra speaks of four lines; one should not let them leave one's side. The foolish man looks at them as mere words..."

A dream: the wise see it as merely real. The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no before or after; being without middle or end, it is neither old nor new. The aggregates (skandhas) are empty and lack substantial characteristics;
relying on what could one perceive a person?

Subhūti said, "Because the Buddha has praised this sutra, stating that wherever it resides, that place shall be as if the Buddha himself were present and should be honored by humans and devas like a stupa or temple;

because this sutra is most supreme, and those who can receive and uphold it will have the greatest merit, I therefore ask what this sutra is named so that I may reverently uphold it. The Buddha [replied] with *prajñāpāramitā*...
Among the six perfections, honey is the foremost. This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*;
it takes the meaning of "that which can cut" and, together with its *prajñā*, dispels all attachments. It is indeed the most supreme, most noble, and unsurpassed Dharma-gate.
Its name is "Most Supreme" (*parama-jyeṣṭha*), for it serves as the supreme cause for all to attain Buddhahood.
Since its name is itself nameless, even its description is without description. Its fundamental nature is non-arising, and its meaning is unsurpassed.

Therefore, when one contemplates the subtle dust-like worlds as coarse phenomenal divisions, they are not separate from the defiled causes of affliction (*kleśa*). Likewise, when one contemplates the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan-lakṣaṇa*)...
As for those who take it as their own objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), they have not yet realized the essence of perfect enlightenment;
therefore, compared to the merit of upholding this sutra, the atoms of the world are not numerous enough, and the thirty-two marks are not remarkable enough.

Because upholding this sutra serves as the cause for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it cannot be compared to the causes and effects of worldly, conditioned, and outflowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena. Although...
To give away one’s life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in alms is not equal to the great merit gained from upholding and reciting even four lines of verse;
how much less could the merit obtained from giving external objects such as the seven treasures compare to it?

Because it is worthy of veneration; because it is worthy of the people’s reverence; because it is the supreme cause of all; because its meaning is unsurpassed;

because it transcends the many [obstacles] of both the external and internal; because it is the superior cause for the Buddha’s physical form; because it transcends the merit of internal giving; because it appears simultaneously with the Buddha;

because it is rare for one to be able to believe and understand it; because it is difficult to practice; because the fruit of believing and practicing is great; and because belief and understanding bring about accomplishment.
Because it is based on the past and because its power is unsurpassed, for what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly explain these various causes and characteristics?
It is because sentient beings practice the giving of material sustenance and seek the fruits of wealth and status, yet do not uphold the True Dharma to sever the causes of all suffering;
therefore, he praises and exhorts them repeatedly. As for what is called "a place worthy of respect," it is [a place where] people...
The expression "veneration" has already been explained above. Now, regarding the supreme cause of all: Subhūti asks what this Dharma-gate should be named.
The Buddha says: "The name of this sutra is *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* (The Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom), for it is able to sever all afflictions, defilements, doubts, and attachments."
If one severs doubt and attachment, the attainment of Buddhahood is certain; is this not superior? Therefore, you should uphold it.
Now, as for why this Dharma-gate is called "Vajra": the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through the Prajñāpāramitā, possess the most supreme understanding of both mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Why is this so? The Buddha taught that Prajñāpāramitā is itself not [a fixed entity].
Prajñāpāramitā refers to the wisdom regarding all phenomena within the three realms that is able to weigh and know them as lacking solidity.
That which lacks solidity is still this shore; whereas that which is most solid through the wisdom of prajñā is called reaching the other shore.
Regarding the shore of the merit of wisdom, there is no one who can measure it. As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "That shore of wisdom is difficult [to reach]."
As for "measure": within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), because the intrinsic nature is unborn, it is difficult to conceive;

how, then, could there be "attainment"? Even the wisdom of *prajñā* must be able to sever [conceptualization]. This dharma-gate serves as the supreme cause for the realization-dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
As the verse says: "By practicing the cause, one realizes the Great Essence. Is this not what that refers to? That which is called...
Regarding the "Unsurpassed Meaning": The Buddha asked Subhūti, "What do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?
Subhūti already knew that all the Dharmas preached by the Tathāgata are neither graspable nor expressible;
thus he replied, "The Tathāgata has preached nothing. This means that there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has preached alone; rather, it is all [the same].
Because all Buddhas proclaim it together. Since it is the nature of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of what the Buddhas have personally realized and attained, it is supreme and unsurpassed.
Whatever they may speak is entirely in accordance with their realization; within realization there is no speech—how could there be any divergent teaching?
The verse says: "By virtue of the excellence of its outflow, it is thus in meaning that there is nothing superior.
This refers to what is called "surpassing the many, both external and internal. The Buddha asked Subhūti: "What do you think?
Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many? Subhūti replied: "They are exceedingly many," for [he considered] the trichiliocosm as reduced to [atoms].
A minute particle (*paramāṇu*). By accumulating these minute particles, one forms the three-thousandfold world system.

Just as by accumulating minute particles one attains the superior fruits of humans and devas through meritorious practice (*puṇya-kriyā*), can this be considered much? That merit from the gift of precious jewels is a cause for defiled afflictions (*kleśa*);
it is able to bring about the fruit of defiled afflictions, and it is able to bring about defiled afflictions themselves.
This is because the cause is that of the *āsravas* (outflows), and the fruit is that of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Thus, these subtle particles of the world are entirely unreal; since both [cause and fruit] are non-existent, the Tathāgata says they are not particles and says they are not elements (*dhātu*).
However, these "earth-particles" are not particles of a nature such as defilement (*rajas*); therefore, they are designated as "earth-particles."
Furthermore, that world is not a realm characterized by the causes of afflictive defilement; it is for this reason that it is called a "world.
By this it is said that the merit of such giving is actually a cause for the dust and grime of delusion and affliction; though that merit may be virtuous, [it is still so].
Even when compared with the indeterminate [actions] regarding external objects, these are still inferior. When measured against the merit of upholding [the sutra], they do not appear to be great.
This is because the giving of jewels does not equal the merit of the physical realm, and the physical realm does not equal the merit of upholding the sutra;

for the former involves the cultivation of afflictions, whereas the latter brings about the severance of those very afflictions and delusions. As the verse says: "That is due to the cultivation of afflictions... [The sutra...]
How could this not be manifest? Because the world contains sentient beings, it is called "internal multiplicity" (adhyātma-bahutva).

Because atoms consist merely of form and color, they are called "external multiplicity" (bahirdhā-bahutva). This merit of upholding the sutra does not fall into the category of the indeterminate (avyākṛta);
therefore, it transcends both internal and external multiplicity. Regarding what is called "surpassing the causes for the Buddha’s physical form," the Buddha asked Subhūti:
"What do you think? Can the Dharma-body Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? He replied, "No.
The Dharma-body Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. For what reason?
It is because the thirty-two marks cannot constitute the Dharma-body Tathāgata. When the Tathāgata speaks of the thirty-two marks, they are not [the Dharma-body]."
The Dharma-body has the characteristic of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), whereas the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) has the characteristic of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This is because the Dharma-body is the true nature (*tathatā*) of the unconditioned, while the Form-body (*rūpakāya*) is a conditioned reflection.

Thus, just as all meritorious deeds performed through practice can bring about the marks of a Buddha-body, these constitute only the Response-body (*sambhogakāya*); yet, regarding the merit of upholding and explaining [the teachings], they can bring about the Dharma[-body].
The body is likewise inferior because its various characteristics are not the essential nature of perfect enlightenment;
yet, it is said to be inferior because it is maintained as the means by which one can attain the nature of great enlightenment.

Although those characteristics are inferior, they still surpass the defiled merit of giving material wealth—how much more so for that which serves as the cause of the Dharma-body? Thus, even that which is inferior is also superior.
The verse says: "This merit that subdues defilement—if it is the most excellent among all merits, one can know that it is capable of further subduing [even that].
Thus, it is called "the superior cause for the Buddha’s form. Regarding what is called "surpassing the merit of internal giving," the Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, practiced giving..."
To give with the seven treasures is to give external wealth; this giving of one’s body and life is what is called internal wealth.
To sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is not to say it is not much; to destroy stinginess and greed is not to say it is not exhaustive.
As for the meritorious retribution obtained, compared to those who give away material resources and precious jewels, its merit is far superior. Why?
For this reason, they sacrifice their bodies and lives because of the suffering of body and mind. As the verse says: "Suffering the body is superior to that;
practicing these causes of suffering without hastening toward Bodhi will ultimately result in nothing but outflowing fruits.

Furthermore, if there should be someone who, from within this sutra, even receives and upholds as few as four lines of verse and explains them to others, this is called the gift of Dharma, which brings benefit to oneself.

Benefiting others enables one to advance toward Bodhi and ultimately achieve the supreme fruit; therefore, its merit is infinitely more vast than that [of external giving], beyond measure and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
This is called "surpassing the merit of internal giving. This comparison based on internal resources further demonstrates the superiority of the Sūtra.
Thus, as for this scripture being named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*: because it is free from the marks of words and letters, there is nothing that is spoken;
because it is free from the marks of afflictions, it is not a mote of dust; because it is free from the marks of humans and devas, it is not a world-system.
Because it is even apart from the Buddha’s physical body, it is not the thirty-two marks; because it is apart from the intrinsic nature of *prajñā*, it is not the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Such a supreme, foremost, and most rare dharma can only be trusted through self-confidence and can only be realized through self-awakening.
If one does not awaken to it, then even if one were to sacrifice immeasurable quantities of the seven treasures to seek it, one would certainly—
It cannot be attained. Even if one were to sacrifice countless bodies and lives in the pursuit of it, it could never be found.
Only Subhūti deeply accords with its essential meaning; how could he fail to shed tears while sighing over its rarity? Huangbo said: "The Buddha has three bodies:
the Dharmakāya preaches the Dharma of the self-nature’s empty penetration; the Sambhogakāya preaches all pure dharmas."

The Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body) preaches the Dharma of the six perfections and myriad practices. The Dharmakāya (Dharma Body) preaches the Dharma in a manner that cannot be sought through speech, sound, form, or written characters;
it has nothing to be preached and nothing to be realized, being merely the spontaneous penetration of intrinsic nature.

Therefore, it is said: "There is no dharma that can be preached; this is called preaching the Dharma. Both the Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body) and the Nirmāṇakāya manifest according to the karmic conditions and capacities of beings. [End of excerpt]

The preaching of the Dharma also accords with specific circumstances and adapts to the faculties [of beings] in order to gather and transform them; none of these are the true Dharma. Therefore it is said:
"The retribution-body and transformation-body are not the true Buddha, nor are they the preachers of the Dharma. It is further stated:

"All that the Tathāgata speaks is for the sake of transforming people, like using yellow leaves as gold to stop a small child's crying; it is certainly not real. If there were any real attainment, it would not be mine."
"A guest from under the lineage of the Zen school—what business do you have with your own fundamental essence? Therefore, the Sūtra says:

'In reality, there is not the slightest dharma to be obtained; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If you can understand this meaning, only then will you know that both the Buddha-way and the Mara-way are equally mistaken.
Originally pure and brilliantly clear, it has no squareness or roundness, no length or shortness, and no greatness."
Small and other such characteristics—outflow-free and unconditioned; neither delusion nor enlightenment. Seeing clearly, there is not a single thing, nor is there a person, nor even a Buddha.
The great trichiliocosm and its myriad worlds are but bubbles on the ocean; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning. Nothing compares to the reality of the mind.
The Dharmakāya, from antiquity to the present, is identical to that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Where [is it not so]?
It lacks not even a hair’s breadth. Having understood this meaning, you must exert yourself with great diligence. The single school of Huangbo is entirely composed of the Great Meaning of the Vajra;
thus, one knows that this sutra is truly the transmitter of the Buddha’s Mind-Seal.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One! That the Buddha should preach such a profound sutra as this.
Since the past, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard a sutra such as this."
Master Fu’s verse says: Hearing the sutra, I deeply understand its meaning; my heart is filled with both joy and sorrow. In the past, I eliminated the obstacle of afflictions;
now, I am able to leave behind the obstacle of the knowable. The imputed nature was understood long ago; the perfected nature is realized at this very moment.
Riding upon the unimpeded wisdom of former lives, I employ skillful means to exhort others to uphold [the Dharma].

World-Honored One, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and, with pure faith, gives rise to the mark of reality, you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
World-Honored One, this mark of reality is precisely the absence of marks.
Therefore, the Tathāgata spoke of it as the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Master Fu’s verse says:
There has never been a mind without an object, nor has there ever been a mind without an object. When the object is forgotten, the mind naturally ceases;

“There are Buddhas; how could minor sages possibly be capable of this?
World-Honored One, for me now to hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.

But if, in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there should be sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it—such persons [will be even more rare].”
This is the foremost rarity. Why is this? This person has no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span. Why is that? The mark of self is precisely no-mark;
the marks of person, sentient being, and life-span are likewise no-marks. Why is this? To be free from all marks is what is called "all Buddhas."
Master Fu’s Verse says: When Śūnyatā-janman heard the wondrous principle, it was like tares growing among hemp. When ordinary people believe this Dharma, it is like a lotus blooming from fire.
Fearing that people might give rise to views of annihilation, the Great Sage preemptively provided both opening and closing [of the teaching].
If one can leave behind all marks, one will certainly enter the House of the Dharma King.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is exceedingly rare."
Master Fu’s verse says: If one is able to resolve the mind [for enlightenment], One should understand the two extremes.
Nirvana has no marks; Bodhi is free from objects of perception. There is neither vehicle nor rider; Both person and phenomena are abandoned.
If you wish to reach the principle of True Suchness, You should recognize the original source.
Why is this? Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not indeed a foremost pāramitā;
it is designated as the foremost pāramitā.
Master Fu’s Verse says: *Pāramitā* is called "the other shore," yet within it there are ten names. High and low arise from deluded consciousness;
their sequence is for the sake of confused sentiment. Seeking water within a mirage, searching for an echo in empty space— How can one gain or lose the True Suchness?
Only now is it called "Perfectly Accomplished."
Tong said: "The profound praise herein for the great merit gained from upholding this sutra refers to the attainment of pure merit, not worldly merit.
To receive and uphold even four lines of verse brings forth immense merit;
how could it be that one gains such merit merely by memorizing words and engaging in verbal discourse? What is valued is faith; what is valued is practice. It is thus."
One receives [the teachings] and practices in this way. By not clinging to the thirty-two marks, one immediately attains the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

How would this differ from that of a Buddha? By not clinging to the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span, one is no longer bound by the causes and effects of the world’s humans and devas.
Because one thus transcends the three realms, the merits within the realms are insufficient.
To illustrate this: because it is no different from the Buddha himself, its merit and wisdom are both complete, such that neither humans nor devas dare to hope for them.
For this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*—which is both prajñā and yet distinct from prajñā—is of unsurpassed power.
It is the most supreme and foremost of rare dharmas; those who can truly believe in it are difficult to find. As for those who are able to believe and understand it, their merit is [immeasurable].
How can it be measured? That which is called "appearing together with the Buddha" means that when a Buddha arises in the world, those of meager merit find it difficult to encounter him;
this sutra is likewise so, for few are those who hear it in advance. At that time, Subhūti, having heard this Dharma-gate, gave rise to profound faith and understanding.
Weeping with tears falling like rain, he wiped away his tears and addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One! As the Buddha has spoken..."
This profound sutra refers to the wisdom of *prajñā*, which perceives that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty.
This deep *prajñā* now explains that *prajñā* is neither *prajñā* nor non-*prajñā*; it is empty yet not empty—this is the most profound *prajñā*.

From the past until now, the eye of wisdom I have attained has only been the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), understanding the emptiness of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-śūnyatā*), but I have never yet attained [the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena].

Having heard such a sūtra as this, one empties the dharmas and further empties that very emptiness, realizing the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and understanding that there is nothing to be attained.
I was originally an arhat who followed the Buddha into the homeless life; even in the past, I had not heard of this True Dharma.
Therefore, it is as rare as the manifestation of a Buddha. Why is such a sūtra so rare? It is because of the aforementioned meaning.
The Buddha taught that Prajñāpāramitā is not Prajñāpāramitā. That shore of wisdom is immeasurable;
only a Buddha can know it, for there is no one else who knows it. Therefore, it is called the "ultimate meaning. It is what is rarely able to be believed and understood.
Furthermore, if there should be a person who hears this sutra and is able to give rise to faith—if such faith arises, it does not believe in [the inherent existence of] all phenomena;
therefore, it is called "pure. Within this [sutra], there is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), because it is not shared with others;
for apart from the Buddha-dharma, no other place possesses the true mark, as that [true mark] has never existed and has never arisen elsewhere. Only by believing in this sutra does [faith] arise.
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As the verse says: "Because it is also not the same as other dharmas.
The true mark refers to the fact that all dharmas are unarisen and have nothing from which they arise; this is the mark of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of True Thusness (*tathatā*).

Once the true mark has been realized, the merits of the three bodies (*trikāya*) are thereby fully perfected. One should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit. Dharma...
Fundamentally there is no arising. How, then, can there be a real characteristic of arising? That which is called the "real characteristic" is spoken of in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
it is precisely the absence of characteristics. For this sutra suddenly eliminates the two attachments and simultaneously reveals the two emptinesses; even the sickness of emptiness is itself empty.

There is absolutely nothing to be attained. Since there is neither attainment nor teaching, what characteristic could there be? If it were exclusively without characteristics, one might fear it would result in nihilism.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, relying on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), speaks of it as the "true characteristic" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Although this true characteristic arises, [it remains without characteristics].
Because one does not destroy non-arising, the non-characteristic is pointed out as the true characteristic.

If a person can believe that all dharmas are unarisen while not destroying conventional designations, they will realize the characteristic within the characteristic and transcend the characteristic; they will realize the non-arising and non-ceasing within arising and ceasing.
For this reason, they achieve the foremost and most rare merit, which only a Buddha can personally verify, and not...
This is what even the minor sages have attained; thus it is said that such faith and understanding are rare. Regarding those who "practice with difficulty," Subhūti said:
"I have now heard such a Dharma-gate, which is firm, substantial, profound, and subtle, having received the Buddha’s words directly from him."
To have faith, understand, and uphold this is not a difficult task.

If, in a future age, during the final five hundred years when the distance from the Sage has gradually increased and the True Dharma is about to perish, one should examine these bequeathed teachings, believe in and understand the emptiness of all phenomena, and remain free from both extremes.
To uphold it in this way is truly rare. Such a person is not merely one who preserves and recites empty words;
therefore, it is called difficult. As for what is meant by "the greatness of the fruit of faith and practice":
it refers to their faithful understanding and upholding. For what reason is this called rare? It is because these sentient beings have faith, understand, and practice this sutra.
There is no longer the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, or the mark of a life-span. This is the thorough realization of the nature of non-self in persons;
it is the non-arising of marks such as "self" and so forth. Why is it that these marks of self and so forth are made non-existent?

It is because when there is an object of appropriation (*grāhya*), the mark of an appropriator (*grāhaka*) arises therein. The essential substance of the mark of self does not exist apart from the mind.
Regarding these dharmas: these mental states and mental factors have been non-existent from the very beginning.
They exist only through reliance on conventional discourse, whereby one speaks of the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span.

If explained according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they are indeed without marks. This is because, by realizing that dharmas are without self, one realizes the twofold emptiness. For what reason does this cause people...?
Are phenomena also empty? If one has not yet departed from signs (*nimitta*), one cannot be called a Buddha.

Only by departing from the mark of persons (*pudgala-nimitta*), departing from the mark of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*), and even departing from the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā-nimitta*)—departing from all of these—is one named a "Buddha. This is the mark of original reality.
Although originally there is not a single thing, this does not fall into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*); truly, there exists the essential body and marks of the Buddhas. This is called...
It is for the sake of the great fruit. Faith is able to receive and uphold it; one realizes this great fruit, and thus it is called rare.

From the time Subhūti heard this sutra being preached until this point, there are six stages of discourse: namely, weeping upon hearing the Dharma; the arising of faith in the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);

the contrast between difficulty and ease; clarifying the absence of self and person (*pudgala*); the simultaneous extinction of attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*); and the complete attainment of the Buddha-way.
All that has been thus spoken consists of words that are entirely true and authentic. Therefore, the Buddha confirmed it, saying: "So it is, so it is.
That he spoke these words twice was to express the ultimate limit of what is appropriate to say. Regarding what is called the accomplishment of faith and understanding, the Buddha said:
Furthermore, if there should be someone who hears this sutra— which is exceedingly profound and subtle, difficult to understand and difficult to know—
and yet, at the time of hearing the Dharma, does not give rise to transgression, fear, or alarm, nor produces dread where it is misplaced, as if one were violating the correct principle,
such that they would be startled or censured; that is, one who is not terrified by the teaching of the non-arising of all phenomena within the paths of rebirth and existence.
Furthermore, when contemplating, one does not give rise to continuous fear; one does not cease the fear of doubt, which is unending.
This means that while the Lesser Vehicle speaks of emptiness and existence, one does not fear the teaching of the Middle Way, which is neither empty nor existent.
When practicing, one does not give rise to dread or obstruction; it is not a matter of fearing the ultimate exclusively.
Because they do not fall into terror; that is to say, they are resolutely directed toward unsurpassed bodhi.

One should know that such a person is already rare in having distanced themselves from the inferior and deluded views of the masses, yet to further proceed toward unsurpassed bodhi and shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata is exceedingly rare.
Only those who possess this state of being neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid [are so].
The mind, regarding this supreme One Vehicle (Ekayāna) wherein there is neither vehicle nor one who rides it, is able to give rise to no doubt;
this alone may be called true faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). As the verse says: "Firmly established in the profound meaning"—this is precisely what that refers to.
Regarding what is called "unsurpassed power," for what reason is it so? It is because hearing [this teaching] does not cause astonishment, fear, or dread, which is rare indeed.
It exists. Because this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost *pāramitā*. As the verse says: "Because it surpasses all other sūtras.
Why is it called the foremost? Because the *dharmakāya* is the greatest, and it is through this that [the Buddha] is accomplished;
there is nothing equal to it. Among all the Buddha-dharmas, it is the most firm and sharp, the most pure and supreme.

Therefore, the verse says: "Because it is the Great Cause and is pure. Furthermore, because it is that which all Buddhas have collectively taught, it is also said to be a lineage of supreme excellence.
If explained according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is not the foremost *pāramitā*;

for it was never lost in the past, nor has it ever been newly attained now. Since originally there was no one who could reach it, who could be called "foremost"? This is merely spoken in accordance with worldly convention.
It is spoken with truth. Because it cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed, it is called the foremost *pāramitā*.
To speak of the foremost *pāramitā* is already the ultimate limit; yet, it is further negated by saying, "It is not the foremost *pāramitā*.
Therefore, it is said that its majestic power is unsurpassed. In each preceding section, the excellence of the Sūtra was revealed, and this excellence—

This is the fundamental principle; it does not exceed this gateway. That external and internal giving of material wealth lacks the power to destroy delusions during the causal stage and lacks the virtue of the Dharma-body during the resultant stage.

There is nothing that so perfectly fulfills such a multitude of virtues as this. Therefore, when compared to the previous accumulation of merit, their relative status—whether superior or inferior—is fundamentally distinct.
Consequently, the merit of upholding and reciting [the scriptures] is the most excellent among all forms of merit.
This is virtue. As stated previously: "The Buddha says that which is not a body is called the Great Body. This refers to the fruit being devoid of any fruit. Here it is said:
"The Buddha speaks of the foremost *pāramitā*, yet it is not the foremost *pāramitā*.
This refers to the cause being devoid of any cause. Since both cause and fruit are inconceivable, why would there be grasping? Therefore, there is grasping.
Doubts may now be resolved. A monk asked Huangbo, "What is the meaning of Mañjuśrī holding a sword before Gautama?

Huangbo replied, "The five hundred bodhisattvas who attained the knowledge of past lives saw that their karmic obstacles from previous existences were none other than these very five-aggregate bodies of yours.
Because they saw these karmic obstacles of past lives, they sought the Buddha, sought Bodhi, and sought Nirvana."
This is why Mañjuśrī took the sword of wisdom and insight to slay this mind that views [the Buddha] as existing; thus he said, "You have slain well. [The monk asked: "What is this sword?
Huangbo said, "The mind of understanding is the sword. [The monk asked: "If the mind of understanding is the sword, it severs this mind that views [the Buddha] as existing.
But as for this very mind capable of severing the view—how can it be eliminated? Huangbo said, "It is precisely by using..."
"You possess non-discriminative wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). It severs this mind of discrimination that views existence. [The questioner] says:

'If one acts as if there were a view of existence and a seeking for Buddhahood, one severs it with the sword of non-discriminative wisdom. But what can be done about the fact that the sword of wisdom itself exists? Baizhang said:
'If non-discriminative wisdom were to harm the view of existence or the view of non-existence, then even non-discriminative wisdom could not be attained. [The questioner] says: 'No.'"
"One may sever wisdom with further wisdom, but one cannot sever a sword with a sword. Huangbo said: "A sword harms itself;
when swords harm one another, even the sword cannot be found. Wisdom harms itself; when wisdoms harm one another, even wisdom cannot be found.
It is the same for the loss of both mother and son. Only Huangbo clearly illuminates this golden [truth]."
The profoundly deep meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is that even *prajñā* itself cannot be apprehended;
this is why it is called the unsurpassed Dharma-gate.

Since the *pāramitā* of wisdom (*prajñā*) is the most supreme, it is sufficient merely to uphold and expound it. Why laboriously practice the other *pāramitās*?

Those who now uphold and expound [this wisdom] are practicing the bodhisattva path; acts such as cutting one’s own thigh to save a dove or throwing oneself off a cliff to feed a tiger—such practices are all termed causes of suffering.
