The Buddha taught that if a bodhisattva has resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta, how could there ever be a self? One should give rise to such a mind of non-self, thinking:
"I shall bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa and cause them to enter nirvana without remainder. Thus one should extinguish [the notion of self].
Having delivered all sentient beings, one does not perceive even a single sentient being who has truly entered parinirvāṇa.
Internally, one does not give rise to the thought of being a deliverer; externally, one does not see a multitude of those to be delivered. When such thoughts do not arise, this is precisely non-self.
This state of non-self is what is called a Bodhisattva. For what reason? Because while universally delivering sentient beings...
Does he not give rise to the thought of sentient beings? If a bodhisattva harbors the thought of "I" who delivers sentient beings, that is the mark of a self (*ātman*).

If he harbors the thought of "sentient beings" who are to be delivered by me, that is the mark of a person (*pudgala*). As long as he has not forgotten self and person, [he has not attained non-arising].
To think that there are sentient beings is the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*). To think that there is a nirvana to be entered is the mark of a life-span (*jīva-nimitta*).
To possess these four marks is inverted conduct; it is not the cause of purity, and such a person cannot be called a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind [on enlightenment].
Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "To practice within the inner mind while maintaining the notion 'I am a bodhisattva'—this is precisely what obstructs the mind."
This contravenes the path of non-abiding. Because it is contrary to the characteristic of non-abiding, it remains far removed from unsurpassed bodhi.
Now, that which brings sentient beings to extinction is the vast mind; that which causes them to enter nirvana is the foremost mind;
that which does not perceive extinction is the eternal mind; and that which remains far removed from the four marks is the mind of right wisdom. To give rise to...
These four kinds of mind that benefit sentient beings can only be said to correspond with unsurpassed bodhi.
If there were even a single dharma capable of giving rise to such a mind, one might say that a self exists.
Yet, when observed now, there is first no objective realm to be transformed, and next no subjective mind capable of transforming; both mind and object are forgotten. This is the capacity...
All things are simultaneously quiescent. In reality, there is no dharma that gives rise to the bodhicitta.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), even the very first moment of giving rise to the bodhicitta does not exist; how much less, then, can there be a "self" who acts as its agent?
Since there is not a single dharma that can give rise to the bodhicitta, bodhi is unattainable.
Because bodhi is unattainable, sentient beings are unattainable. Because sentient beings are unattainable, the four marks are unattainable.
In the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single dharma exists. This is precisely why the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is of such profound meaning.
Huangbo said: "Because you give rise to the thought of becoming a Buddha, you say there is a Buddha to be attained;
because you give rise to the view of sentient beings, you say there are sentient beings to be saved. To give rise to thoughts and stir the mind is entirely your own sphere of perception."
"If there were no views whatsoever, where would the Buddha be? For instance, as soon as Mañjuśrī gave rise to the view of a Buddha, he was banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains.
A monk asked, "At this very moment of awakening, where is the Buddha? Baizhang said, "From where does the question come? From what does the awakening arise?
Speech and silence, movement and stillness—all sounds and forms—are entirely the work of the Buddha. Why [seek it elsewhere]?"
Seeking the Buddha within these abodes, the world of empty space is brilliantly clear; there is not even a hair’s breadth of anything that can serve as an object for your views and understandings.
Therefore, all sounds and forms are the Buddha’s eye of wisdom. Phenomena do not arise in isolation; they manifest only by relying upon conditions.
For the sake of sentient beings, he possesses manifold wisdom; yet though he speaks all day long, when has he ever spoken?
Though one hears him all day long, when has one ever heard? Therefore, although Śākyamuni taught for forty-nine years, he never uttered a single word.
A monk asked, "If this is so, where is Bodhi? Baizhang said, "Bodhi has no such place; even the Buddha did not attain Bodhi."
"Ti! Sentient beings likewise do not lose bodhi. It cannot be attained through the body; it cannot be sought through the mind.
All sentient beings are themselves the mark of bodhi. The monk asked, "How does one give rise to the bodhicitta? Huineng said, "Bodhi is non-attainment.
You should now simply give rise to a mind of non-attainment. If you are resolutely unable to attain a single dharma, that is bodhi."
"Awaken the mind. Since bodhi has no place of abiding, there is no one who attains it. Therefore, it is said:
"At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I did not obtain even the slightest dharma; for this reason, the Buddha immediately conferred upon me the prediction [of my future enlightenment].

This makes it clearly known that all sentient beings should not further seek to attain bodhi. As for your current question regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta, you speak of taking up a single mind.

"Study and take up the Buddha; it is intended solely for the path of Buddhahood. Even if you were to practice for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, you would only obtain a *nirmāṇa-buddha* or a *saṃbhoga-buddha*.
What connection could these have with your original source, the true-nature Buddha? Therefore it is said: 'Seeking externally for a Buddha with form is not like you.
How marvelous this discourse is! It is sufficient as a commentary on this section."
Regarding the twelfth [point], the severing of the causes for Buddhahood: there is the doubt that "there are no bodhisattvas.
This doubt arises from the perspective that, in reality, there has never been anyone who has generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

The *Guṇapradīpa-śāstra* states: "If there were no bodhisattvas setting out upon the Mahāyāna, then there would be no cause for realizing the fruit of Buddhahood, nor would it be brought to fulfillment."
There are four kinds of beneficial matters. Why was the World-Honored One granted a prediction of enlightenment by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, saying:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni, who will be able to accomplish four kinds of beneficial matters for sentient beings"?
To dispel this doubt, the sutra says:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, obtain any dharma called ‘anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi’?

“No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there was no dharma that the Buddha obtained as ‘anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi’ while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha. The Buddha said, “So it is.”
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. Truly, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as 'anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as 'anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,' then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me this prediction: 'In a future age, you shall become a buddha, named Śākya-'"
Śākyamuni, there is in truth no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, Dīpaṃkara Buddha conferred upon me the prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni."
The Master said: "Subhūti’s doubt regarding the existence of a self was extremely subtle.
Initially, he doubted that those who dwell in and subdue [the mind] must harbor a self; thus, he took the wisdom of subduing to be the self.
Once he heard that there is truly no dharma by which one generates the bodhicitta, and that wisdom itself does not arise, how could there be a self? Having [resolved this], he then again doubted..."
When one generates the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), there is no such thing as a "Bodhisattva. Who, then, would act as the cause for Buddhahood?
One does not know that at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was truly no dharma through which he generated the mind of enlightenment; how then can one have doubts regarding the Bodhisattva?
That not a single dharma can be apprehended is precisely the cause for becoming a Buddha. Yet, one further doubts that there is no dharma to be attained and no Buddha to be realized.

Will this not lead to falling into the view of emptiness? Not knowing the meaning of the suchness of all phenomena—that they are neither existent nor non-existent—is precisely the Middle Way, the ultimate truth.
Because they are neither existent nor non-existent, all phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma.

It is not that one possesses a "great body" and thus is called "one with a great body"; how could it ever come to the point where the Buddha-dharma is utterly absent? Since the Buddha is thus, so too are the Bodhisattvas.
It is thus. If there were even a single dharma to be apprehended, one would immediately be attached to the four marks; this would not be adornment.

Only when that which is neither Buddha-dharma nor non-Buddha-dharma, neither adornment nor non-adornment, constitutes the realization of the meaning of non-self, can one be called a Bodhisattva, and can one become a cause for attaining Buddhahood. These four sections of doubt originally belong to...
Because they share a single essence, they are all subsumed here. The *Kanding ji* states: "Within your own mind, do you perhaps think that I attained bodhi under Dīpaṃkara Buddha?
In the past, I purchased flowers to offer to the Buddha and spread my hair to cover the mud;
I was then granted a prediction by the Buddha that I would become a buddha named Śākyamuni. Do you consider these to be the practices of a bodhisattva?"
"Does one practice? Is there anything to be attained in unsurpassed enlightenment? Subhūti replied, "No.
It is not my intention to say that the Tathāgata attains enlightenment. I have understood the meaning of what the Buddha has taught:
the dharma of enlightenment is quiescent and unarisen, free from all conceptual discrimination. When the Buddha was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he beheld his own body..."
Pure. Seeing the Buddha as pure, there is no mind that can attain, nor is there any dharma that can be attained;
this is the sound of the prophecy, yet it does not reach the ear. In reality, there is no dharma by which one attains unsurpassed bodhi.
The Buddha then confirmed this, saying: "So it is, so it is. The Tathāgata truly has no dharma by which he attains unsurpassed bodhi. If [one were to] maintain...
If the subject and object, mind and境 (the objective sphere), are not extinguished, then there is the existence of dharmas. Because of the existence of dharmas, one does not accord with Bodhi;

therefore, the Buddha does not bestow a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) upon such a person. Only when subject and object are abandoned and both mind and境 are forgotten is there no existence of dharmas.
Because of the non-existence of dharmas, one accords with Bodhi; therefore, the Buddha bestows a prediction of enlightenment upon them. Regarding the various practices I cultivated at that time—
Practice. In reality, there is not a single dharma that attains bodhi. In terms of practice, there is no attainment in each act of practicing;
in terms of thought, there is no attainment in each moment of thought. As the Bodhisattva Maitreya said in verse: "The prediction was given at a later time;

the practice under Dīpaṃkara was not supreme. This means that when Dīpaṃkara Buddha gave the prediction to Śākyamuni that he would become a Buddha in the future, it was not because [the practice] was particularly superior.
Regarding causal practice: one may realize Bodhi in that state precisely because there is nothing to be attained; thus, one receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Furthermore, why do you harbor doubts regarding the fact that for a Bodhisattva who has resolved upon unsurpassed Bodhicitta, there is truly no dharma whatsoever?
Xuansha asked Jingqing: "The ancients said, 'Not seeing a single dharma is a great calamity. Now tell me, what do you say about this?"
"What dharma have you seen? Jingqing pointed to a pillar and said, "Is it not this very dharma? Xuansha said, "The clear water and white rice of Zhejiang, you may eat as much as you like;
as for the Buddha-dharma, you have not even dreamed of it. Tiantong took up the case, saying:
"When Jingqing answered in such a way at that time, and when Xuansha finally spoke in such a way—did they accord with each other or not? Nevertheless..."
"Jingqing has long ceased having dreams of the Buddha-dharma; it must be one who was a fellow student of Xuansha who can truly understand this.
○ Thirteen: Severing the doubt that 'if there are no causes, then there is no Buddha-dharma.
This doubt arises from the fact that the Śākyamuni of old, while practicing the causal path under Dīpaṃkara, actually attained nothing at all. If there were none..."
If one practices with causes, then one cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If there were no bodhi, then there would be no Buddhas, Tathāgatas.
Would it not follow that everything is non-existent? To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says:
Why is this? "Tathāgata" means the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, as for the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the Tathāgata—
Subhūti, herein there is neither reality nor unreality. Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti, that which is called "all dharmas" is precisely not all dharmas; therefore it is named "all dharmas."
“Subhūti, it is as if there were a person with a large body. Subhūti said, “World-Honored One, what the Tathāgata calls a ‘large body’ is precisely not a large body;
it is merely designated as a ‘large body.’”

Tong said: "The previous statement that one receives the prediction of honor 'because of having nothing to obtain'—does this so-called 'having nothing to obtain' mean that it is like a tortoise's hair or a rabbit's horns, being utterly non-existent?
The essence of the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm."
"Suchness is immovable. This is the meaning of what is taught in all the sūtras: that all phenomena (dharmas) are suchness. True Suchness (bhūtatathatā) is neither real nor unreal.
If there were something obtainable, then obtaining it would be called "real" and losing it would be called "unreal.
Since there is only non-attainment, both of these [extremes] are discarded. This correctly reveals the Middle Way, the Supreme Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). Why is it so called?
Non-substantiality means that all phenomena are not all phenomena; it means that the great body is not a great body—this is non-substantiality.
Why is it called non-emptiness? That which is not all phenomena is named "all phenomena," and that which is not a great body is named "the great body"—this is non-emptiness.
Being neither substantial nor empty, one remains far removed from the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
Thus, we know for certain that what is called "non-attainment" (anupalabdhi) likely transcends the realm of existence and non-existence;
it cannot be discussed in terms of existence or non-existence. The *Puṇyavardhana-śāstra* states: "Buddha means awakening (*buddha*); *bodhi* also means awakening.
Since awakening should not further attain awakening, the Tathāgata has not a single dharma that can be attained. Although there is not a single dharma that can be attained..."
There has never been a time when the Tathāgata was not present, because True Suchness (tathatā) is the Buddha. True Suchness is the meaning of the suchness of all phenomena (dharmas).
Tathāgata is simply another name for the true nature of reality, True Suchness. It is fundamentally unborn and fundamentally unceasing;
because it is free from inversion, it is called the "true nature" (bhūtatā), and because it is without change, it is called "True Suchness. If there should be someone who says:
Since there is a Tathāgata and since there is bodhi, it is only by attaining bodhi that one is called a Tathāgata.
If the Tathāgata, while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did not perceive any dharma capable of attaining bodhi, then it would be impossible for him to have ascended the seat of awakening.
Such a person, by asserting that there is a real practitioner of the bodhisattva path, speaks what is not true; for [he does so] regarding that...
To say that there is something to be attained regarding bodhi is also not the truth. The Dharma is itself the Dharma of bodhi; the Buddha is himself bodhi.
How could there be anything to be attained? A verse says: "Because bodhi and those practices are equal. When a bodhisattva practices these practices, in reality there is nothing to be practiced.
It is the same for all Buddhas: there is no dharma that can be realized as perfect, complete enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
If that is so, does the Tathāgata ultimately not attain bodhi?

Indeed, the unsurpassed bodhi attained by the Tathāgata is "attainment as non-attainment," because within it there is neither reality nor unreality. Therefore, the bodhi attained by the Tathāgata is not a truly existent conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
A conditioned phenomenon refers to that which is produced by causes, such as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth.
That Dharma of Bodhi has no such characteristics as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; therefore, it is said to be "without reality.

It is precisely because it does not possess the characteristics of form and so forth—that the absence of such characteristics is its own characteristic—and because that itself is the characteristic of Bodhi. As the verse says:
"It is the characteristic of the non-characteristic," which is spoken of as being "non-false" because it is not deceptive. This does not mean that one realizes a dharma of non-attainment.
Yet it does not encompass everything. Therefore, the Buddha taught that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are the Buddha-dharma.
All phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane, ordinary or noble—do not take their own intrinsic nature as their essence; rather, they all take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their essence.
Since True Suchness is that which is realized only by the Buddha, all phenomena are called the Buddha-dharma. (Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Verse)
He said: "These dharmas are the dharmas of all Buddhas; they are the self-nature and characteristics of all things.

However, regarding what are called all dharmas such as form and sound, not a single dharma possesses the nature of being obtainable. Only that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot maintain its own self-nature and characteristics, and thus it is not a 'dharma' at all.
If all dharmas such as form and sound are not dharmas, [then what are they?]"

What is meant by "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*)? Because they are designated through conventional expression within the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), that which is not a phenomenon is precisely because it does not possess the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
This constitutes its being a phenomenon; this "all" is the all of *tathatā* (suchness).
These phenomena are the very self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the phenomenon of *tathatā*. Since those characteristics of phenomena do not exist, it never abides.
Maintaining those characteristics of phenomena ultimately means being able to maintain the characteristic of non-existence.
The essence of the *dharmakāya* of true suchness is inherently thus. It is, for example, like a human body that has grown large;

as in the previous passage where the body is like Sumeru, the King of Mountains, it becomes a great entity without self-discrimination. Based upon that *dharmakāya*, this metaphor of the "great body" is taught. Why is this so?

Is it called the "Great Body"? It is because the two obstacles—the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—are absent that it is named the "Perfectly Complete Body," which is the fully endowed Dharmakāya. This has two meanings: first, it pervades all objects.
This refers to the nature of *tathatā* (suchness). Because it does not differ regardless of where it is located, and because it is shared equally by all sentient beings, it is called "Great.
Second is the greatness of merit: the merit of cultivation is inconceivable and corresponds to the Great Body (*mahākāya*).
For this reason, it is termed the "Great Body. Subhūti profoundly accords with this meaning; therefore—
This means that when the Tathāgata speaks of the great stature of the human body, he does not speak merely of the existence of a physical form.
He speaks of the *rūpakāya* based on its ultimate meaning (*tattvārtha*). Within the nature of *tathatā*, there are no conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*);
since its arising is not perceived, how could there be "greatness"? Thus, it is a non-great body. Because it has the essence of *tathatā*, it is precisely non-arising.
Its nature is called "non-body. This very non-body is named the "wondrous great body"; it is not what is meant by a physical body (*rūpakāya*).
As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "Relying upon that Dharmakāya Buddha, the metaphor of the 'great body' is taught."
The body is free from all obstructions and pervades all objects; because its qualities and its great essence are thus, it is called the "Great Body.
That which is not a body is itself the body, and for this reason it is called "non-body. One is able to know that what is non-body is the Great Body.
One can surely believe that non-attainment is itself true attainment; why then doubt the absence of the Buddha-dharma?
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the teaching for a single generation? Yunmen replied, "I speak to each one. This is precisely what is meant by "all dharmas.
Xuedou’s verse comments: "To speak to each one—how vast and solitary! An unperforated iron hammer."
Driving in the wedge once more. Under the Jambū tree, he laughs heartily. Last night, the black dragon snapped its horns. Parting, parting!
The old man of Shaoyang has obtained a single peg. A monk asked Yunmen: "It is not the mechanism before one's eyes, nor is it the matter before one's eyes.
What is it? Yunmen said: "Turn the statement upside down. This is precisely what is meant by "not any dharma whatsoever. Snow.
Dousong said: "To overturn one statement and divide one section—'dying together and living together' is your secret instruction.
The eighty-four thousand [teachings] are not the phoenix feathers; thirty-three people entered the tiger's den. Separately, separately;
in turmoil, in haste—like the moon in the water. Furthermore, a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the pure Dharma-body? Yunmen said, "Flowers in the medicinal hedge. This...
This refers to what is called the "great body" of a human being. The monk asked, "What is it like when one goes forth in this very manner?
Yunmen said, "A golden-maned lion. This is what is meant by not having a great body. Xuedou’s verse says: Flower-adorned balustrade—do not be negligent!
The star is on the scale, not on the platter. To go forth in such a way is a great causeless error. Golden-maned...
Great masters, look! The meaning of these dharmas as they truly are is exceedingly profound and exceedingly subtle;
one must pass through Yunmen’s "cloudy tangles" before even a small portion of accord can be granted.
○ Fourteenth: Dispelling the Doubt that There is No One to Deliver Beings or Adorn the Buddha-land.
This doubt is identical to the twelfth doubt; both arise from the eleventh doubt concerning the fact that there is no dharma by which one awakens the mind.
If there is no dharma by which one awakens the bodhicitta, then there would be no Bodhisattvas; whom, then, would they teach to deliver?
[He asks: "Once [the Buddha] has been born, who is to adorn the land? The former doubt was that there is no Buddha; this doubt is that there are no bodhisattvas.
Therefore it is said, "The bodhisattva is also like this. To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says:
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva. If one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then one is not called a bodhisattva.
Why is that? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that is called a "bodhisattva.
Therefore, the Buddha has said that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span. Subhūti, if...
If a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva. Why?
The Tathāgata has said that what is called "adorned buddha-field" is itself non-adornment; it is merely designated as "adornment.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the dharma of selflessness, the Tathāgata declares him to be a true bodhisattva. (The term "bodhisattva" is repeated in the Wei, Chen, and Tang translations.)
Master Fu’s verse says: Person and phenomena depend upon each other; their two aspects are originally such. Phenomena are empty and the person is illusory;
the person being empty, phenomena are also dispelled. If both person and phenomenon were real, then the bestowal of prediction would not be false.
All things are like illusions; who can say there is existence or non-existence?
The Master said: "In the previous explanation, it was said that when a bodhisattva generates the bodhicitta, there is still a 'bodhi' to be attained.
Reaching this point, however, there is in fact no dharma whatsoever that generates the mind; if even the generation of the mind does not exist, how much less so the bodhi?

In the previous explanation, it was said that a bodhisattva does not perceive any sentient beings to be saved, yet there was still a 'bodhisattva' to be attained. Reaching this point, however, in reality..."
There is no dharma that can be called a "bodhisattva. Since even a bodhisattva does not exist, how much less so a sentient being?
Thus we know that what was previously severed was the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*), while what is severed here is the innate grasping at dharmas (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*).
This is indeed most subtle. Master Fu said: "If both person and dharmas were real, then the bestowal of prophecy would not be false. It is only the person..."
Since both phenomena and the self are empty, the bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is not something real. This resolves the first three doubts. First, regarding the "exhaustion of the path":
the *Guṇapradāna-śāstra* states that the characteristics of the purity of causes described above are not yet complete in meaning; therefore, to fulfill them, the previous intent is restated.
Thus, it is said that at the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, the Tathāgata did not obtain even the slightest dharma through his cultivation of causes.
It is pure. It is not only the Tathāgata who is thus; all bodhisattvas are likewise.
If one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then one perceives oneself as the savior and sentient beings as those to be saved.
As long as the dualistic mind and its objects are not forgotten, this is a perversion, and such a person cannot be called a bodhisattva. For what reason is this so?
If one harbors thoughts, can one still be called a bodhisattva? Within the nature of true suchness (*tathatā*), not even a hair’s breadth exists;
in reality, there is not the slightest dharma that can be apprehended which is named "bodhisattva. If one raises the mind or stirs a thought, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma.
Therefore, the Buddha said that all dharmas are themselves the Buddha-dharma, being without self, without person, without sentient beings, and without life-span. First.
Within the ultimate meaning, there is no bodhisattva and no ordinary person. Because the true realm is equal, it is inappropriate to give rise to conceptual discrimination.
To oppose this is to perceive the four marks, which is to be a sentient being; to accord with it is not to perceive the four marks, which is to be a bodhisattva.
Ultimately, not a single dharma can be apprehended. If a bodhisattva were to say: "That which is cultivated..."
The six perfections and myriad practices are for the purpose of adorning the Buddha-land. Without pure causes, how could there be pure fruits?
Since these are the causes of attachment to the aggregates of form and so forth that constitute the Buddha-land, such a person is not called a bodhisattva.
For what reason is "adornment" also not called a "bodhisattva"?

Regarding that which the Tathāgata has described as "adorned Buddha-fields," in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), one does not perceive a subject who adorns nor an object that is adorned. Because the true meaning is non-arising (*anutpāda*), it is not adornment at all.
Since there is fundamentally no arising, why would there be such a name? It is merely expressed according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Therefore, as for that which is adorned by right and wrong, adornment and non-adornment are equal and without duality; this is called true adornment.

Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "Failing to realize the true Dharma-realm, yet giving rise to the intention to deliver sentient beings and purify buddha-lands—such a thought is itself a perversion.
Now, to truly adorn a buddha-field is the mark of great wisdom; whereas [to do so] inferiorly...
To deliver sentient beings is what constitutes great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). These are all matters within the domain of a bodhisattva.
If one gives rise to even a single thought [of self], one is no longer a bodhisattva. Thus, what kind of mind must arise to be called a bodhisattva?
If there are sentient beings and bodhisattvas who have thoroughly realized the dharma of non-self (*anātman*), there are two kinds of this dharma of non-self: the first is sentient beings...
Regarding all dharmas: first, there are the dharmas possessed by a bodhisattva.
If one can have faith through their own wisdom—whether it be worldly wisdom or supramundane wisdom—they will believe and understand that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

That all dharmas are without intrinsic nature means not only being free from the self of persons (*pudgala-ātman*), but also being free from the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*). Though they adorn [themselves] throughout the day, they never truly adorn.

Venerable One, throughout the entire day one delivers sentient beings, yet never actually delivers them; this is true formlessness, this is true non-abiding. The Tathāgata calls such a person a true Bodhisattva.
To speak again of "Bodhisattva" refers to two types: first, the Bodhisattva of the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
second, the Bodhisattva of the supramundane truth (*lokottara-satya*), who is truly worthy of receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood. The verse of Maitreya Bodhisattva states:
It is said: "Ordinary beings and bodhisattvas know that all dharmas are without self. It is not through the self-knowledge of non-sages that they have faith;
rather, it is through the wisdom of sages. Although one may not yet be a bodhisattva, if one can believe through one's own wisdom, one is indeed a bodhisattva, because of possessing this wisdom.
Huangbo said: "The Buddhas and bodhisattvas, as well as all wriggling insects and sentient beings, share this same Great [Mind]."
The nature of nirvāṇa is the nature, which is the mind; the mind is the Buddha; the Buddha is the Dharma.
A single thought that departs from reality is entirely a delusive conception. One cannot seek the mind further through the mind; one cannot seek the Buddha further through the Buddha;
one cannot seek the Dharma further through the Dharma. Therefore, the practitioner of the Way directly realizes the state of no-mind through silent resonance.
This is all there is to it. To direct the mind toward it is already a deviation. Transmitting mind by means of mind—this is the correct view.

Be careful not to pursue external objects or mistake objects for the mind. When greed, hatred, and delusion arise, one then establishes the precepts, concentration, and wisdom; yet fundamentally, afflictions do not exist.
What use is there for bodhi? Therefore, the Patriarch said: "The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to eliminate all mental states.
Since I have no mental states, what use are all dharmas? The source is pure and pristine; above the Buddha, one does not further attach to a single thing. It is like empty space:
even if adorned with immeasurable treasures, they can ultimately find no place to abide. The Buddha-nature is the same.
Although space is adorned with immeasurable merit and wisdom, it can never abide there; it is merely that one’s own fundamental nature is deluded, causing one to fail to see it.
This is what is called the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground: all things are established in dependence upon this mind.
They exist when encountering objects and do not exist when no objects are present. One must not misinterpret the Pure Land as being an external object. As it is said:
Concentration and wisdom are like a mirror: their function is vividly clear, silent yet alert. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all merely forming interpretations upon objects;
this may suffice for those of middling or inferior capacity who speak provisionally. However, if you wish to realize it directly, none of these interpretations should be maintained.
All such things are merely objective phenomena (*dharma*) that possess a place of immersion; they sink into the ground of existence. Therefore, regarding all phenomena— [The original text ends here.]
Not forming views of existence or non-existence is precisely seeing the Dharma. Huangbo directly scraped away and exhausted everything from the very essence of the Dharma he had realized;
he was truly one who had attained thorough penetration of the dharma of non-self.
15. Severing the doubt that the Buddhas do not perceive all dharmas:
This doubt arises from the fact that the aforementioned Bodhisattvas do not see sentient beings who are to be saved, nor do they see Buddha-lands that are to be purified.
If a Bodhisattva does not see those as sentient beings, and does not see himself as a Bodhisattva, then he does not see a self.
They are identical in their characteristics. If this were so, the Buddhas would not perceive any phenomena and would possess no eye of wisdom at all.
Would there be an object to be apprehended? Or would there be no object to be apprehended? Herein it is said that there are no objects; thus the Sūtra says:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? “Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? “Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? “Yes, World-Honored One...”
“Venerable One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.”
Master Fu’s verse says: The celestial eye has unimpeded penetration; the fleshly eye is obstructed and lacks penetration. The Dharma-eye observes only the conventional;
the wisdom-eye directly takes emptiness as its object. The Buddha-eye is like a thousand suns; though illuminating diverse forms, they are seen as identical.
Within the perfectly luminous Dharma-realm, there is nowhere that is not encompassed.

The Tathāgata Viśeṣaprabha explained it as follows: "As for what is called the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), it illuminates and perceives the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the physical bodies (*rūpa-kāya*) born from the womb, the egg, moisture, or transformation.

As for what is called the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), it illuminates and perceives the palaces of the various heavens, clouds and rain, light and darkness, and the causes and conditions for the revolution and submergence of the five planets and the two luminaries.
As for what is called the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), it illuminates and perceives the wisdom of sentient beings."

The nature [of these eyes] ranges from shallow to profound, representing the superior, middling, and inferior grades of rebirth within saṃsāra as they take up residence in various forms; this is the causal condition for their manifestation. As for what is called the "Dharma-eye" (dharmacakṣus):
it illuminates and perceives that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) pervades the triple world, being formless and signless, exhausting all of empty space and permeating the entire Dharma-realm;

this is the causal condition for its manifestation. As for what is called the "Buddha-eye" (buddhacakṣus): it illuminates and perceives that the Buddha-body is incomparable throughout the worlds, emitting light that shines universally to shatter all [obscurations].
It is darkness, unobstructed and unhindered, pervading the ten directions. By seeking the light, one perceives the essence and knows that there exists the realm of Nirvana.

Among these five eyes of the Tathāgata, if there is a person of superior faculties and superior wisdom who can recognize these five kinds of causes and conditions, they are immediately named a Mahayana Bodhisattva.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River truly sand, as the Buddha has described them?
"Yes, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata has described them as sand. "Subhūti, what do you think?

If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and if one were to count all the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—" the Buddha, the World-Honored One... [continued].
"World-systems such as these—would they not be many? "They would be very many, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Within all those world-systems, the various kinds of minds possessed by all sentient beings, the Tathāgata knows them all.
Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that all minds are 'not-minds'; it is for this reason that they are called 'minds. Why is that, Subhūti? Because the past mind..."
It can be attained. The present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. Master Fu’s verse says:
"Based on the dependent nature, a single thought arises; Together they constitute the realm of delusion. Thus they divide into sixty-two views, And nine hundred distractions surge in all directions.
The past has perished, yet there is no perishing; The future will arise, yet there is no arising. One should always be able to act [thus]."
In this contemplation, truth and falsehood are both level and even.
Tong said: "The previous statement that 'with the Buddha’s wisdom he fully knows these people and fully sees these people' emphasizes the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
As for the Buddha-eye, all four [eyes] are preeminent; beyond the Buddha-eye, there are no other four eyes. It is like...
Coming to know that seeing and knowing are non-dual, the Tathāgata fully knows the five eyes previously mentioned and the various kinds of minds subsequently mentioned.

Since the minds of sentient beings are all but small portions of phenomena manifested from the true mind, and the Tathāgata has realized this true mind, how could there be any delusions that he does not perceive?
Therefore, one who thoroughly penetrates the dharma of non-self is precisely [the same as]...
The Tathāgata is in accord with the true mind; therefore, he is able to know and see all things completely. The *Kanding ji* states:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are far removed from the discrimination of subject and object, and do not perceive even a single dharma as obtainable. How could it be that they have no vision at all?
Nevertheless, when the eye of true wisdom illuminates and discerns external objects, there are briefly five kinds [of vision]. The first is the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*)."

The first is the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which consists of pure material sense-faculties that perceive forms within obstructions; because the Buddha possesses all sense-faculties, he has this physical eye.
The second is the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), which draws upon the pure divine faculty adjacent to the physical eye to perceive forms beyond obstructions.
The third is the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which penetrates and analyzes ultimate truth through fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*). The fourth is the subsequent...

Attaining wisdom and preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is called the "Dharma-eye" (*dharmacakṣus*). The first four [eyes] reside in the Buddha and are vastly distinct from what is attained by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and bodhisattvas;
these are collectively termed the "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakṣus*). Thus, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the five eyes, seeing all things without exception.

This section defines "purity of vision" (*darśana-viśuddhi*) based on the five eyes as the means of seeing. Below, "purity of wisdom" (*jñāna-viśuddhi*) is defined based on the various minds that are known. Furthermore...
The Bodhisattva Vairocana spoke in verse: "Though one does not perceive all phenomena, it is not that there is no eye that comprehends the objects.
Because the five kinds of reality of the Buddhas are seen as inverted, [the Buddha] desires to clarify that the wisdom of the Tathāgata is subtle and capable of knowing;
therefore, he manifests it by means of the vast multiplicity of the objects known. What do you think? It is like the number of grains of sand in the Ganges River."
"Does the Buddha say these are grains of sand? "It is so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata says these are grains of sand.
This refers to counting the grains of sand within a single Ganges River. "What do you think?
If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River—this refers to counting rivers by means of the number of sands in a single river—then all those Ganges Rivers..."
"Are all the grains of sand in those rivers as numerous as the Buddha-worlds? Would they be many?
This refers to counting world-systems by means of the sands in the various Ganges Rivers. The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Within all those lands, there are sentient beings."
There are various kinds of minds; within such realms, the mental capacity of sentient beings is as vast as that.
These various kinds of minds do not transcend the two categories of defilement and purity. As for why the Tathāgata is able to know them all:
those various minds grasp at false objects and are entirely the delusions of the six consciousnesses, which constitute the mind.
Regarding the various distinctions of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*): for what reason does the Tathāgata say it is "not mind"?
Because it lacks a sustaining support, the mind is dispersed; for it abides in falsehood and does not abide in reality—it is not that which the mind dwells upon.
Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke in verse: "Various kinds of inverted consciousness arise because one is separated from true mindfulness;
by not abiding in that true wisdom, they are therefore called 'inverted. If one does not abide in this manner, one remains far removed from those four foundations of mindfulness."
Since there is nothing that can be grasped or maintained, it constantly revolves according to conditions; this is precisely the continuity of inversion, termed "the nature of falsity.
Why, then, is it said that all minds are inverted consciousness?
It is because they cannot be found when sought in the past, present, or future: the past mind has already ceased, and the future mind has not yet arisen. Thus, the past...
By using the past to verify the present, one sees that the present’s false conceptualization is precisely the nature of the parikalpita (imagined) aspect;
it lacks intrinsic existence. Therefore, this mind of cyclic existence is entirely an object of deluded consciousness, for it possesses no nature across the three times.
Thus, the Tathāgata knows and perceives all of this and designates it as "non-mind. That which is esteemed as the Buddha-eye is not...
One takes up that which can know the deluded mind of sentient beings; one takes up that which knows the deluded mind is entirely unobtainable.
Since the deluded mind is unobtainable, it is itself the true mind. That the true mind does not perish is what is called "mind. This is termed right knowledge and right view.
How could it be reached by the limited wisdom of those with physical eyes? Formerly, there was one from the Western Heaven...
The Tripitaka Master Da’er arrived at the capital and claimed to have attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds. Emperor Suzong ordered National Teacher Zhong to test him.
As soon as the Tripitaka Master saw the Master, he prostrated and stood to the right.
The Master asked, "Have you attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds? He replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "Tell me, where am I right now? He replied:
"The Master is the teacher of the entire nation. How can you go to West River to watch the boat races?

How is it that you are instead watching monkey tricks at Tianjin Bridge? The Master remained silent for a long while, then asked again, "Tell me, where am I, this old monk..."
“Where is the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃgha now? Zang was unable to fathom this. The Master rebuked him, saying, “You wild fox spirit!

Where is your supernatural power of knowing others’ minds? Zang had no reply. Later, a monk asked Yangshan, “For what reason did the Tripiṭaka Master Dairi not see the National Teacher during his third visit?
Yangshan said, “The first two visits were when his mind was still involved with objective realms; the later [visit]...”
He entered the samādhi of self-enjoyment, which is why he was not seen. Furthermore, a monk asked Xuansha, "Do you say that you saw him during those previous two occasions?
Xuangjue said, "I saw him during those previous two occasions. Why then did you not see him later?
Tell me, where does the point of significance lie? Again, a monk asked Zhaozhou about the Tripitaka Master Dier.
For the third time he could not see the National Teacher and wondered where the National Teacher might be.
The Master said, "He is on top of the Tripitaka Master’s nostrils. Later, a monk asked Xuansha, "If he is on top of the nostrils, why can he not be seen?"
Sha Yun said, "It is simply because it is too close. Tiantong took up the case and said, "Setting aside for a moment that the Tripitaka Master did not see the National Teacher, tell me:
do you say the National Teacher knew his own place of descent? If you say he knew it himself, then all the birds will carry flowers to him."
The devas made offerings without ceasing for a single day. But tell me: at such a time as this, where does it fall?
Formerly, when Deshan arrived at Liyang, he saw an old woman selling cakes on the road; he rested his shoulder and bought some cakes for refreshment.
The woman pointed to his pack and asked, "What kind of text is this? Deshan replied, "The *Qinglong Shu* (Blue Dragon Commentary)."
The laywoman said, "What sutra are you lecturing on? Shan said, "The Diamond Sutra. The laywoman said, "I have a question.
If you can answer it, I will provide you with refreshments; if you cannot answer it, you must go elsewhere. "The Diamond Sutra says: 'The past mind cannot be apprehended;
the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. I wonder—"
The Elder asked, "Which mind does one point to? The Mountain was silent. He then went to Longtan, where he clarified his own realization.
He piled his commentaries and sub-commentaries before the Dharma Hall, held up a torch, and said: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void;
to exhaust all worldly mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a vast abyss. Thereupon, he burned them. Thus, he came to know for himself.
One can attain the mind. Those such as National Teacher Zhong and Deshan may be said to possess the Buddha-eye.
(16) Regarding the severing of the delusion of merit and virtue:
this doubt arises from the inversion of the fundamental state of mind. The Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of sentient beings.
The mind. Furthermore, one fully knows that the accomplishment of immeasurable merit is of a nature that is illusory.
Since the mind is in a state of flux, all accumulations of merit likewise become empty. If this is illusory, it is identical to perversion; how, then, can it be called a wholesome dharma?
"In that case, does the practice of all wholesome dharmas not fall into emptiness? To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti, what do you think?
If someone were to fill the three-thousandfold world system with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, gain much merit?
[Subhūti replied: "Yes, World-Honored One, that person would [gain much merit]. By means of this, the World-Honored One...
By this cause and condition, one obtains a vast amount of merit. Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one obtains a vast amount of merit;
because merit is non-substantial, the Tathāgata says that one obtains a vast amount of merit.
The Tathāgata Sovereign Power King explained: "Although this is indeed such a gift, it is merely a treasure with obstructions;
it is not the unconditioned, pure merit. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not say it is much.
If there is a bodhisattva who, by means of the seven factors of enlightenment within the body of Vairocana, observes the fast, pays homage, and praises [the Buddha] from their heart..."
Lamp. It transforms into merit; it is neither born nor extinguished, as firm as a diamond.
Riding upon clouds of fragrant flowers, it enters boundless realms and raises a platform of radiance to make offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions.

This is the unconditioned merit of the giving that perceives the nature of reality. It transforms into a Bodhisattva. The verse says: Extensively taking the seven treasures to hold as an offering, as if...
He did not say that the field of merit is vast. If one uses the lamp of the mind as an offering, its majestic radiance will shine everywhere, filling the Sahā world.
Tong said: Subhūti previously stated, "This merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata..."
It is said that his merit is great; however, because the nature of merit does not fall within the realm of numerical calculation, it cannot be discussed in terms of much or little.
When it is said that his merit is great, this merely refers to worldly merit. Subhūti is comparing the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) with the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Therefore, the abundance of worldly merit is not equal to its absence. The World-Honored One regards the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as identical to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
it is precisely because merit is non-existent that he speaks of its abundance. Furthermore, if merit possessed an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it would mean that merit possesses substantial reality.
Now, by negating even that intrinsic nature, one abides neither in the ultimate nor in the conventional. It is exactly for this reason that—
This reveals the Truth of the Middle Way. The *Kanding ji* states: "The mind that undergoes cyclic existence may indeed be illusory;

however, the substance of what is called the 'accumulation of merit' is not unreal. For instance, if one takes giving as the cause and the seven treasures as the conditions, and if such giving extends throughout the great trichiliocosm, then the merit likewise extends throughout the great trichiliocosm—how could it not be exceedingly vast? Nevertheless..."
If it is not sustained by the wisdom of right awakening, it becomes a cause for outflows (*āsrava*);

though one may acquire much merit, there would be a substantial nature of merit that could be apprehended, and the Tathāgata does not call this "much. This is because giving while abiding in signs is a perversion.
If one practices giving without abiding in signs, it is sustained by the wisdom of right awakening and thus becomes [unconditioned].
Regarding the cause of outflows (*āsrava*): although no merit can be obtained, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of merit does not exist, its abundance is immeasurable.

Therefore, the Tathāgata says that one obtains much merit. From the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are fundamentally no appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*), and thus nothing possesses real existence.
Because it exists only as verbal expression according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), he speaks of its abundance. This is precisely—

That which is sustained by wisdom is not inverted. The previous state of sentient beings' minds abiding in signs is called inversion, because it contradicts the originally empty and quiescent essence.
This giving does not abide in signs and is therefore not inverted, because it accords with the originally empty and quiescent essence. — Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Verse.
It is said: The root of the Buddha’s wisdom is not a merit based on inversion. Because it possesses the characteristics of such merit, he speaks again through parables.
That which is seen by these five eyes is entirely without anything to be apprehended; this is the realm of the Buddha.
By this, one should know that the pure cause free from marks has no objective realm to be attained. Therefore, for one who penetrates the dharma of non-self, there is no knowing.
There is nothing he does not know; there is nothing he does not see, even when it appears not to be seen.
Deshan ascended the hall and said: "If you have no concerns within yourself, then do not seek falsely. Even if you were to obtain something through false seeking, it would still not be attainment.
You need only be without mind regarding phenomena, and without phenomena within your mind; then you will be empty yet spiritual, vacant yet wondrous. Even a hair’s breadth—so it is said."
Regarding the fundamental and the derivative, both serve only to deceive oneself. Why is this? A thought as slight as a hair’s breadth becomes the karmic cause for the three miserable realms;
a fleeting emotion gives rise to shackles that bind one for ten thousand kalpas. Holy names and mundane titles are all but empty sounds;
extraordinary features and inferior forms are all but illusory colors. If you seek them, will you not be burdened? And when you come to weary of them, they again become a great affliction.
In the end, it is of no benefit. Because Deshan was thoroughly matured in the purport of the *Vajracchedikā*, these words flowed forth spontaneously;
as stated above, only when each and every expression is free from delusion can it be called the wisdom of *prajñā*.
The Essential Meaning of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five;
The Essential Meaning of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Six:
Chapter Seventeen, Severing Doubts Regarding the Absence of Marks and the Presence of the Marks and Signs of a Buddha.
This doubt arises from the premise that the Tathāgata comes from the meaning of the "suchness" (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. "Suchness" means the sense of being unmoving like *tathatā*.

This is precisely the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Since it has already been stated that the unconditioned *dharmakāya* is the Buddha, why is it that the accomplishment of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) is also called the Buddha?
This is a doubt concerning the *rūpakāya* based on [the discussion of] the *dharmakāya*. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of a body of perfect form? No, World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of a body of perfect form. Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls a "body of perfect form" is...
It is not the perfection of the physical body; it is called the perfection of the physical body. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of the various marks? "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the possession of the various marks. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls the possession of the various marks is itself not a possession; it is called the possession of the various marks."
The perfection of the marks.
Master Fu’s verse says: "The eighty secondary signs, And the thirty-two primary marks— They manifest in ten thousand forms according to objects, Yet in principle, they are neither one nor many.
Both person and phenomena are cast aside; Form and mind are equally abandoned. Thus, realization is attained."
"Bodhi is truly realized through the departure from all marks.
Tong said: "Master Fu was originally an emanation of Maitreya who appeared in response to the spiritual capacities of this land.
His verses on the profound meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* are truly the key to this sutra. Regarding the principle that 'all marks are non-marks'—"
This is certainly not merely a matter of repetition; how could it be that such a profound reiteration is devoid of meaning?

Because Subhūti has already realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), he knows that the thirty-two marks are themselves non-marks, thereby clarifying the reality at the boundary of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Reaching this point, he further empties those dharmas; thus he knows that what are called "non-marks" are in fact named "marks," thereby clarifying the reality that transcends the Dharma-body.
This refers to the simultaneous relinquishing of both person and phenomena. By clarifying that there is no characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), one has already discarded form (*rūpa*).
By clarifying that there is no non-characteristic, one further discards mind (*citta*). This is what is meant by the simultaneous and equal relinquishing of both form and mind.

When person and phenomena are both empty, and form and mind are equally discarded, one thereby realizes *bodhi*. It is neither empty nor form; it is neither one nor different. Thus he preached the Dharma.
The body is not merely the physical body, yet the physical body has never failed to be the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body certainly cannot be seen through marks, yet it likewise cannot be seen apart from marks. It is marks without marks; it is without marks yet marks.
Is this not the most wondrous, the most wondrous of all? The *Puṇyapradāna-śāstra* states: "The Dharma-body is ultimately not the form-body.
Such things as the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are all the form-body. The Dharma-body is ultimately not a phenomenon of marks.
Such things as being fully endowed with eighty-four thousand marks and characteristics, or being fully endowed with the spiritual marks of the ten bodies, are all [the form-body]."
This is the characteristic of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "The ultimate essence of the Dharma-body is not that body of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*).
Because it is not accomplished by means of marks, it is not that Dharma-body. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should not see [the Buddha] by means of the perfected form-body;
one should not see him by means of the perfection of the various marks. Now, these two types—marks and signs—are also...
It is not that they are not Buddhas, for these two are not separate from the Dharmakāya.
Just as gold is ultimately neither a lion nor is it not gold, because the lion is not separate from the gold; so too, Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verse says:
"Not separate from the Dharmakāya, those two are not non-Buddhas. Therefore, he speaks again of their accomplishment, which is neither dual nor existent. Thus it is said:
The Sūtra says: "This is called being fully endowed with the form-body; this is called being fully endowed with the various marks.
According to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one should not perceive the Dharma-body through physical characteristics; therefore, it is said to be "non-body.

According to conventional discourse (*saṃvṛti*), one perceives the Dharma-body within those very physical characteristics; therefore, it is said to be "fully endowed. Thus, it may be described as non-existent, and it may also be described as existent.
Therefore it is said: "There is neither duality nor existence. It is non-existent yet not non-existent;

this is called true non-existence. It is existent yet not existent; this is called wondrous existence. Without the profoundly deep wisdom of *prajñā*, it is truly difficult to comprehend this. Huangbo said:
The Buddhas of the ten directions truly have not the slightest dharma that can be obtained which is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is simply the one mind;
it truly has no differentiated characteristics, no radiance, and no victory or defeat. Because there is no victory, there is no mark of a Buddha.

Because there is no attachment, there is no mark of a sentient being. The monk asked, "If the mind is already without marks, how can it be entirely devoid of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics in order to transform and deliver sentient beings? Baizhang said, "The thirty-two marks belong to the realm of marks."
"All that has form is entirely false and illusory. The eighty minor marks belong to the realm of form (*rūpa*).

"If one perceives me by means of form, such a person walks upon a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. Huangbo’s words clarify exclusively the non-sentence, causing people to directly perceive their own nature.

"Eh? A monk asked Zhimen, "Dongshan said, 'Three pounds of flax. What is the meaning of this? Zhimen said, "Flowers clustered, brocade clustered.

The late Master has been gone for so long! Later, Changqing heard of this and said, "The Great Official should have laughed, not wept."
This caused [Dongshan] to weep. Xuedou combined these elements into this single verse and subsequently added the word "yi" (a sound of realization), thereby meeting with Dongshan once again.
If you can understand this clearly, you will finally know that what is called "three pounds of flax" refers to a sign—is it a sign?
Is it not a sign? Is it the Buddha who can be seen? Is it the Buddha who cannot be seen? You must possess a pair of eyes of your own to discern this.

The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical characteristics; likewise, the Tathāgata necessarily teaches the Dharma apart from physical characteristics.

If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has preached some dharma, they would be slandering the Buddha, for they would not understand what I have preached.
Subhūti, as for one who preaches the Dharma, there is no dharma that can be preached; it is called "preaching the Dharma" (the latter part [of this passage] is from the Wei translation).

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings. Why is this?

Sentient beings. (In the second year of the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, the monk Lingyou died suddenly. Manifestation cannot be manifested apart from verbal expression. To speak without speaking is what constitutes sublime speech.
The previous statement—that there is no fixed dharma for the Tathāgata to speak—implies that although the dharma is not a fixed dharma, the trace of "dharma" still remains;

He preached the Dharma. Yet, as for this, not even a single dharma exists. Fundamentally, there is nothing that can be preached. The body is the very body that is no-body; preaching is the very preaching that is no-preaching.
Unless one possesses the capacity of a supreme sage, it is truly difficult to believe. The *Kanding ji* says: "Do not say that the Tathāgata has any dharma he preaches.
The Dharmakāya is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); in reality, there is no one who can preach. It is just like...
It is like the echo in an empty valley; in reality, there is no one who produces the sound. Whenever one preaches the Dharma, one must first form this thought:
"Although the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he has no mind that preaches the Dharma;
