One might think: "The Tathāgata has taught some Dharma. For what reason should one not entertain such a thought?
Because the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of the Tathāgata is not separate from the *dharmadhātu*. The *dharmadhātu* is equal; speech is itself silence, and silence is itself speech.
Since that which is spoken lacks intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is fundamentally no speaking. If one were to say that the Tathāgata has taught some Dharma, it would be...
This is to slander the Buddha. It is because they cannot understand my teaching of "non-teaching" that they do so. Now, one who preaches the Dharma should preach it in accordance with the Dharma;
this is called true preaching of the Dharma. The Dharma is fundamentally detached from all names, marks, and conceptual discriminations.

Not even the slightest real essence or nature can be found that might be preached. Since the teaching itself has no substance, what is there to be taught? If one speaks in accordance with this teaching—
This is the teaching according to the Dharma; therefore, it is called "teaching the Dharma. Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "As is the Buddha, so too is the Dharma;
the two distinctions thus spoken do not depart from the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). The teaching of the Dharma has no intrinsic characteristic (svabhāva).

Since the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) does not depart from the Dharma-realm, the Dharma that is taught likewise does not depart from the Dharma-body; therefore, it is established as non-existent. Indeed...
The teaching of the Dharma is thus; when has there ever been anything taught? Subhūti was foremost in understanding emptiness and took wisdom as his life.
That he heard this teaching and did not oppose it with faith was not yet difficult to achieve. Therefore, he asked concerning future beings:
as the True Dharma grows ever more distant, will there perhaps be those who, hearing these words, give rise to faith? World-Honored One.
This is because sentient beings are not necessarily [fixed as] sentient beings. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
how can it be known that there are none capable of faith? Therefore, it is said that such a person is neither a non-sentient being nor not a sentient being.

To say they are capable of faith means they originally possess the essence of the Sage and are thus not [ordinary] sentient beings; yet, as they have not yet departed from the category of ordinary beings, they are not "not" [sentient beings].
They are sentient beings. For what reason is it said that they are not sentient beings, yet are also called sentient beings?

As for the term "sentient beings," the Tathāgata says they are not sentient beings because, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are distinct from the five aggregates;
when one seeks their essential substance, it is entirely unattainable. Therefore, they are said to be not sentient beings. Why is it not the case that they are not [sentient beings]?
Sentient beings are designated as such through conventional discourse, based upon the correspondence between the five aggregates and the fruits of karma;
therefore, they are called "sentient beings. Yet, these so-called sentient beings are in truth not sentient beings.
Since sentient beings possess the noble nature (*āryatva*), which serves as the very root of faith, why should one worry that they cannot believe in this profound *dharmadhātu*?
Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke in verse: "What is taught and the teacher are profound; it is not that there are none capable of believing.

It is neither a sentient being nor a non-sentient being, neither a saint nor a non-saint. What is called a 'sentient being who is not a sentient being' cannot be called a saint, yet it has never been the case that they cannot become saints.
One who can contemplate sentient beings in this way realizes that sentient beings are themselves free from the nature of sentient beings."

Furthermore, how can one have doubts regarding the teaching of non-teaching? When the Venerable Subhūti was sitting in meditative seclusion within a mountain cave, the devas rained down flowers and offered praise.
Someone asked, "Who is this raining flowers from the sky and offering praise?
What is he praising? The deva replied, "I am Brahmā. I revere the Venerable One’s excellent exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā. The Venerable One said:
"I have never spoken a single word regarding Prajñāpāramitā. Why do you praise it? The deva said, "It is so.
Venerable sir, there has been no speaking; I have heard nothing. This absence of speaking and hearing is the true teaching of Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, "What is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality? Mañjuśrī—
Ratnākara said: "According to my understanding, regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is no speech and no discourse; there is no demonstration and no cognition;
it is free from all questioning and answering—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: "We have each spoken for ourselves;
you, O Benevolent One, should now speak: what is the Bodhisattva’s entrance into non-duality?"

Regarding the second dharma-gate: Vimalakīrti remained silent. A Celestial Youth offered this verse: When Mañjuśrī inquired after his illness, the Elder of Vaiśālī opened the gate of non-duality; let us observe the master at work.
When the manifest is extinguished and the essence remains within, who can truly appreciate it? Let go of past and future, and do not lament.
He who earnestly presented the uncut jade was the man from the court of Chu who had his kneecaps removed; he who brilliantly returned the pearl was the one from the city of Sui who slew the snake.
Do not point it out; it is free from all flaws and blemishes. Though worldly taints are entirely absent, there remains a slight distinction.
Thus, as for this teaching that is beyond words, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise so; why then should one harbor doubts regarding the World-Honored One?
19. Regarding the doubt as to how one can cultivate and realize the Dharma when no dharma exists:
this doubt arises from the previous doubts concerning numbers twelve and thirteen, specifically regarding the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the non-existence of dharmas.

The *Puṇyadatta-śāstra* states: "If the realm of the Buddha in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) is such that neither the form body (*rūpakāya*) nor the speech body (*vākkāya*) can be apprehended, and there has never been any dharma that is an object of cognition, how can one speak of 'unsurpassed perfect enlightenment' apart from the sequence of correct knowledge?
Since there is no essence of dharmas, who is it that cultivates and realizes [it]? To dispel this [doubt]:...
Because of this doubt, the Sūtra says:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, when the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Regarding my attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. There is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal, without high or low; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because it is without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span, one cultivates [it] as one...
All wholesome dharmas lead immediately to the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, as for what are called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata has said that they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely designated as "wholesome dharmas."
The Tang translation says: Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal; within it there is nothing that is not equal.
Therefore, it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Because it is equal in its lack of selfhood, lack of sentient-beinghood, lack of life-principlehood, lack of personhood, and lack of individualhood (*pudgala*), it is therefore called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
There are no wholesome dharmas that are not directly realized; there are no wholesome dharmas that are not perfectly awakened to.

Subhūti, as for "wholesome dharmas, wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata has declared them all to be non-dharmas. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of them by the name "wholesome dharmas, wholesome dharmas."
Master Fu’s verse says: In water and on land, all share the same true limit; Whether flying or moving, their essence is one and the same. Within the Dharma, how can there be "self" and "other"?
Within principle, how could there be intimacy or estrangement? Discriminations between self and other are dispelled; Cognitions of high and low are eliminated.
Realizing this nature of equality, All together enter the realm of non-remainder.
Tong said: "In the previous doubts concerning verses twelve and thirteen, the Tathāgata stated that there is truly no dharma by which one attains unsurpassed bodhi.

Subhūti surely did not disbelieve its non-existence; however, he feared that future sentient beings, taking the fact that 'it is neither body nor speech' and that 'everything is non-existent' to mean that even the Dharma-body is non-existent, would consequently ask whether the Buddha attained unsurpassed bodhi."
Is it called "non-attainment"? That which is termed "non-attainment" is indeed correct;
it does not mean that because there is no attainment, there is consequently no unsurpassed *bodhi*. Therefore, it is said: "This is called unsurpassed, right, and equal *bodhi*.
If even the slightest dharma existed, there would be high and low. Since not even a single dharma exists, all things are equal. By means of this equality...
Therefore, the sage and the ordinary person are of one essence. By realizing this through self-attestation, one finds that no bodily form can be apprehended.
By using this to deliver sentient beings, one finds that no characteristic of verbal expression can be apprehended.

This causes all sentient beings to enter nirvana without remainder, yet in reality, not a single sentient being has attained extinction. It is precisely for this reason. The Qin translation says: "Cultivate all wholesome deeds."
If one practices the dharmas, then one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Previously it was said that there is not even a slight dharma;

here it is said to cultivate all wholesome dharmas. Previously it was said there is nothing to be attained; here it is said that one then attains it. These words seem to contradict one another in meaning.
The Tang translation states: "Because it is equal, it is called unsurpassed, right, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

There are no wholesome dharmas that are not fully realized; there are no wholesome dharmas that are not perfectly awakened to. Regarding this enlightenment, it speaks only of the name and not of its attainment;
regarding all wholesome dharmas, it speaks only of realization and not of cultivation. This appears to point toward the 'transcendental' (the upward path)."

The *Lù* (Commentary) further refines this point. The *Kāndìngjì* (*Record of the Collation and Determination*) states: "In the preceding text, it was repeatedly said that there is no dharma by which one attains bodhi.
If the Tathāgata does not obtain even a single dharma, how can he transform and abandon the two obstacles and transform and attain the two fruits?

Since he has already transformed and attained bodhi, how could it be that he does not obtain even a single dharma? The Buddha’s response is threefold; the first is that there is no dharma to be obtained.

One attains perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). The second answer is that equality constitutes perfect enlightenment. The third answer is that the correct and auxiliary cultivation of goodness constitutes perfect enlightenment.
The first answer is as can be seen in the text: "There is not even the slightest dharma to be attained" refers precisely to the locus of bodhi.
There is not even the slightest dharma that can be realized as bodhi; nor is there any dharma whatsoever that can surpass it.
Therefore, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). This takes the absence of dharmas as perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, the following four lines take equality as perfect awakening, because the Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya* is equal and without differentiation. Its...
The Dharma is without anything that is not equal; there is not even the slightest increase. Therefore, it is called "unsurpassed. Because it does not increase among the noble ones, it has no height;
because it does not decrease among ordinary beings, it has no lowness. All things are equal, fundamentally never lost;
what more could there be to attain? Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "In that place, there is not the slightest dharma; thus one knows enlightenment to be unsurpassed. The Dharmadhātu..."

It neither increases nor decreases; it is the pure equality of self-characteristics. Although there are no phenomena, and although it is equal, this does not mean that one does not attain perfect enlightenment through cultivation.
Furthermore, that dharma has the characteristic of selflessness and is free from all marks; this is precisely equality.
Moreover, that dharma is selfless, its essence is reality, and ultimately not a single dharma can be apprehended. Therefore—
It is called "unsurpassed. Furthermore, among all skillful means, it is also unsurpassed because all wholesome dharmas are fully perfected;
thus, it is named "unsurpassed. How can wholesome dharmas, which possess a substantial nature that can be apprehended, serve as the cause for realizing the principle of non-apprehension?
Since these phenomena are not analogous, how could they constitute a valid cause? As for what are called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata has taught them to be—
It is unrighteous (*adharma*). Because it cannot be sustained due to its nature as being with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is designated as non-virtuous (*akuśala*).

Because it is definitively able to be sustained by its nature as being without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is virtuous (*kuśala*) in nature. Those outflows are not pure phenomena; this state of being free from outflows is itself a pure phenomenon.
Therefore, it is called "that phenomenon. If it were a phenomenon with outflows, it would be called a non-virtuous phenomenon. Because it is without...
Because they are *sāsrava* (with outflows), they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*). This is because they are definitively wholesome dharmas that are free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
It is like saying, "Is this a gentleman? Yes, he is a gentleman. Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verse says:

"There is the unsurpassed skillful means, And the departure from dharmas with outflows; Therefore, what is not a pure dharma Is itself the pure dharma. Thus, it is through cultivation and realization.
Regarding equanimity (*samatā*): although it is not a pure phenomenon, one cultivates it without cultivation and realizes it without realization;
since there is not even the slightest dharma to be attained, it is called "purity.
One day, Guishan pointed to a field and asked Yangshan, "In this field, which end is high and which end is low? Yangshan replied, "Actually, this end is high."
The other end was low. Guishan said, "If you do not believe me, stand in the middle and look at both ends.
Yangshan said, "There is no need to stand in the middle, nor should one dwell at either end. Guishan said, "If it is so, look at water; water can level things.
Yangshan said, "Water has no fixed nature; it simply levels that which is high by being high and that which is low by being low. Guishan then—
Rest! How profound is the difficulty of realizing equality! To abide in the two extremes is inequality;
to stand in the middle is inequality. Water can be level, but objects cannot. Only when there is not even the slightest dharma is there equality.
High is equal; low is equal. Only by seeing it thus can one truly know that self and others share the same nature of nirvāṇa.
It is like the ocean.
○ Twenty: Severing Doubt Regarding the Indeterminate (avyākṛta) Not Being a Cause.
This doubt arises from the preceding cultivation of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). As it is said: "By cultivating all wholesome dharmas, one attains Bodhi."
The term "提" (ti) is subsumed under wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), not under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

If what was previously mentioned—such as upholding or reciting the four-line verse and so forth—were subsumed solely under the indeterminate nature of names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*), then since there is no cause or effect within indeterminate dharmas, how could there be any principle by which one could attain *bodhi*? To dispel this obstacle, the Sūtra says:

Subhūti, if someone were to take all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm and offer them as a heap of these seven treasures as a gift, and if another person were to [offer] this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra—
Even if one were to receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain to others even as little as a four-line verse from it, the previously mentioned merit would not equal a hundredth part of this;
it would not equal a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or a hundred-millionth part, nor could it be reached by any calculation, analogy, or comparison.
Master Fu’s verse says: Giving away treasures as numerous as grains of sand only produces causes for outflows (*āsrava*). It is not equal to the contemplation of non-self;
realizing delusion is what is called the True. If one wishes to realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one must rely on detachment from greed and anger.
Knowing that both persons and phenomena are without self, one wanders freely beyond the six sense-objects.
Tong said: "The comparison of the precious gift has already been made more than twice; yet this is raised once more to dispel the doubt that neutral states (*avyākṛta*) are not causes.
It is taught that practicing all wholesome dharmas without attachment to signs (*nimitta*) constitutes the cause of Bodhi."
This is indeed so. Nevertheless, all the teachings spoken by the Buddha flow forth from within the nature of untainted goodness;

they transcend the characteristics of verbal expression, yet those who uphold and expound them are truly able to demonstrate the causes of bodhi. Through this, one may perceive the wondrousness of Prajñā.
Not only do all wholesome dharmas realize bodhi by way of being devoid of marks;

even those dharmas that are indeterminate by nature realize bodhi through their marklessness. How could this be accessible to those who regard the giving of jewels as something comparable to sand, thereby creating causes for outflows?
Therefore, the Buddha cites the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, taking one such world...
Within it stands a single Sumeru King of Mountains, immeasurable in height and breadth, equal in magnitude to a vast accumulation of the seven treasures.
If someone were to take this and offer it as a gift, their merit could indeed be called great.
Yet, if a person were to take even as little as a four-line verse from this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on signlessness and non-abiding, and uphold it, [their merit would be even greater]. Self-...

It is for one's own benefit. To expound it through teaching is for the benefit of others. Within the sūtras, regarding the expression of ultimate truth, it is by means of this that awakening and understanding arise, leading to the initiation of practice and the ability to proceed toward Bodhi.
Since it is impossible to attain Bodhi apart from this, we know that it is only by relying upon this that one accords with Bodhi.
Therefore, he proclaims that the measure of this Dharma-jewel is equal to space and is inconceivable.
Compared to the merit of giving away countless jewels previously mentioned, this [merit] is more than a hundred thousand billion times greater;
it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy. Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "Though it is called an indeterminate dharma, its cause is nevertheless revealed.
Therefore, this single jewel of the Dharma surpasses immeasurable worldly treasures; in terms of number and power, there is no comparable excellence, for there is no comparable cause."
It is likewise so. No worldly phenomena can serve as a metaphor for it;

that is to say, regarding these four kinds of distinctions—excellence in number, excellence in power, excellence in category, and excellence in cause—there is no metaphor capable of being compared to them. First is excellence in number, reaching a point beyond the reach of calculation.
Second is excellence in power, such that strengths and weaknesses cannot coexist. Third is excellence in category.
Just as the noble and the lowly are not alike, fourth is the superiority of the cause. It is said that the former cannot serve as a cause for the latter.
Since the merit of upholding and expounding [this teaching] is such, how could one not exert oneself with diligence, vigor, and a courageous mind?
Formerly, King Xiangzhi bestowed a priceless jewel upon the twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra. The Patriarch...
Taking the pearl he had bestowed, he asked the three princes: "This pearl is perfectly bright; is there anyone capable of matching it?
The first prince and the second prince both said: "This pearl is the most honored among the seven treasures; certainly nothing surpasses it.
Without the power of the Venerable One's Way, one could not grasp or receive it. The third prince said: "This is merely a worldly treasure; it is not sufficient."
Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme; this light of the world is not yet supreme.
Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme; this illumination of the world is not yet supreme. Among all illuminations—
The clarity of the mind is supreme. This luminous jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must rely on the light of wisdom to discern it. Once it has been discerned, one knows it is a jewel.
Once it is known to be a jewel, its preciousness is revealed. If its preciousness were revealed by itself, the jewel would not be precious;
if it were discerned by itself, the jewel would not be a jewel. That the jewel is not a jewel by itself—this is the meaning.
One must rely on the jewel of wisdom to discern the worldly jewels. Since jewels are not inherently precious, one must rely on the jewel of wisdom to illuminate the Dharma-jewel.
Thus, when the Master possesses the Way, his jewels manifest; when sentient beings possess the Way, their mental jewels are likewise so.
The Patriarch praised his discerning wisdom and asked again: "Among all things, what thing is without form? He replied:
Among all things, do not give rise to the notion of signlessness. Again, he asked: "Among all things, which is the greatest? He replied:
"Among all things, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the greatest. The Patriarch, knowing him to be his Dharma heir, entrusted to him the Tathāgata’s True Eye of the Dharma.
Later, the Sixth Patriarch also said: "One may spend an entire lifetime seeking pearls upon a boat, yet remain unaware that one's own body is the seven treasures."
These two patriarchs deeply understood the Dharma-treasure, which cannot be equaled by worldly treasures.
○ XXI. Severing Equality: What is meant by "crossing over the doubt"?
This doubt arises from the nineteenth doubt concerning the equality of this Dharma. The *Puṇyadatta-śāstra* states:
This Dharma is equal; it has no high or low. Thus, there are no sentient beings to be delivered.
If the Tathāgata says they are not sentient beings, how is this not in contradiction with other teachings? For instance, as a sutra states:
"Because immeasurable sentient beings have taken me as their spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they are all liberated from birth and other such sufferings. Since they have been delivered...
Birth itself entails distinctions of high and low; how, then, can there be equality?
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has the thought:
'I shall deliver sentient beings. Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is this? In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers."
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata says that there is a self, it is not a self; yet ordinary people imagine there is a self.
"Subhūti, those who are called 'ordinary beings' (pṛthagjana) by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, ordinary beings; they are merely designated as 'ordinary beings. Tong said:
"Although this doubt arises from the perspective of equality regarding the salvation of sentient beings, it is in fact through the salvation of sentient beings that equality is manifested.
Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verse says: "In the true dharma-realm of equality, the Buddha does not save sentient beings. Because...
Names are shared with those aggregates, yet they do not depart from the dharma-dhātu. Within the one true dharma-dhātu, the five aggregates are all empty;
holy names and mundane designations are entirely non-existent. Sentient beings depend upon the aggregates for their existence; since the five aggregates are absent, [they likewise do not exist].
Thus, there are no sentient beings. Since even the name "sentient being" does not exist, by what means could one deliver them?
Therefore, in reality, there is no sentient being who attains parinirvāṇa; this is the true realization of the nature of the equal Dharma-realm.
The *Kanding ji* states: "The first five phrases refute erroneous interpretations. The subsequent two phrases demonstrate the correct view."
The question asks: For what reason does [the Buddha] cause [beings] not to entertain such thoughts? The explanation states:

Because, in reality, there are no sentient beings who are delivered by the Tathāgata. The One True Dharma-realm is fundamentally equal from the beginning. The Buddha is one who has attained ultimate realization and is already entirely identical with the Dharma-realm.
Although sentient beings have not yet attained realization, they likewise lack intrinsic substance as dependently originated phenomena.
They share the same dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). How could one use the dharma-realm to deliver the dharma-realm? Therefore, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were truly sentient beings distinct from the Tathāgata who were to be delivered, this would not accord with the dharma-realm.

It would indicate a failure to understand dependent origination, resulting in the conceptualization of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, and so forth; thus, the fire of grasping would not yet have been extinguished.
This is called the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*). The Tathāgata does not possess this. Maitreya Bodhisattva states in verse:
"To grasp at a self and [claim] deliverance is a fault; To grasp at those dharmas is likewise so. Because one grasps at delivering sentient beings, One should know that such grasping is absent.
"Those" refers to the four aforementioned marks. Why does the Tathāgata lack the grasping of a self? Regarding that which the Tathāgata speaks of as having a "self":
The meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature is precisely non-self. Since it is fundamentally selfless from the beginning, what could possibly be grasped?
Therefore, there are no marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, because no intrinsic substance can be found.

If a Tathāgata were to grasp at the existence of sentient beings as those to be delivered by him, this would be the fault of grasping at marks; for he would be attached to those dharmas of the five aggregates.
Because it arises, it shares the same fault as the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). For those who wish to bring sentient beings to liberation, such characteristics must not be apprehended.
Since there is no grasping at a self, why say further that one should not apprehend it?

It is because ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) perversely and falsely grasp at things, clinging to them as having a self and thus being unable to attain liberation, that it is said they falsely grasp at a self.
These are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Not yet being noble ones (*ārya*), they are unable to give rise to the noble dharmas;

therefore, they are called "ordinary persons. Those ordinary persons each cling to a self, arising with distinctions; this is called the "arising of ordinary persons. However, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), no ordinary person can be found at all.
It is only by means of conventional discourse (*saṃvṛti-vyavahāra*) that one speaks of the "arising of ordinary persons. This is because...
The preceding passage successively clears away these traces, stating that the Tathāgata has been without a self from the beginning;

it is only because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cling to it as a self that he teaches the dharma of non-self (*anātman*) to deliver them. Ultimately, ordinary beings are likewise fundamentally without a self.
Not only are they without a self, but they are not even ordinary beings. It is like a person in a dream who sees a tiger: both the tiger and the dreaming person are unattainable.
Where else could there be sentient beings to be saved? In the four preceding sections, it is stated that though there is saving, there is no one who saves.

In the first, he was made to abandon the notion of a self that saves beings. In the eleventh, he doubted that the savior was the self. In the fourteenth, he doubted that if there is no self, who is it that saves?
This doubt concerns the equality of the true realm (*tathatā-dhātu*); it is not appropriate for the true realm to save beings. It is here that the reality is revealed.
"There is no sentient being who attains *nirvāṇa*. This is extremely detailed and manifest. One day, while Guishan was feeding crows with raw rice, he turned his head and saw Yangshan.
Guishan said, "Today I have ascended the hall for them once. Yangshan said, "I too have heard it according to the custom.
Guishan asked, "As for what you heard, what was it? Yangshan replied, "The crows cawed like crows; the magpies chirped like magpies."
[The birds] were chirping. Guishan said, "What can one do about sound and form? Yangshan asked, "What did you just say, Master?
Guishan said, "I simply said that for his sake, I went up to the hall once. Yangshan asked, "Why do you call it 'sound and form'?
Guishan said, "Even so, there is no harm in having verified it. Yangshan asked, "As for the Great Matter, what then?"
Shengyan asked, "Master, you raised your fist and said, 'In the end, this is pointing east while drawing west.
Miaoyan said, "What were you just asking? Shengyan replied, "I was asking about the Great Matter of the Patriarchs.
Miaoyan asked, "Why do you call it 'pointing east while drawing west'? Shengyan replied, "Because of attachment to sound and form, I therefore asked about this transgression. Miaoyan said, "..."
Yangshan did not yet understand this matter. Yangshan asked, "How can one come to understand this matter?
Guishan said, "Ji-zi [Yangshan] is sound and form; I, the old monk, am east and west. Yangshan said, "The single moon in a thousand rivers—the essence does not divide the waters.
Guishan said, "One must be like this before it is attained. Yangshan said, "It is like gold and gold; ultimately there is no difference in color, so how could there be different names?"
Miaoyan said, "What is the principle of that which has no different names? Yangshan said, "Vases, dishes, hairpins, bracelets, contracts, bowls, basins.
Miaoyan said, "Ji’s son speaks Chan like a lion’s roar, startling and dispersing the foxes, wolves, and jackals.
Only by clearly realizing the principle of that which has no different names here can one know that names are shared with those aggregates (skandhas)."
To be detached from the dharma-realm is the supreme ultimate truth.
(22) This doubt concerning the discernment of the true Buddha through comparison is derived from the seventeenth doubt,
wherein it was stated that the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the physical body or its various marks.
Come forward. The preceding text states, "It is not a complete body of form," and yet it also says, "This is called a complete body of form.
Since it further states, "It is not the possession of all marks," and yet also says, "This is called the possession of all marks," the intended meaning therein is as follows:
The Dharma-body is ultimately devoid of marks and signs; yet marks and signs are not non-Buddha. Because it is without marks, it manifests marks without departing from the Dharma-body.
Therefore, one may doubt: "Since it is able to manifest marks precisely because it is without marks, then by seeing only the marks, one knows the absence of marks.
Since the Dharma-body does not depart from form and appearance, one thereby knows the Dharma-body.
Because the marks of merit are accomplished, they may be known through analogy and comparison. To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is;
the Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if [one perceives him] by means of..."
Regarding those who view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks: a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) is indeed the Tathāgata. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
The Tang translation says: The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the possession of all marks?
Subhūti replied: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the Tathāgata should not be perceived by means of the possession of all marks."
Regarding the contemplation of the Tathāgata, the Buddha said: "Subhūti, excellent, excellent! It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
One should not contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the possession of the various marks.

Subhūti, if one were to contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the possession of the various marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King would also be a Tathāgata. Therefore, one should not [contemplate him] by means of the possession of the various marks."
One should contemplate the Tathāgata in this way: one should contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the marks and yet not by means of the marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Those who perceive me by my form, And seek me by my voice, They have entered upon a false path; They cannot see me."

One should contemplate the nature of the Buddha-dharma; it is the Dharma-body of the Teacher. Since the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not an object of cognition, it cannot be fully understood by them.
Master Fu’s verse says: Nirvana contains the four virtues; only I am in accord with the true permanence.

Equal in fame to the eight masteries, I alone am the most spiritual and supreme. Neither form nor sound is its characteristic; how could mind or consciousness measure it? When looking at it, it is not...
It can be seen that when one awakens to the principle, its form is immediately manifested.
Tong said: "The 'equal dharma-realm' mentioned above refers to the state where there is neither Buddha nor sentient being.

As the Tathāgata said, 'An ordinary person is not an ordinary person,' for there is no characteristic of a sentient being to be found. Although there are no sentient beings, how could it be that [the dharma-realm] does not exist?"
"O Tathāgata! Indeed, all marks are that which the Tathāgata manifests—namely, marks that are markless.
All marks are not separate from the Dharmakāya—namely, marks that are markless.
Since one can manifest the markless through marks, and likewise manifest the markless through marks, if one observes by way of analogy, it seems one might know the Buddha through these marks."
Knowing that all marks lack intrinsic nature and are not the true essence of dharmas, they cannot be apprehended through inferential contemplation.
Furthermore, the true nature of dharmas not only transcends sound and form, but is also remote from cognition and vision. By what means, then, could one contemplate it?
Therefore, know that what is called the "self" is precisely the self of the four virtues of *nirvāṇa*; it is fundamentally not an object of cognition. Cognition—
Furthermore, it cannot be so. How could one see its existence? This means that even the "self" of delivering sentient beings is absent.
The four-line verse in the Qin translation merely concerns the "self" of sound and form; the final four lines of the Tang translation concern the Dharma-body free from cognition and views.
When these are combined and viewed together, the meaning becomes complete. Furthermore, Subhūti said:
"It is so, it is so. To perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks contradicts what was previously answered.
It is unclear whether the Tang translation abbreviated this correctly. The *Kanding ji* states: "What do you think?"—these two phrases mean:
can one perceive the signless Dharma-body Tathāgata by means of comparison? Subhūti says: "The three phrases" mean the Dharma... [text continues].
Since the physical body manifests as the marks of the body, one realizes the Buddha and attains the signless *dharmakāya* by means of these very marks. The Buddha spoke of three points:
it is difficult for the noble and the ordinary to distinguish one another. That is to say, since a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) also possesses these marks, he might be taken for a Tathāgata;
thus, the physical marks of the body cannot be used to definitively discern a Tathāgata. Furthermore, regarding the physical characteristics of the Wheel-Turning King and the Buddha...
Although they are the same in being the basis for marks (*lakṣaṇa*), there are differences between the two. The marks of a Buddha are manifestations of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

the marks of a king arise from karmic causes. Since the gap between the ordinary person and the sage is as vast as that between clouds and mud, how can one find a standard for comparison? Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse:
The Tathāgata cannot be known by means of the characteristics of the physical body; all Buddhas possess only the Dharma-body. A Wheel-Turning King is not a Buddha.
It is not through the retribution of the marks and signs, which are accomplished based on merit, that one attains the true Dharma-body.

Because these are merely different manifestations of skillful means, Subhūti addressed the Buddha in four statements to realize that the Buddha cannot be seen by means of his physical marks. This is the intended meaning.

It is said: "The provisional arises based on the real; the provisional does not depart from the real. Yet, when seeking the real by means of the provisional, the real does not depend upon the provisional.
That which is accomplished by relying on merit and virtue is the *vipākakāya* (retribution body), not the true *dharmakāya*.
From this it follows that the power of merit can only produce these marks, but the power of merit cannot attain the Great [Vehicle]."
Bodhi cannot, in truth, be seen through marks. At that time, the World-Honored One’s five phrases are beyond the reach of seeing and hearing.
The *dharmakāya* of true suchness (*tathatā*) is not an object of consciousness;
because it is free from all marks and verbal expression, it can only be realized and known as the domain of true wisdom. Therefore, those who seek it by means of form or sound—
They do not know the Buddha. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The form-body is not the Buddha; sound is likewise so. It further states:
"One who does not understand that true nature does not see the Buddha. This refers precisely to this point. Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verse says:
"To see only forms and hear only sounds, such a person does not know the Buddha; for the Dharmakāya of True Suchness is not an object of consciousness."
Because it is an object of perception. The *Guṇaprabha-śāstra* says: "Those who see us by means of form—what is the meaning of this?

It refers to those who, seeing the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of light, say they see the Buddha; and those who, hearing and receiving the words and letters of the sūtras and so forth, say that they have followed [the teaching] and attained the Tathāgata.
They take as their objects of focus (*ālambana*) the body of marks and signs and the body of speech, and cultivate [their practice] therein."
Because they abandon this view, it is said: "These people walk in a deviant path; they cannot see the Tathāgata.
Since the nature of form and of letters is not real, to grasp at them is a deviant path. How could one who walks such a path be able to see the Buddha?
How, then, should one see him? The Sūtra says: "The Dharma is the body of the Tathāgata; one should contemplate only the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). The nature of phenomena..."
That which is called emptiness, the absence of intrinsic nature, the absence of arising, and so forth—this is the ultimate body (*paramārthakāya*) of all Buddhas.
To perceive this is what is meant by "seeing the Buddha. Although one takes the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as an object of focus, this does not constitute grasping;
rather, one realizes the *dharmatā* with a mind of pure wisdom. Is the *dharmatā* itself something that can be realized? Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Dharma..."
The nature [of phenomena] is not an object of vision; even that [nature] cannot be known. As a sutra states:
"The nature of all dharmas is like space and so forth; it serves as the basis for all things, yet its essential nature is neither an existent thing nor a non-existent thing.
To be able to remain tranquil and without cognition within this is called "thoroughly knowing"; therefore, one is called a "knower."
This is merely in accordance with conventional worldly discourse. Guṇabhadra’s explanation of the latter four lines is extremely detailed and is most worthy of contemplation.
Formerly, Mazu was constantly practicing seated meditation at Mount Heng.

Zen Master Nanyue Ruang, recognizing that he was a vessel for the Dharma, went to him and asked, "Virtuous One, what do you hope to achieve by practicing seated meditation? Mazu replied, "I hope to become a Buddha. The Master then said:
He took a brick and began grinding it on a stone in front of the hermitage. The Patriarch asked, "What are you grinding that for? The Master replied, "I am grinding it to make a mirror.
The Patriarch said, "How can grinding a brick produce a mirror? The Master said, "If grinding a brick cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha?
The Patriarch asked, "What then is the way? The Master replied, "It is like a cow pulling a cart; if the cart..."
"It is not so. To drive a cart is it; to drive an ox is it. The Patriarch had no reply. The Master spoke again:

"Are you studying seated meditation, or are you studying the seated Buddha? If you study seated meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If you study the seated Buddha, the Buddha has no fixed form.
Regarding the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you sit as the Buddha, that is to kill the Buddha. If...
He maintained his seated posture, yet had not yet penetrated its underlying principle. Upon hearing the Patriarch’s instruction, it was as if he were drinking *amṛta* (clarified butter).
He prostrated himself and asked, “How should I apply my mind so that it accords with the signless samādhi? The Master said, “Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground is like sowing seeds;
my teaching of the essential Dharma is like the rain from heaven. Because the conditions have converged, you shall perceive the Way.”
He asked again, "The Way has no form or characteristics; how can it be seen? The Master said, "The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way;
the same is true for the signless samādhi. The Patriarch asked, "Is there arising and ceasing?
The Master said, "If one were to constitute the Way through arising and ceasing, or gathering and dispersing, that would not be seeing the Way. Listen to my verse: "The mind-ground contains..."
All kinds of seeds sprout when they encounter moisture. The flower of samādhi is formless; what could be destroyed, and what could be formed?
When the Patriarch received enlightenment, his mind transcended all bounds. Yunmen gave this instruction:
"Everyone possesses radiance within them, yet when one looks for it, it is dark and obscure. What is this radiance of everyone? He spoke on their behalf: "The kitchen and the storehouse."
The Three Gates. It is further said: "Better that good things not exist. Xuedou said: "Self-illumination reveals solitary clarity; for your sake, I open a single thread.
When the flowers fall, the tree has no shadow; when looking, who does not see? See or not see—riding a cow backward, one enters the Buddha Hall.
Consider these two cases together. Although the signless samādhi is [attained] through the Dharma-eye of the mind-ground...
One can see. Yet, seeing while not seeing—like riding a cow backward—is how one may contemplate the Tathāgata.

23. Dispelling the Doubt that the Buddha-Fruit is Unrelated to the Marks of Merit:
This doubt arises from the preceding statement that one "should not view the Tathāgata by means of his marks.

Although it is the same thirty-two marks, when they reside in a Buddha, they are called the "Buddha-fruit" (*buddha-phala*); when they reside in a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), they are called the "marks of merit. Since this is the stage of fruition...
This is not the case. One need only cultivate wisdom; it is not necessary to cultivate merit.

It would seem that one does not need to possess the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) to realize *bodhi*. If bodhisattvas were to practice in this manner, they would lose both their merit and their karmic rewards.
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says:
Subhūti, if you should have this thought: "The Tathāgata has not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection," Subhūti, do not have such a thought.
The Tathāgata has not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection. Subhūti, if you should have this thought... [that he has] set forth...
Regarding the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, do not entertain the thought that it teaches the annihilation or cessation of all phenomena. Why is this?
One who has resolved upon the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the characteristics of annihilation or cessation regarding phenomena.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them...

[The Buddha said: "Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is someone who knows that all dharmas are without self and attains patience (*kṣānti*), this bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that a bodhisattva does not accept merit? Subhūti...
"Subhūti, the merit produced by a bodhisattva should not be clung to with greed; therefore it is said that one does not 'receive' merit.
Subhūti replied: "I have always understood emptiness, and I have always maintained that one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
The Buddha then confirmed this, saying: "If one were to view him by means of his marks, then even a wheel-turning monarch would be a Tathāgata."
The Buddha further elaborated on this with a verse, saying: "To see in form or seek in sound is to walk upon a deviant path.

This discourse on the deconstruction of marks (*lakṣaṇa*) can indeed be called ultimate. However, if one clings to this deconstruction as being correct, it becomes equivalent to biased emptiness (*ekānta-śūnyatā*), leading ultimately to the severance of cause and effect.
Those who give rise to the bodhicitta should practice the union of wisdom and compassion; they ought not to be like this.
Although one realizes Bodhi without relying on merit, one does not lose merit nor remain ignorant of cause and effect;
rather, it is simply that there is no grasping or attachment toward merit. Because one possesses yet does not accept it, the cause becomes a pure cause and the fruit becomes a pure fruit.
Thus, the thirty-two marks obtained differ inherently from the auspicious marks of a universal monarch (cakravartin). *Kanding* (Determination).
The commentary states: "If you should entertain these eight phrases, they serve to negate thoughts that disparage the marks of excellence. The underlying intent is this:
"If you should say that the Tathāgata did not attain bodhi by means of the complete marks, do not entertain such a thought. The phrasing of the text seems redundant.

In truth, the intention is not serious; it merely precedes the subsequent refutation. If you entertain these five propositions, you fall into the fault of manifesting characteristics of disparagement.

For if [the fruit] definitely exists, one clings to eternalism; if it definitely does not exist, one clings to nihilism. Now, if you interpret this as being "without characteristics," you are precisely falling into the view of annihilationism.
This results in the loss of the adornment of merit at the level of the fruit, and the loss of the five perfections at the level of the cause.

Such a practice destroys the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The view that all phenomena are annihilated is the partial understanding of emptiness held by the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), for there is no such severance of dharmas in the vision of a Bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because where there is arising, there is cessation; yet all phenomena possess the nature of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharmatā*).
Therefore, one remains far removed from the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism. To remain far removed from these two extremes is the characteristic of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, those who give rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta must accord with the *dharmadhātu*.

They must necessarily rely upon compassion, wisdom, practice, and vows to perform deeds that benefit sentient beings; they do not speak of the characteristic of the annihilation of all phenomena. As Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse:
"One does not lose the cause of merit, nor its supreme retribution; for all phenomena are simply not subject to annihilation."
Therefore, through the adornment of wisdom and the adornment of merit, one is able to achieve all accomplishments.

How is it known that such a person attains the supreme fruit? If a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them as a gift, the worldly merit thus obtained would indeed be immeasurable. Yet, if there were another person who understood all phenomena...

Non-self means the absence of such characteristics as a self and so forth; thus one achieves patience (*kṣānti*). "Non-self" refers to both the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Having attained these two kinds of emptiness, one no longer gives rise [to conceptual proliferation]; this is called patience.

Once one has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the merit one cultivates is pure and stainless. Compared to that which dwells upon signs while practicing giving, it does not fall into the outflows (*sāsrava*).
It is more than a hundred thousand million times greater. Therefore it is said: "It surpasses the merit obtained by the previous Bodhisattvas.
Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verse says: "Having attained superior patience and not losing it, one thereby attains the stainless fruit.
Only through non-self can one hasten toward unsurpassed Bodhi; therefore, it is called 'superior. If all dharmas are unarisen, then whatever merit..."
All virtues should be severed; how then could merit arise? It is because Bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
This clarifies that by not accepting it, they do not lose merit. However, "not accepting" means not being attached to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
If one dwells in birth-and-death, one accepts merit; yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no merit to be grasped.
"What does it mean for a bodhisattva not to accept merit? The explanation of this intent is as follows:
If a bodhisattva performs meritorious deeds and gives rise to attachment, then because the cause is already tainted (*sāsrava*), the fruit will also be tainted.

Since any retribution thus summoned is something to be loathed, one should know that such grasping is itself "transcendent grasping" (*atigraha*). In this way, both cause and fruit are lost, which confirms the point of the doubt raised. Now, regarding what is...
When one performs meritorious deeds without giving rise to greedy attachment, the cause is already untainted (*anāsrava*), and thus the fruit is also untainted.
Because this merit has no retribution—since it lacks that tainted retribution—one who grasps in this manner does not grasp excessively.
How could one doubt that such a person loses either the cause or the fruit? Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "To demonstrate the characteristics of superior merit, he therefore spoke."
An analogy: this merit has no retribution; thus one receives it without grasping. Merit has never failed to be produced because of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
yet once produced, one should not be greedily attached to it because of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, all dharmas should not be annihilated. That being so, what hindrance could there be between the fruit of Buddhahood and the characteristics of merit? Thus asked the monk.
Chan Master Yunyan Cheng served as Baizhang’s attendant for twenty years. Why was the lamp of his mind not transmitted?
Yunyan said, "The jeweled flower crown upon my head. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the jeweled flower crown upon my head'?"
Yan said: "The Emperor of the Great Tang and the King of the Netherworld.
A monk asked Chan Master Jiufeng Qian, "What is the meaning of 'The Emperor of the Great Tang and the King of the Netherworld'? Jiufeng said, "I recall the words of Dongshan. Danxia’s verse says:
"The jade whip raised high strikes the golden gate, Drawing forth coral of a price beyond measure. A sovereign king transcending antiquity."
With full resolve and spirit, one does not manifest the precious seal; naturally venerable. Furthermore, a monk asked Chan Master Changsha Cen:
"Does the person of original nature become a Buddha? Changsha said: "Do you think the Emperor of the Great Tang cuts thatch and mows grass?
Touzi composed a verse on this: The moss-covered halls are layered, the purple qi deep; The stars divide their positions, the heavens and earth set right.
The Golden Wheel does not govern the realm of Jambudvīpa; how could it be equaled by the precious seals of the feudal lords?

Judging from these two cases, the merit and virtue of a Wheel-Turning King already surpass those of the feudal lords, let alone the Tathāgata’s merit and virtue, which transcend even that of the Wheel-Turning Kings.
Since he is already without self, he has attained patience (*kṣānti*); thus, he does not himself undergo being cut.
The matter of mowing the *mao* grass: thus, not receiving merit is the ultimate merit.
○ Twenty-fourth: Dispelling the doubt regarding the appearance of transformation bodies to receive merit.
This doubt arises from the preceding point on not receiving merit. The *Puṇyapradāna-śāstra* states: "If, in the ultimate sense..."

There is no merit to be acquired. Why, then, do other sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s accumulations of merit and wisdom are perfected, and that he proceeds to nirvāṇa while seated upon the bodhi-maṇḍa? To dispel this doubt, the sūtra says:
Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Tong said: "The Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of physical form, nor can he be described as being subject to annihilation.
This is because he dwells neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa, but constantly proceeds from True Suchness (tathatā) to deliver sentient beings.
Yet, although nirvāṇa has no real location, arriving there is termed 'going. The same applies to saṃsāra."
There is no real location from which it emerges; this is what is called "coming. To neither go nor come is the meaning of "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One).
Therefore, one cannot seek it by grasping at signs, nor can one seek it by abandoning signs. One should know that the emanation body appears, yet though it appears, it has never appeared.
Since there is originally no enjoyment-body within the fruit, how could there be one within the cause?
[Is it] accepted? The *Kanding ji* (Record of Determination) states:
"If a person says that the Tathāgata appears and comes, enters parinirvāṇa and goes, or dwells in the world—whether sitting or reclining—they do not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
For what reason is he called the 'Tathāgata'? Because the true Buddha is fundamentally without coming or going; [it is only] the nirmāṇakāya that comes and goes."
The Buddha is the Tathāgata, who is the Dharmakāya. He is fundamentally unmoving.
If the Tathāgata were subject to the distinctions of coming and going, one could not say that he dwells eternally as such. To dwell eternally as such means that he is neither changing nor different.
Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke in verse: "The transformation-body Buddhas of the past and future—the Tathāgata is eternally unmoving.

This is not a difference within what is non-different. Someone asked: "If there is no coming or going of Buddhas, for what purpose do they appear to receive offerings and be enjoyed by sentient beings?
He replied: "This is because when the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, they perceive the Buddha's arrival. His 'coming' [is thus a reflection of their own purity]."
There is nowhere from which [the Buddha] comes. When the water of the mind is turbid with defilements, one perceives the Buddha departing; yet his departure goes nowhere.

This is because the Buddha acts spontaneously and without mind, appearing only in accordance with what sentient beings perceive. Since there is not even a Buddha who appears, how could there be any matter of receiving blessings?
Maitreya Bodhisattva said in verse: "This retribution for merit and virtue is for the sake of transforming all sentient beings."
Such is the nature of karma. The Buddhas manifest throughout the ten directions; as other sutras state, they appear in forms according to the needs of beings, like the moon reflected in water.
While the reflections in the water come and go, the moon itself remains ever unmoving.
Grand Master Lu Xun asked Nanquan: "In my home, there is a stone slab upon which I sometimes sit and sometimes lie."
Lu asked, "If one wishes to become a Buddha, can one attain it? Quan said, "One can. Lu asked, "Is it not possible that one cannot? Quan said, "One cannot."
Yunyan said, "When sitting, one is a Buddha; when not sitting, one is not a Buddha. Dongshan said, "When not sitting, one is a Buddha;
when sitting, one is not a Buddha. Tiantong commented: "To turn function into position, and to turn position into function—this belongs to the Dongshan school."
"Father and son. Now tell me, what was Nanquan’s intention? It is truly such that neither a needle nor a锥 (chui) can penetrate it. Wuzu Yan said:
"O assembly, one who acts as a true spiritual friend must possess clear discernment. Why is it that others are able to speak [of this]?"
"It can be said; others cannot say it. It also cannot be said. Do you know where Nanquan has landed?
Baiyun, not begrudging his own eyebrows, shall explain this for you: 'Attaining'—who says that? 'Not attaining'—who says that?
If you still do not understand, I, the old monk, will provide you with an illustration tonight."
He then raised his hand and said: "I take the three realms and twenty-eight heavens to be the head of a Buddha;
the golden wheel and the limits of the waters to be the feet of a Buddha; and the four great continents to be the body of a Buddha.
Although I have thus fashioned this Buddha, where, you sons of the Buddha, do you establish yourselves and find your livelihood? Has the assembly understood yet, old man?"
The monk has gone to create a second model: he makes one Buddha in Pūrvavideha, one Buddha in Jambudvīpa, one Buddha in Aparagoyānī, and one Buddha in Uttarakuru.
Grasses, trees, and forests are the Buddha; all wriggling and breathing creatures are the Buddha. Since it is thus, furthermore—
What do you call a "sentient being"? Do you understand yet? It is not as it is with Pūrvavideha;
let Pūrvavideha remain Pūrvavideha. Jambudvīpa remains Jambudvīpa. Aparagoyānī remains Aparagoyānī.
Uttarakuru remains Uttarakuru. Grasses, trees, and forests remain [as they are].
To the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests; to all wriggling and moving sentient beings—leave them as wriggling and moving sentient beings.
Therefore it is said: "This Dharma abides in its own station; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Since this is so, what do you call "Buddha"? Do you understand?
Suddenly, if there were a man who came forth and said, "White Cloud, stop your drowsy talk!"—the assembly, take note of this!

[The Master] turned [the seat]. The aforementioned venerable masters, regarding the Buddha of the Original Source and Innate Nature, each brought forth their own hands and eyes to engage in mutual investigation.
If one can penetrate this through contemplation, only then may it be called "seeing the Tathāgata."
○ Twenty-five: Severing Doubts Regarding the Identity or Difference between the Dharmakāya and the Nirmāṇakāya.
This doubt arises from the preceding point that dharmas are neither annihilated nor do they come or go. As the *Guṇaprabha-śāstra* states:
If both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are unattainable, then there is no coming or going.

How could the Tathāgata abide as a single, composite accumulation like Mount Sumeru? This is said to dispel the views of oneness, permanence, partlessness, and having parts, as well as the view of a composite whole.
By stating that "there are many atoms," it dispels the view of a partless composite whole.
Furthermore, "not a collection of atoms" is intended to eliminate the view that there is a composite whole formed by the conjunction of parts.

As for "that which is called a collection of atoms," it means that I do not grasp a composite object as being a collection; this is further intended to eliminate the view of accumulation. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to grind this trichiliocosm into fine particles of dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of dust be very much? "It would be very much, World-Honored One. "For what reason?"
If this multitude of atoms were substantially real, the Buddha would not have called it a "multitude of atoms.
Why is that? The Buddha said: "The multitude of atoms is precisely not a multitude of atoms; it is designated as a 'multitude of atoms.
World-Honored One, the so-called 'trichiliocosm' spoken of by the Tathāgata is precisely not a world; it is designated as a 'world. Why is that? If [the world]..."
If the elements were substantially existent, they would be a "unified whole. The Tathāgata has said that a unified whole is not a unified whole;
it is merely called a "unified whole. Subhūti, that which is a unified whole is inexpressible;
yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.

wondrous forms as space; wondrous sounds as an echo; the lands of all Buddhas as a city of the Gandharvas; and the Buddha-activities as..."
Dreams: the Buddha-body is like a shadow; the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is like a reflected image; the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is like a magical creation;

with the exception of the wondrous voice, which is like an echo, the remaining [attributes] are listed as nine metaphors. Although their names and characteristics differ slightly, they can for the most part be understood through the mind.
This profound wisdom of Prajñā-pāramitā observation—though the Buddha’s activities are like a dream and the Buddha’s body is like a shadow—correctly realizes the One.
All phenomena are like illusions. From the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to bodhi and nirvana, everything is like an illusion;
this is the fundamental Prajñāpāramitā school that deconstructs all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Those who uphold this sutra and preach its Dharma must deeply understand its meaning and intent.
He is able to expound the Dharma for others, yet does not grasp at appearances; he remains as suchness, unmoving.
He is thus well-able to contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being like dreams or illusions, devoid of any real nature—suddenly arising and suddenly perishing.
While fools perceive them as having birth and extinction, the wise observe that they are fundamentally non-moving from the start; they have never truly arisen, nor have they ever ceased.
Since there has never been extinction, and since there is neither arising nor extinction, there is likewise no coming or going.

For this reason, the *nirvāṇa* of all Buddhas does not abide within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), nor does it abide within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Since they do not abide in either birth-and-death or *nirvāṇa*, they are eternally suchness itself (*tathatā*).
Whether preaching in a mote of dust or in a world-system, they have never been interrupted from the very beginning; how then could one be dogmatic about "entering quiescence"?
...of its characteristics. Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke in verse: The nirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas is neither conditioned nor apart from it.

Because of the correct contemplation of sublime wisdom regarding the nine kinds of conditioned phenomena—namely, the perceived object (*nimitta*), consciousness (*vijñapti*), the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), the body (*deha*), and the objects of enjoyment (*upabhoga*), as well as past and present dharmas, and likewise contemplating the future world, the perceived object, and the experience [of them]—one contemplates these three.
Regarding worldly affairs: within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), one attains stainless sovereignty.
This clarifies that the nirvāṇa of all Buddhas is neither a conditioned phenomenon, nor is it separate from conditioned phenomena; for they abide neither in nirvāṇa nor in the world.
He specifically manifests worldly conduct for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

The reason he does not abide in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is that he possesses sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) which observes nine kinds of dharmas. What are these nine? First, he contemplates them as being like stars:

although the mental factors (*citta-dharma*) can still be seen and are not without their brilliance, they vanish and do not appear when the sun of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) shines brightly. Thus he contemplates...

The characteristics are like a visual obscuration. All external objects that serve as conditions are mere false manifestations, like the appearance of floating hairs; they are fundamentally not real. Contemplate consciousness as being like a lamp:

it relies upon craving and attachment, yet it is not without the power of illumination. Moment by moment it undergoes transition and passes away, continuing in an unceasing succession. Contemplate the vessel-world as being like an illusion:
the various phenomena of the world arise from delusive conditions and are produced through the transformative power of illusion; they have no [independent existence].
The body is a single reality; contemplate it as being like dew, for it abides but momentarily. Upon encountering the sun, it dries up; once met with impermanence, it immediately withers away.

Contemplate that which is enjoyed as being like a bubble: through the conjunction of the three factors—the sense organs, objects, and consciousness—experiences of pleasure and pain arise and disperse respectively.
Contemplate the past as a dream; all that was accumulated and created is identical to a dream.

Objects arise only through recollection; fundamentally, they have no substantial reality. Contemplate the present as like lightning: it perishes at the very moment of arising and does not abide for even an instant.
Though existing for a brief time, it vanishes in a flash. Contemplate the future as like clouds:
consciousness contains seeds, just as clouds contain rain, and it can serve as the root of all things. If one can, with a mind like a vajra...
If one with sublime wisdom contemplates these nine kinds of phenomena: first, one observes the object and consciousness;

this is the investigation into the characteristics of the conditioned that is accumulated and constructed. Second, one observes the vessel-world, the body, and the objects of enjoyment—specifically, by what means one dwells, by what kind of body, and what is enjoyed;
this is the observation of the phenomena currently being experienced before one’s eyes. Third, one observes the three...
The differentiation of worlds: what are these conditioned formations? They are precisely the observation of phenomena that flow and do not abide.
By means of this observation, one is able to attain unimpeded mastery according to one's will among all conditioned phenomena.
For this reason, even while dwelling amidst the defilements of birth and death, one’s wisdom remains unstained;

and even if one attains parinirvāṇa as ashes, how could one’s compassion ever be obscured? Thus, that which is immaculate and eternally sovereign is precisely suchness, immovable, fundamentally devoid of any characteristic of entering quiescence.
If one can contemplate in this manner, one will neither abide in the conditioned nor—
One grasps at marks, yet does not dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) while remaining free from marks. By means of this, one delivers oneself;
by means of this, one delivers others. Therefore, regarding the protection and entrustment to all bodhisattvas, this single verse alone is the most urgent and essential.
How could it be possible to falsely speculate upon it with coarse and shallow views? Formerly, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty requested that Fu...
The Great Being was lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. As soon as he ascended the seat, he struck the desk once with a ruler and immediately descended.
The Emperor was astonished. Master Zhigong asked, "Your Majesty, do you understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand.
Zhigong said, "The Great Being has finished his lecture on the sutra. Xuedou’s verse says: "He did not take up residence at the Twin Śāla Trees, but instead [appeared] in the land of Tang."
It stirs up dust and dirt. Had it not been for Old Master Zhi Gong at that time, he too would have been one of those restless wanderers from the land of Qi.
With this single stroke of his ruler—like lightning, like an illusion—he broke through with the great meaning of the Vajra, speaking it in a mere snap of the fingers.
Were it not for Zhi Gong’s wondrous wisdom, [this teaching] would have almost gone in vain. Furthermore, when a monk passed away, Chan Master Cen of Changsha rubbed [the body] with his hand.
He said, "Great assembly, this monk is truly setting forth the essential principles for you all to deliberate upon.
Do you understand? He then spoke a verse: "Not a single dharma before the eyes, Nor a person present in that very place. The vast and boundless diamond body— Neither false, nor real.
Furthermore, a monk asked, "After a deceased monk has passed away, where does he go? The Sha... [text ends]
He said: "Not recognizing the adamantine essence, one instead calls it 'dependently arisen. Throughout the ten directions, there is true quiescence; who is present, and who is practicing?
Xuefeng, upon seeing a deceased monk, also composed a verse: "Looking down, I do not see the earth; Looking up, I do not see the sky.
If you wish to recognize the adamantine essence, Just look before the skull. Furthermore, a monk asked Fayan about the deceased.
A monk asked, "When a monk passes away, where does he go? Danyuan said, "When has a deceased monk ever passed away?
The monk said, "What about right now? Danyuan said, "You do not recognize the deceased monk. These venerable masters revealed the essence of the *vajra*:
it is fundamentally without birth or death, nor coming or going. Thus, one knows that suchness is immovable; this is the teaching of the Buddhas throughout all time.
Thus it was. When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Elder Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the world— including devas, humans, and asuras— having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly filled with joy.
"Believing, accepting, and practicing accordingly.

The *Kanding ji* (Record of Determination) states: "Regarding the phrase 'After the Buddha had spoken this sutra,' it was originally because Subhūti had posed a question that the Buddha answered with [the stages of] descending, abiding, and practicing.
Since the answers to the questions were concluded, the sutra ought to have ended there. Yet, [the text] continues by following up with the arising of doubts."

The twenty-seven sections of the *Huán* [commentary] conclude with this text. All doubts are now cleared away like melting ice. Since Subhūti had no further questions, the Tathāgata ceased his teaching.
Although both teacher and disciple are present within this single fascicle of the sutra, it is attributed solely to "the Buddha’s teaching" because the superior authority prevails.
Regarding the phrase "all were greatly rejoiced, believed, accepted, and practiced," there are three meanings to their joyful acceptance. Rejoicing and practicing...
[The teaching is] pure in three ways: first, purity of practice, because one is not defiled by attachment to gain and offerings;
second, purity of the teaching, because one knows the essence of phenomena as they truly are, explaining principles according to principle and facts according to fact;
third, purity of attainment, because one gives rise to practice based on understanding and attains the untainted (*anāsrava*). Those present in the assembly were monks and nuns.
As for the laymen and laywomen, who are known as the four assemblies that constantly follow [the Buddha],
it goes without saying that they will hear this sutra and believe it without opposition. Furthermore, if all those in the world— gods, humans, asuras, and others—

from the highest realms of the formless world down through the gods of the form realm and the desire realm, including those with form and without form, those with perception and without perception— [should hear it...]
Neither-perception-nor-non-perception is included therein as well.

Yet, by mentioning only humans and asuras, the four modes of birth—namely, womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—are likewise included therein. That all are able to believe, accept, and practice accordingly is evident;
that is to say, the principle of causing them to enter nirvana without remainder and thereby bring them to extinction is already clearly established. Thus, then:
Is there any provision for the World-Honored One’s protection and entrustment of the various bodhisattvas beyond this?

Zen Master Guling Zan attained enlightenment upon meeting Baizhang; he returned to his place of training, where his original master asked him, "While you were away from me, what work or accomplishments did you achieve?
He replied, "I have achieved nothing at all. Thereupon, the master sent him to perform menial labor. One day—
While washing his body, he instructed his teacher to remove the dirt from his back. The teacher then patted his back and said, "What a fine Buddha hall this is, yet the Buddha is not holy.
The Master turned his head to look at him, and the teacher said, "Though the Buddha is not holy, he is at least able to emit light.
On another day, while the Master was reading a sutra by a window, a bee flew against the window paper, seeking an exit. Seeing this, the teacher said:
The world is this vast, yet you refuse to emerge; you cling to old rags, so when will it ever end? Thereupon he spoke a verse:
"Refusing to leave the gate of emptiness, To throw yourself through the window is great folly. Drilling into old rags for a hundred years— When will you finally emerge?
His Master held up a scripture and asked, "Whom have you encountered on your travels? I have seen you before and after."
His speech was extraordinary. The Master said, "I have received from Venerable Baizhang the indication of a place of rest; now I wish to repay his compassionate virtue.
Thereupon, the Abbot informed the assembly and prepared a vegetarian feast, requesting the Master to preach the Dharma.

The Master then ascended the seat and proclaimed the tradition of Baizhang’s school, saying: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects; its essence reveals the truth."
"Constantly, it is not constrained by words; the nature of mind is unstained, fundamentally and spontaneously perfected. Simply by detaching from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness.
Upon hearing these words, the Original Teacher was awakened and said, "Who would have expected that in my old age I would hear such ultimate matters?"
Baizhang’s few words are indeed sufficient to encapsulate the essential purport of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

They enable those who hear them to be struck with sudden realization and inspiration, so that they no longer laboriously bore into old books in search of meaning. Who would have thought that in this final five-hundred-year period, there would be those born with such faith?
How difficult it is to find such a person!
*The Scripture on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā: The Essential Penetration*, Scroll Seven.
